chapters.title: Chapter 851
paragraphs: It was an especially beautiful day.
Warm sunshine, a cool breeze, and wisps of pure white cloud.
The people working up a sweat wore smiles, and the well-kept main road bustled with crowds.
Perhaps that was why someone who always seemed pressed for time suddenly spoke to his coachman just as the man was about to set off in a hurry.
“Could we take it a little slower today? There’s no particular rush.”
“Pardon?”
“I’d like to take my time on the way back. Look around outside, too.”
The coachman wondered at his employer’s uncharacteristic mood, but put the question aside and eased the reins.
All he had to do was follow orders, after all. And he much preferred guiding the horses slowly and safely to shouting at people to get out of the way.
Still, he’s acting strange today. Did something happen inside?
The coachman glanced sideways. A sturdy wall, built up in two and three layers like a fortress, filled his view.
At their usual pace, it was one thing. At this rate, it would take a full fifteen minutes to reach the end of that wall.
Good grief. It’s impressive no matter how many times I see it.
The enormous estate stood not on the outskirts, but right in the heart of the city. The land was as valuable as it came.
Owning so much of it was proof enough of the family’s tremendous power, but that wasn’t what amazed the coachman most.
It was nothing like this when I first saw it.
A fallen great family.
There had been no better way to describe it. That was the cold reality, as the coachman and everyone else nearby had seen it.
Yet no one could have guessed that a family slowly declining, its past glory behind it, would rise in barely more than two years to rule an entire city.
Just goes to show, you never know what’ll happen.
The coachman looked up at the flag flying high above the stone wall. A breeze caught the silk, and four characters written in a bold, flowing hand caught his eye.
Jin Family of Taiyuan.
The owners of that enormous estate had become a symbol of Shanxi Province.

The changes to the Jin Family of Taiyuan had been swift and unmistakable. The pavilions and walls, shabby and crumbling when the coachman first saw them, had been repaired until they looked as solid as a fortress. Supplied with fine weapons and elixirs, the family’s martial artists now had a righteous light in their eyes that hadn’t been there before.
And that wasn’t all.

The entrance, once crowded with debt collectors demanding payment for the reckless Third Young Master’s unpaid bills, was now so packed you could hardly set foot there—but for entirely different reasons.

Merchants from other regions came to entrust their business to the Jin Family Escort Bureau. At the end of each month, shopkeepers of every kind lined up to pay tribute, along with the martial arts sects and Branch Leaders under the Jin Family of Taiyuan.

So many of Shanxi Province’s most important people came and went that they nearly wore out the threshold. Some people with nothing better to do even loitered nearby, spreading whatever they’d seen and heard.
Just like the two men squatting beside the roadside wall now.
“Didn’t she come today, either?”
“Didn’t who come?”
“Oh, come on. You know perfectly well who I’m waiting for. Why do you keep asking?”
“Don’t tell me you’re at it again...”
“What do you mean, ‘again’? I’ve been devoted to her from the start.”
“Cut the nonsense. If your wife catches you, she’ll beat you to death—and I’ll get killed, too.”
“It’s fine. You only die once, don’t you?”
“I’m telling you, it’s not fine. Your wife’s arm is thicker than my calf.”
“Good grief. You call yourself a man, getting scared like that? Just answer my question. Didn’t she come today, either?”
“She was here just four days ago. Of course she didn’t come today. Do you think she’s an unemployed layabout like us, with nothing but time on her hands?”
“Damn it. I thought maybe this time I’d get to see her up close.”
“Just give it up already. What would you do if you saw her up close?”
“Do I need another reason to see Shanxi’s foremost beauty? I saw her from far away once, half a year ago, and my blurry old eyes cleared right up.”

“Have you considered that one good whack from your wife might make everything go dark? And calling her Shanxi’s foremost beauty hardly does her justice. She leads the Mount Heng Sword Sect despite being a woman—and she’s formidable. If you cross her the wrong way, you won’t walk away in one piece.”
The man gazed dreamily into space, then swallowed.
“...Well, I heard she’s got some old man following her around like a shadow, and he’s got one hell of a temper.”
“If temper were all he had, would they have called him the Tiger of Mount Heng? Quit acting up and go home while both your legs still work. Take care of your kid.”
“Take care of him? He’s all grown up.”
“Already? Time flies. I remember him being born just about this time last year.”
“Yeah. That’s right.”
“...Are you insane?”
The two men’s voices gradually faded.
Listening from his seat, the coachman gave a quiet laugh and gathered up the reins he’d let slacken for a moment.
Clip-clop. Clip-clop.
Drawn by four fine horses, the carriage made its slow way down the main road, just as his employer had asked.

In the past, a single four-horse carriage would have taken up half the street. But now the road was several times wider, and the crowds packed into it simply moved aside a little and carried on talking.
Most of what they said was idle chatter, but some of it was worth the coachman’s attention.
“Have you heard? The Jin Family of Taiyuan’s blacksmith shop has been making nothing but weapons lately.”
“I thought you were about to say something important. That’s been going on for a while, hasn’t it? The Jin Family of Taiyuan is a Murim sect. It’s hardly strange.”
“True. But for the past six months, they’ve dealt exclusively in weapons. If you want farming tools, you’ll have to go at least as far as Gohyeon.”
“Well, now. Gohyeon’s a good three or four days on foot. Luckily, the tools we bought earlier are so sturdy we won’t need more.”
“That’s because the craftsmen Old Man Jang brought with him know their trade.”
“Hey, don’t call him Old Man Jang. The Jin Family of Taiyuan trusts him with important work. You ought to call him Elder Jang Taebo now.”
“Ah, it’s a habit. Anyway, the more I think about it, the more worried I get. They say things in the martial world are tense these days. Do you think something big is about to happen...?”

“Put your worries aside and finish your game of Go. Dark Heaven or whatever can make all the trouble it wants; in the end, it’s a Murim affair. We have the Great Nation farther afield and the Jin Family of Taiyuan standing firm right here. What’s there to worry about?”

“I only brought it up because the rumors coming from all over don’t sound good. And things up on the northern plateau have changed after being quiet for the past year or two. Something isn’t right in the martial world.”
“What’s going on up north now? I thought the Jin Family of Taiyuan had wiped out the mounted bandits.”
“Do mounted bandits disappear just because you uproot them once? They’re like weeds. They keep coming back. And a few merchant caravans that headed north last month...”
Even with his employer’s instructions, there was only so long the coachman could keep the horses moving slowly.
Come on, get to the point.
He was still trying to catch the rest of the story as the carriage left the main road when his employer, who had spent the ride silently watching the scenery, suddenly spoke.
“Everyone has a lot to worry about. Then again, it’s happening around them. How could they not notice?”
“Y-yes?”
“I mean those people. You’ve had your ears pricked up this whole time. Why are you so surprised?”
“Uh, well. It’s just...”
The coachman swallowed and stammered on.
“You’ve never spoken to me first while we were traveling, so it caught me off guard.”
“Ah. Well, I suppose it would.”
The coachman glanced over his shoulder. Through the pearl-bead curtain, he caught a glimpse of his employer nodding as though it were nothing.
He also glimpsed skin powdered white and lips red as cherries.
He’s definitely acting differently today.
What had gotten into him?

The coachman had served him for nearly a year, but his employer remained a mystery. He was always smiling, yet somehow it never seemed genuine. And there was only one occasion when he ever spoke to the coachman first.
When they reached their destination.
A brief “Thank you for your hard work” was both the beginning and the end of their conversations.
But today he spoke first, and he hasn’t even looked at his bamboo slips on the road.
His high-ranking employer was always busy. He had a mountain of work to handle and people to meet everywhere.

After nearly a year of seeing him like that, perhaps it was only natural that today’s change felt so strange. Perhaps that was why the coachman let a pointless curiosity he would normally have kept to himself slip out.
“Um, has something happened?”
“Hm?”
“Ah, well...”
The coachman regretted the question the moment he asked it. Nothing good could come of upsetting his employer, especially one so high-ranking.
But his employer was more forgiving than he’d expected.
“Hm. Something happened? Yes, I suppose it did. I heard some bad news not long ago.”
“I-I’m sorry.”
“No, why apologize over that? When you bow and scrape too much, it makes me uncomfortable, too. Brings back old memories.”
“Pardon?”
“Memories I never want to go back to. For example...”
His employer trailed off and gazed out the window.
Beyond the wooden lattice, children were laughing in a clean, orderly street.
“Going three whole days without food, then standing in the street singing to please people dressed in silk. Memories like that.”
“Oh, don’t get the wrong idea. I’m not saying it to make you feel bad. It’s just something that happened.”
The coachman’s mouth fell open at the thought that someone of such high standing had lived through that. His employer watched the people passing slowly by and smiled faintly.
“It’s nice to see everyone looking so happy.”
It had happened a very long time ago.
But in someone’s memory, it remained a brand that would never fade.
Poverty. Death. Sorrow. Anger.
The days he had spent doing everything he could to escape the shackles that had gripped his throat since birth flashed past.
“I managed it somehow back then...but can I do it this time, too?”
The quiet mutter scattered on the wind.
The coachman didn’t dare say another word. He kept guiding the horses while his employer took in everything passing slowly around him.
As they drew nearer to their destination, hoofprints in the dirt came into clearer view. At last, his employer knew the time had come.
“Could I ask you a favor?”
“A favor...sir?”
His employer nodded at the coachman’s question.
“Yes, a favor. Consider it an apology, too, for not being very warm toward you until now.”
“Th-there’s no need to say that, sir. If you need anything, please give me an order, Deputy Military Commissioner.”
His employer—or rather, Hong Jin, Deputy Military Commissioner of Shanxi Province—parted his red lips.
“I’ll get off here. Go to Honghwaru right away and tell them. Or should I say the Lower District Sect’s Shanxi branch?”
“You thought I wouldn’t know, didn’t you? But they’ve probably figured it out to some extent already. No matter how secretly the Embroidered Uniform Guard operates, they can’t avoid that many eyes.”
The fact that Hong Jin knew his identity, and the existence of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, said to act only on the Emperor’s orders.
The coachman couldn’t decide which shocked him more. Then he realized what he needed to ask.
“What would you have me do, Deputy Military Commissioner?”
“Tell them everything that’s happening. Then have them use every bit of the Lower District Sect’s information network to find one person.”
“One person?”
“Someone who can protect us in any situation—or rather, His Highness Prince Shangshan. The most trustworthy person in all Murim.”
Hong Jin spoke slowly, emphasizing every word.
“The Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, Jin Taekyung.”
“Go. Hurry.”
That was all.
The carriage sped away like the wind. Hong Jin watched it until it vanished, then turned.
A group of riders descended on him amid the thunder of hooves.
“By imperial decree, you must come with us, Deputy Military Commissioner.”
“And His Highness Prince Shangshan?”
“Rest assured. He is unharmed—for now.”
“For now... All right, then.”
Hong Jin smiled.
Then he walked toward his young lord.

chapters.title: Chapter 852
paragraphs: The ways a Murim martial artist could get information were extremely limited.
The easiest places to start were inns and pleasure houses.
They were full of people from every walk of life. Listen for a while and you could hear all kinds of stories.
The downside was that none of the important information was there. Most of it was unverified rumor.
So martial artists whose heads weren’t just for decoration, and who’d spent some time earning their keep with a sword, went to information merchants instead.
These professionals bought and sold information in every region. Their prices were steep, but their information was reliable.
The problem was that there were clear limits to what they could gather.
They could provide high-quality information about the region where they were based, but that was as far as it went.
For people with money, a respectable sect behind them, and a few useful connections, that left two natural choices.
The Lower District Sect.
And the Beggars’ Sect.
They had taken root throughout the land. The weeds of this world had gathered one by one and grown a vast forest of their own.
The Beggars’ Sect was one of the Nine Sects and One Gang, so its importance went without saying. But the Lower District Sect couldn’t be dismissed, either.
Waiters and courtesans, coachmen and pickpockets. Back-alley gamblers and merchants running shops of every size.
Like the beggars of the Beggars’ Sect, they were everywhere.
Their vast networks let them cast a net across the land and haul in a wealth of information. Even the Sect Leaders of the most prestigious Murim sects couldn’t treat them carelessly.
Of course, there were exceptions to every rule.
“Gather everyone.”
“Pardon?”
“Gather everyone. You have half a day. At the Sichuan Tang Clan.”
At least for today, Jeok Cheongang was a Grand Mage.
In precisely half a day, he’d summoned the Lower District Sect and the Beggars’ Sect, along with the Qingcheng and Emei Sects, and seated them all in one place.
“Um, may I ask why you’ve called us here so suddenly...?”
“Plant yourself quietly in a corner. You need to hear this, too.”
Of course, Tang Sadok, the Family Head of the Sichuan Tang Clan, was there as well.
But what surprised everyone except Jeok Cheongang was that the Sect Leaders of Qingcheng and Emei had come in person.
“I, Bicheonja of the Qingcheng Sect, a junior of the Murim, pay my respects to you, Senior.”
Sect Leader of the Qingcheng Sect or not, in front of Jeok Cheongang, he was a junior of the Murim.

Bicheonja looked as though he’d run hard enough to sweat through his soles. Jeok Cheongang nodded at his cupped-fist greeting. Bicheonja—or Cheongpung the Ancient Sword, as he was better known in Murim.
“So, is your master still doing well these days?”
“...He passed away twenty years ago.”
After a brief silence, Jeok Cheongang spoke without batting an eye.
“I was asking whether you’ve been tending his grave. No matter how busy you are, visit often and pull the weeds.”
“...Yes. I’ll remember that.”
Anyone could see Jeok Cheongang had forgotten, but Cheongpung the Ancient Sword showed the patience of a Daoist and took his seat.
No, it was probably more accurate to say he let it slide because this was the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang.
No one in Murim could match Jeok Cheongang’s seniority, and his age and martial arts were overwhelming.
But Extinction Divine Nun, who’d taken the vacant post of Emei Sect Leader after the Sichuan Blood Tragedy, was someone even Jeok Cheongang couldn’t treat carelessly, given her age.
“You’re here, old hag.”
I take it back. I must’ve been mistaken.
He’s treating her however the fuck he wants. Seriously.
I pressed a hand to my forehead. Everyone else’s mouths fell open.
At least there was one saving grace: Extinction Divine Nun, famous for rampaging like a madwoman on the battlefield, was usually an exceptionally gentle person.
“Benefactor Jeok, you’re the same whenever I see you. In more ways than one.”
“Old hag, you’ve gotten older since I last saw you. It feels like forty years, not four months. I mean that literally.”
“Amitabha. At your age, you should’ve grown up long ago. When are you going to start acting your age?”
“I’ve grown about a hundred years younger, so I plan to live like this for another hundred. Though by then, Venerable Nun, you’ll no longer be of this world.”
“...Amitabha. That was too harsh.”
“If you’re that offended, you should Return to Youth yourself.”
“Amitabhaaaaa!”
I sensed we were in deep shit and hurriedly stepped between them. It was the best move I could’ve made.
If they’d traded one more line, Extinction Divine Nun’s wooden prayer block would’ve come down on Jeok Cheongang’s skull.
Of course, Jeok Cheongang wouldn’t have just let her hit him. The important thing was that Extinction Divine Nun’s anger quickly subsided when I appeared.
“Oh, Benefactor Jin.”
“Have you been well, Venerable Nun? No—I mean, Sect Leader.”
“You needn’t be so formal. Call me whatever feels comfortable. In any case, you’ve become even more striking since I last saw you. And such a full head of hair.”
Extinction Divine Nun added that last part while looking at Jeok Cheongang, then patted my shoulder with her deeply wrinkled hand.

Perhaps because she thought so highly of the way I’d rushed around trying to minimize the damage during the Sichuan Blood Tragedy, both she and Cheongpung the Ancient Sword looked at me so fondly their eyes might as well have been dripping honey.
“Before we begin, I must say you’ve been through a great deal. I hear you distinguished yourself against Dark Heaven’s fiends in Nanman and even brought the Nanman Beast Palace into the alliance?”
“Fellow Daoist Jin’s chivalrous spirit is truly remarkable. I, too, can’t help but admire you.”
Words could travel a thousand li without legs.
The story had already begun making the rounds among people with decent information networks. And that certainly included everyone gathered here.
Two Sect Leaders from the Nine Sects and One Gang, not to mention leaders of the land’s foremost information organizations.
“Congratulations, though belated, Great Hero Jin Taekyung. Our Shaanxi Branch Leader was delighted when she heard the news.”
“I only wish that brat Gung Gibang—or rather, the Successor Beggar—could measure up to you even halfway. Anyway, what you did was incredible.”

“Where’s your Sect Leader? Why’s some mere Elder hanging around?”
“...Sir Jeok, how could we bring the Sect Leader here from Henan in half a day?”
“Henan? That bastard’s in Henan right now?”
“Yes.”
Getting from Henan to Sichuan in half a day would’ve been impossible without a jet.
Jeok Cheongang seemed to accept that the Elder had a point and looked for another target.
“Hey. Lower District Sect.”
“Yes, sir.”
“Where’s your Sect Leader?”
“I’d dearly love to bring him here, but even I don’t know where he is. Our sect is organized into cells, so his location is a closely guarded secret...”

For a Lower District Sect with countless members, a Branch Leader was on the same level as a Beggars’ Sect Elder. The Sichuan Branch Leader swallowed hard under Jeok Cheongang’s pressure.
“Of course not. Whatever information you want, we’ll find it by any means necessary and bring it to you as quickly as we can!”
“Whatever you want. By any means necessary. As quickly as you can?”
“Yes, sir.”
“That sounds good. I’ll remember it clearly, so you remember this one thing, too. Understand?”
“I’m not sure what you mean...”
The Lower District Sect Branch Leader’s eyes wavered. Then Jeok Cheongang’s voice sounded, low and heavy.
“If even a single word of what’s said here today gets out...”
Whoooosh.
He didn’t finish the sentence, but he didn’t need to.
The terrifying wave of qi that rolled out from Jeok Cheongang was a wordless warning against the slightest chance of a leak.
And there wasn’t a single person here too slow to understand what he meant.
They understood, too, that something important was about to be discussed.
“Around noon today, the City Lord of Sichuan Province died.”
With Jeok Cheongang’s first words, the curtain rose. Every eye turned toward the Divine Physician and Namho as they stepped forward.
“The late City Lord died of illness. His physical and mental strength had declined sharply over the past few months, and that led to his death.”
“The renowned physicians in the area have already examined the body at the City Lord’s Residence and reached the same conclusion. The Divine Physician here has as well.”
I added quietly, “A death by illness, beyond all suspicion. That’s how it will be reported. Officially, at least.”
I could feel the air around us shift.
Officially.
Anyone could hear the implication. That one word told them there was a secret the outside world didn’t know.
At my quiet glance, the Divine Physician nodded, took a small wooden case from his robe, and carefully opened it.
“This is known as Blood Soul Gu.”
The people who saw it stared wide-eyed. It was smaller than any insect I’d ever seen, and red as blood.
By the time everyone had left, evening had fallen.
Jeok Cheongang and I were the only ones left. We talked as we looked out at the pitch-black darkness that had settled all around us.
“How long do you think it’ll take?”
“Who can say? All we can do now is trust them and wait.”
“If we wait, we’ll be too late. We need to move.”
“One wrong turn, and it’ll take even longer to find our way back. Besides, haven’t we already learned something from their information?”
I nodded without a word.
Just as Jeok Cheongang said, we’d already received information from the Lower District Sect and the Beggars’ Sect.
The Embroidered Uniform Guard.
No one living in this land could fail to know that name.
One of the Great Nation’s most powerful and secretive forces, acting only on the orders of a single person.
They’d shown themselves—and well before we arrived in Sichuan.
In Anhui Province, not Zhejiang Province, where the Great Nation’s capital and the Emperor’s residence were located.
And they’d been disguised, unlike usual.
Why had the Embroidered Uniform Guard—an agency directly under the Emperor—appeared in Anhui Province in disguise, unlike usual?
We had no way to learn more. The informants who’d caught their scent and followed them had been found dead. But I couldn’t help imagining the worst.
If they hadn’t stopped in Anhui and had kept heading northwest...
That would take them to Shanxi Province. And he was in Shanxi Province.
Prince Shangshan, Zhu Bao.
The only direct member of the imperial family the current Son of Heaven had spared after winning the horrific power struggle over the throne.
The only vassal king in the land and, with the Son of Heaven having no heir, the current successor to the Great Nation’s throne.
But the Emperor, who’d been quiet until now, has set the Embroidered Uniform Guard in motion. And so secretly, too.
If their destination was Shanxi Province... I could only foresee the worst.
The shadow of Dark Heaven had reached the Great Nation’s imperial family.

The Captain of the Guards said the City Lord of Sichuan Province had started showing signs of madness right after the Son of Heaven took his favorite concubine. And the Blood Soul Gu found in his body was so rare that I’d never even seen one in the Poisonblood Grounds in Nanman.
There was enough evidence. I silently stared up at the night sky, lit only by hazy moonlight.
A question that would reach no one.
What the hell are you after?
And then—
A faint sound came from somewhere in the sky and reached my ears.
No. It reached both our ears.
Flutter.
“Old Master.”
“This is...”
It wasn’t the wind. It was the beating of wings as something flew through it toward us.
A messenger pigeon!
The moment I realized it, Jeok Cheongang and I looked toward the distant sky. Our eyes widened.
Whooosh!
The shadows of more than ten birds raced toward us, cutting through the wind.

I take it back.
I must’ve been mistaken.
He’s treating her however the fuck he wants.
Seriously.
I pressed a hand to my forehead.
Everyone else’s mouths fell open.
At least there was one saving grace: Extinction Divine Nun, famous for rampaging like a madwoman on the battlefield, was usually an exceptionally gentle person.

chapters.title: Chapter 853
paragraphs: Information is a puzzle. One piece alone can never give you the whole picture.
Unless you gather the pieces and fit them together, they’re not information at all—just questions with no value.
The Embroidered Uniform Guard appearing in Anhui about fifteen days ago had been just such a piece.
At least, until the City Lord of Sichuan Province died suddenly and the Blood Soul Gu was discovered.
Things are different now.

Emei and Qingcheng belonged to the Nine Sects and One Gang. Then there were the Sichuan Tang Clan and the Beggars’ Sect. Even the Lower District Sect, whose members were largely commoners, was a Murim organization.
With a full-scale war against Dark Heaven underway, information about the government had naturally fallen down their list of priorities.
If your own neighborhood was on fire, you’d have to be crazy to go looking around the one next door.
But if the fire spread there, that changed everything.
We needed to dig up every piece that, for one reason or another, had never been reported—or had been set aside as mere suspicion.
And the dozen or so messenger pigeons that had just arrived at the Sichuan Tang Clan were carrying those very pieces.
“Old Master. You’re here. And you too.”
Important matters went to the Family Head first, of course.
Tang Sadok greeted Jeok Cheongang and me briefly. In front of him lay a scattering of tightly sealed missives.
“Are those all... about this?”
“Probably.”
At Tang Sadok’s brief reply and glance, the old man beside him—who had been carefully inspecting the messenger pigeons and their missives—spoke up.
“From what I’ve seen, there’s no sign the messenger pigeons were attacked, and none of the missives have been damaged.”
“Are you certain? This is important.”
“I stake my life on it.”
“That’s enough for me. I’ll send for you when the time comes. Until then, don’t let anyone in.”
“Yes, Family Head. I won’t let so much as a rat near.”
The old man bowed politely and left the room. His presence quickly faded into the distance.
Tang Sadok caught the meaning in Jeok Cheongang’s eyes and spoke first.
“He’s a household retainer absolutely loyal to me. He’s handled messenger pigeons here for more than half his life, so I had him check them as a precaution.”
The place Tang Sadok called “here” looked less like a pavilion than a huge aviary.
Even standing still, the sharp, musty smell of birds stung my nose. Iron cages of all sizes filled the space, and feathers of every color fluttered through the air.
It was clear that this place had been used for years solely to train messenger pigeons and send and receive their messages. Dozens of unopened missives were piled up inside.
“There are more than I expected. A lot more missives than pigeons we saw on the way here.”
Tang Sadok gave a small nod.
“I’m surprised, too. Usually, they send only the bare minimum of information to keep the messenger pigeons from attracting attention. But sending several pages on each one means...”
“They had that much information to send, even if this was the only way to do it.”
Jeok Cheongang spoke up, then added quietly,
“And it was that urgent.”
I opened the first missive and read it. What they’d said was no exaggeration.
“What does it say?”
I was silent for a moment before answering Jeok Cheongang.
“After Anhui, people suspected of being members of the Embroidered Uniform Guard appeared in Hubei.”
“Hubei? When did the information come in?”
“About twenty days ago.”
“Twenty days. Damn, that’s late.”
“By then, their trail in Anhui had already gone cold, and it seems neither the Beggars’ Sect nor the Lower District Sect in Hubei guessed they were the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
Tang Sadok frowned.

“Isn’t it possible they weren’t the Embroidered Uniform Guard at all? If your guess is right and their target is Prince Shangshan, they’d have no reason to detour through Hubei to reach Shanxi. They could go straight from Anhui to Henan.”
He was right. Anhui was closest to Henan, and they could enter Shanxi by heading just a little farther north.
But Tang Sadok had forgotten one important thing.
“If they are the Embroidered Uniform Guard, and they disguised themselves to hide their identities from the start, of course they’d avoid Henan.”
“What does that mean...? Ah.”
Tang Sadok let out a small exclamation.
“The Murim Alliance.”
“Exactly. Their trail was nearly picked up even in Anhui. Henan is practically an impregnable fortress right now.”
The vast storm of war was reaching its peak, and the full-scale war with Dark Heaven had begun.
With everyone in the Central Plains Murim on high alert, crossing Henan—the home of the Murim Alliance’s headquarters—to reach Shanxi would be no different from giving away their identities.
The Murim Alliance wasn’t made up of fools.
Dark Heaven’s agents or the Embroidered Uniform Guard—it didn’t matter. Anyone suspicious would be identified in no time.
Even if the Sword Saint, Mae Jonghak, leader of the Murim Alliance, merely stood by with a gentle smile and watched, one old fox beside him would be different.
Song Ho, the Thousand-Faced Fox.
He had another title: Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.
At that very moment, as I pictured the Thousand-Faced Fox’s face, always marked by a faint smile—
Rustle.
A faint sound came from the crack beneath the firmly shut door. But no one in the room, myself included, was surprised or flustered.
We’d already sensed someone approaching and had a fair idea who it was.
Creeeak.
At Jeok Cheongang’s glance, I reached out. A gentle current of qi pushed the door open, revealing a person.
No—more accurately, two people who looked like one.
The Tang Family retainer who had left earlier had Namho pinned in an embrace from behind, a blade pressed to his Adam’s apple.
What the hell was going on?
My brain stalled for a moment, but the answer came quickly.
The Tang Family retainer who would do anything Tang Sadok said had been guarding the place so faithfully that not even a rat could get near. Then he’d found Namho.
The minor problem was that Namho had nearly died for it.
“You’re still young at heart. It’s not easy to get fired up at your age.”
Namho, restrained with the retainer pressed up against his back, replied with a face like he’d bitten into a turd.
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
“Nothing. Anyway, stay still. Your Adam’s apple moves when you talk, and the blade will cut you.”
“There’s a limit to how far you can take a threat—”
Slice.
“Fuck, it really does.”
“I told you not to talk.”
“That’s why I’m using ventriloquism now.”
“Oh, ventriloquism. Teach me sometime.”
“Maybe, if I get the chance... Damn it. Cut the crap and get this man to stand down. I’ve explained, but he won’t listen to a word.”
Jeok Cheongang stroked his chin, looking amused by Namho’s predicament.
“You were right about him being loyal. If he were just a little more reliable, he’d have killed an innocent man.”
“...Sometimes his loyalty goes too far. Let him go. He’s one of ours.”
At Tang Sadok’s sighing words, the retainer blinked, finally withdrew his dagger, and stepped back.
Namho watched him leave without so much as an apology and muttered,
“I’ve seen all kinds of lunatics, but this is something else. No wonder the Sichuan Tang Clan is—”
“Is what?”
Namho met Tang Sadok’s pointed gaze and changed course at the speed of light.
“That of one of the Five Great Families under Heaven.”
An impressive drift. Then again, however long you’d already lived, you wouldn’t want to spend the rest of your life worrying about being poisoned.
“Anyway, why did you take so long? It’s been ages since I sent for you.”
“I was trying to remember something. Maybe I’m getting old, but my memory isn’t what it used to be.”
“Your memory?”
“Yes. My memory.”
Before I could ask what he meant, Namho nodded toward the missive in my hand.
“That information you’re reading—where did it come from?”
“The Hubei branches of the Beggars’ Sect and the Lower District Sect.”
“No, the one beside it.”
I opened another of the dozens of missives scattered across the table and checked it.
“It says Hoyeon Trading Company. I’ve never heard of it. The contents say...”

“It’s a trading company under the Qingcheng Sect. More precisely, Hoyeon Sword, a lay disciple of the Qingcheng Sect, has been running it for twenty years. He’s a Peak master, but he’s much better at running a trading company than at martial arts. Hoyeon Trading Company is one of the five largest in Shandong.”
“What?”
“Oh, and you don’t need to tell me what it says. I’m looking for a different name. Just check the source of each message and tell me.”
I didn’t know what to ask first.
As far as I knew, he hadn’t set foot in the Central Plains since the Great Faction War. How did he know so much about something from twenty years ago?
And if he didn’t care what the missives said, what source was he looking for?
Jeok Cheongang and Tang Sadok stared at him with wide eyes. I could only look at him, dumbfounded and silent. Namho clicked his tongue, displeased.

“I’m no Jiang Taigong. Did you think I spent all those years in Nanman just sitting around fishing? I kept up with news from the Central Plains through the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s Hidden Thread while I was there. There’s nothing to be so surprised about.”
“This seems like more than just keeping up with the news. Even if I heard some of that, I wouldn’t remember it.”
“Call it an old man’s pastime. Anything else?”
It was probably closer to an occupational habit, but my curiosity about that didn’t matter right now.
I kept quiet and hurriedly began opening and reading the remaining missives.
They’d all come through the Sichuan Branch, but each had a different source. And since I had to read them to find what Namho wanted, I began piecing together their contents as I went.
What emerged was shocking.
It wasn’t just Anhui and Hubei.
Anhui, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangsu, Shandong.
If the missives were accurate, people suspected of being members of the Embroidered Uniform Guard had appeared in all five provinces, then vanished.
This is...
They were traveling in separate groups.
It looked less like an attempt to cause confusion than a way to move without attracting attention.
They had split into groups of between ten and thirty, scattered across the provinces, then disappeared upon reaching Shaanxi or Shandong.
Shanxi. They gathered in Shanxi.

There was no doubt. Avoiding Henan and drawing as little attention as possible, they’d gone around it, slipping into Shanxi through Shaanxi and Shandong—the provinces that lay along the continent’s flank.
And in Shanxi...
Prince Shangshan Zhu Bao.
My heart sank. I picked up another missive almost mechanically, and my teeth clenched as I read it.
Grind.
“What is it?”
“What does it say?”

Assigned: Fire King Jeok Cheongang, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung, and all members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion.

Only one place in the world could give an order to me—or rather, to Jeok Cheongang.

He was right. There was no more time to hesitate.
I shot off into the darkness.
We had a little over fifteen days left. We had to hurry, even if it was only by a single hour.

sentences.text: Information is a puzzle.
One piece alone can never give you the whole picture.
Unless you gather the pieces and fit them together, they’re not information at all—just questions with no value.
The Embroidered Uniform Guard appearing in Anhui about fifteen days ago had been just such a piece.
At least, until the City Lord of Sichuan Province died suddenly and the Blood Soul Gu was discovered.
Things are different now.
Emei and Qingcheng belonged to the Nine Sects and One Gang.
Then there were the Sichuan Tang Clan and the Beggars’ Sect.
Even the Lower District Sect, whose members were largely commoners, was a Murim organization.
With a full-scale war against Dark Heaven underway, information about the government had naturally fallen down their list of priorities.
If your own neighborhood was on fire, you’d have to be crazy to go looking around the one next door.
But if the fire spread there, that changed everything.
We needed to dig up every piece that, for one reason or another, had never been reported—or had been set aside as mere suspicion.
And the dozen or so messenger pigeons that had just arrived at the Sichuan Tang Clan were carrying those very pieces.
“Old Master.
You’re here.
And you too.”
Important matters went to the Family Head first, of course.
Tang Sadok greeted Jeok Cheongang and me briefly.
In front of him lay a scattering of tightly sealed missives.
“Are those all... about this?”
“Probably.”
At Tang Sadok’s brief reply and glance, the old man beside him—who had been carefully inspecting the messenger pigeons and their missives—spoke up.
“From what I’ve seen, there’s no sign the messenger pigeons were attacked, and none of the missives have been damaged.”
“Are you certain?
This is important.”
“I stake my life on it.”
“That’s enough for me.
I’ll send for you when the time comes.
Until then, don’t let anyone in.”
“Yes, Family Head.
I won’t let so much as a rat near.”
The old man bowed politely and left the room.
His presence quickly faded into the distance.
Tang Sadok caught the meaning in Jeok Cheongang’s eyes and spoke first.
“He’s a household retainer absolutely loyal to me.
He’s handled messenger pigeons here for more than half his life, so I had him check them as a precaution.”
The place Tang Sadok called “here” looked less like a pavilion than a huge aviary.
Even standing still, the sharp, musty smell of birds stung my nose.
Iron cages of all sizes filled the space, and feathers of every color fluttered through the air.
It was clear that this place had been used for years solely to train messenger pigeons and send and receive their messages.
Dozens of unopened missives were piled up inside.
“There are more than I expected.
A lot more missives than pigeons we saw on the way here.”
Tang Sadok gave a small nod.
“I’m surprised, too.
Usually, they send only the bare minimum of information to keep the messenger pigeons from attracting attention.
But sending several pages on each one means...”
“They had that much information to send, even if this was the only way to do it.”
Jeok Cheongang spoke up, then added quietly,
“And it was that urgent.”
I opened the first missive and read it.
What they’d said was no exaggeration.
“What does it say?”
I was silent for a moment before answering Jeok Cheongang.
“After Anhui, people suspected of being members of the Embroidered Uniform Guard appeared in Hubei.”
“Hubei?
When did the information come in?”
“About twenty days ago.”
“Twenty days.
Damn, that’s late.”
“By then, their trail in Anhui had already gone cold, and it seems neither the Beggars’ Sect nor the Lower District Sect in Hubei guessed they were the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
Tang Sadok frowned.
“Isn’t it possible they weren’t the Embroidered Uniform Guard at all?
If your guess is right and their target is Prince Shangshan, they’d have no reason to detour through Hubei to reach Shanxi.
They could go straight from Anhui to Henan.”
He was right.
Anhui was closest to Henan, and they could enter Shanxi by heading just a little farther north.
But Tang Sadok had forgotten one important thing.
“If they are the Embroidered Uniform Guard, and they disguised themselves to hide their identities from the start, of course they’d avoid Henan.”
“What does that mean...?
Ah.”
Tang Sadok let out a small exclamation.
“The Murim Alliance.”
“Exactly.
Their trail was nearly picked up even in Anhui.
Henan is practically an impregnable fortress right now.”
The vast storm of war was reaching its peak, and the full-scale war with Dark Heaven had begun.
With everyone in the Central Plains Murim on high alert, crossing Henan—the home of the Murim Alliance’s headquarters—to reach Shanxi would be no different from giving away their identities.
The Murim Alliance wasn’t made up of fools.
Dark Heaven’s agents or the Embroidered Uniform Guard—it didn’t matter.
Anyone suspicious would be identified in no time.
Even if the Sword Saint, Mae Jonghak, leader of the Murim Alliance, merely stood by with a gentle smile and watched, one old fox beside him would be different.
Song Ho, the Thousand-Faced Fox.
He had another title: Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.
At that very moment, as I pictured the Thousand-Faced Fox’s face, always marked by a faint smile—
Rustle.
A faint sound came from the crack beneath the firmly shut door.
But no one in the room, myself included, was surprised or flustered.
We’d already sensed someone approaching and had a fair idea who it was.
Creeeak.
At Jeok Cheongang’s glance, I reached out.
A gentle current of qi pushed the door open, revealing a person.
No—more accurately, two people who looked like one.
The Tang Family retainer who had left earlier had Namho pinned in an embrace from behind, a blade pressed to his Adam’s apple.
What the hell was going on?
My brain stalled for a moment, but the answer came quickly.
The Tang Family retainer who would do anything Tang Sadok said had been guarding the place so faithfully that not even a rat could get near.
Then he’d found Namho.
The minor problem was that Namho had nearly died for it.
“You’re still young at heart.
It’s not easy to get fired up at your age.”
Namho, restrained with the retainer pressed up against his back, replied with a face like he’d bitten into a turd.
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
“Nothing.
Anyway, stay still.
Your Adam’s apple moves when you talk, and the blade will cut you.”
“There’s a limit to how far you can take a threat—”
Slice.
“Fuck, it really does.”
“I told you not to talk.”
“That’s why I’m using ventriloquism now.”
“Oh, ventriloquism.
Teach me sometime.”
“Maybe, if I get the chance...
Damn it.
Cut the crap and get this man to stand down.
I’ve explained, but he won’t listen to a word.”
Jeok Cheongang stroked his chin, looking amused by Namho’s predicament.
“You were right about him being loyal.
If he were just a little more reliable, he’d have killed an innocent man.”
“...Sometimes his loyalty goes too far.
Let him go.
He’s one of ours.”
At Tang Sadok’s sighing words, the retainer blinked, finally withdrew his dagger, and stepped back.
Namho watched him leave without so much as an apology and muttered,
“I’ve seen all kinds of lunatics, but this is something else.
No wonder the Sichuan Tang Clan is—”
“Is what?”
Namho met Tang Sadok’s pointed gaze and changed course at the speed of light.
“That of one of the Five Great Families under Heaven.”
An impressive drift.
Then again, however long you’d already lived, you wouldn’t want to spend the rest of your life worrying about being poisoned.
“Anyway, why did you take so long?
It’s been ages since I sent for you.”
“I was trying to remember something.
Maybe I’m getting old, but my memory isn’t what it used to be.”
“Your memory?”
“Yes.
My memory.”
Before I could ask what he meant, Namho nodded toward the missive in my hand.
“That information you’re reading—where did it come from?”
“The Hubei branches of the Beggars’ Sect and the Lower District Sect.”
“No, the one beside it.”
I opened another of the dozens of missives scattered across the table and checked it.
“It says Hoyeon Trading Company.
I’ve never heard of it.
The contents say...”
“It’s a trading company under the Qingcheng Sect.
More precisely, Hoyeon Sword, a lay disciple of the Qingcheng Sect, has been running it for twenty years.
He’s a Peak master, but he’s much better at running a trading company than at martial arts.
Hoyeon Trading Company is one of the five largest in Shandong.”
“What?”
“Oh, and you don’t need to tell me what it says.
I’m looking for a different name.
Just check the source of each message and tell me.”
I didn’t know what to ask first.
As far as I knew, he hadn’t set foot in the Central Plains since the Great Faction War.
How did he know so much about something from twenty years ago?
And if he didn’t care what the missives said, what source was he looking for?
Jeok Cheongang and Tang Sadok stared at him with wide eyes.
I could only look at him, dumbfounded and silent.
Namho clicked his tongue, displeased.
“I’m no Jiang Taigong.
Did you think I spent all those years in Nanman just sitting around fishing?
I kept up with news from the Central Plains through the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s Hidden Thread while I was there.
There’s nothing to be so surprised about.”
“This seems like more than just keeping up with the news.
Even if I heard some of that, I wouldn’t remember it.”
“Call it an old man’s pastime.
Anything else?”
It was probably closer to an occupational habit, but my curiosity about that didn’t matter right now.
I kept quiet and hurriedly began opening and reading the remaining missives.
They’d all come through the Sichuan Branch, but each had a different source.
And since I had to read them to find what Namho wanted, I began piecing together their contents as I went.
What emerged was shocking.
It wasn’t just Anhui and Hubei.
Anhui, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangsu, Shandong.
If the missives were accurate, people suspected of being members of the Embroidered Uniform Guard had appeared in all five provinces, then vanished.
This is...
They were traveling in separate groups.
It looked less like an attempt to cause confusion than a way to move without attracting attention.
They had split into groups of between ten and thirty, scattered across the provinces, then disappeared upon reaching Shaanxi or Shandong.
Shanxi.
They gathered in Shanxi.
There was no doubt.
Avoiding Henan and drawing as little attention as possible, they’d gone around it, slipping into Shanxi through Shaanxi and Shandong—the provinces that lay along the continent’s flank.

Prince Shangshan Zhu Bao.

paragraphs: Jang Il, a junior military officer in Hubei Province, knew how to be satisfied with his life.
Some people who knew him would click their tongues and say he had no ambition, despite being born a man. But Jang Il himself was proud of who he was.
I’ve done well enough. Damn right I have.
He’d been born into a commoner family with next to nothing, yet he’d risen to become an officer.
His low rank meant the government paid him a pittance, but what mattered was that he was one of the seven gate commanders in Yichang, a major city in western Hubei Province.
And what kind of place was Yichang?
A port city on the Yangtze, which ran across Hubei Province. Poets and scholars flocked there to admire its splendid scenery.
Countless people and goods passed through every day, and naturally, each gate collected hefty tolls.
There were also the little extras called bribes, which never found their way into reports to the higher-ups.
Wonder what big shots will come through today.
Jang Il rose early, eager to get ready for work.
He put on a silk robe with a lustrous sheen and belted on his finely decorated sword.
It stung a little that he couldn’t see himself in a mirror—they were far too expensive for him to buy—but his elderly servant offered some comfort.
“You truly have the bearing of a hero, my lord.”
“Ahem. You think so, too?”
“Yes, my lord. Whoever passes through the gate, none of them will dare raise their heads properly in the face of your authority.”
“Now, now. What a silly thing to say.”
For all his protests, the corners of Jang Il’s mouth twitched upward. The elderly servant laughed and waved a hand.
“When have you ever known me to flatter you? But you’re wearing your best silk robe and even carrying your sword today. Something important must be happening.”
“You’re always quick to catch on. Some real big shots might be coming through. A trading caravan that left for Chongqing about two months ago is due back around now.”
“Goodness. But haven’t things been getting strange around Chongqing lately?”
“Who told you that?”
“A traveling merchant I know. He said there’s been a bloodbath among martial artists, not just around Chongqing, but in Guangxi as well...”
“It’s all nonsense, so ignore it. I’ve heard a little about Guangxi myself, but Chongqing only has a few disorganized bandits and river pirates. This caravan is bound to bring in a fortune.”
Jang Il straightened his clothes and smiled with satisfaction.

Chongqing lay between Sichuan Province and Hubei Province. It wasn’t quite a province in its own right, but its abundant resources and local specialties had countless trading companies eager to do business there.
The profits were high, and so was the competition. The trading companies that won out were enormous.
Especially this caravan.
Three trading companies had joined forces. Between their guards and caravan porters, they’d brought a staggering five hundred people.
They’d loaded more than a hundred carts onto ten merchant ships and set out about two months ago. Jang Il couldn’t help looking forward to the little extras coming his way.
After everything it took to get this post, I ought to get something out of it.
The old saying “you reap what you sow” meant something entirely different to Jang Il.
He’d scattered a fortune in bribes to become a gate commander in Yichang. In less than two years, he’d collected more than he’d spent, but he had no intention of stopping there.
As long as I keep collecting like this, that’s plenty. No need to get greedy. Just enough to buy a respectable estate.
One greed was soon forgotten in pursuit of another.
Proud to be a conscientious official who was only moderately corrupt and moderately lazy, Jang Il left home.
The moment he arrived at his post at the West Gate, he realized something was wrong.
What is this?
The air felt taut.
The soldiers who would usually be standing around yawning with their arms folded were drenched in sweat and running in every direction. Bloodied stretchers and charred debris lay scattered about.
So did the three flags that had flown proudly when the caravan left for Chongqing two months ago.
“What on earth...”
“My lord! Officer Jang!”
The sudden call snapped Jang Il out of his daze.
A familiar subordinate stood before him, pale as a sheet.
“What—what happened here?”
“Th-that is...”
“Tell me the truth, now!”
The subordinate flinched at his superior’s sharp shout, then stammered out an answer.
As Jang Il listened to his rambling account, his mouth fell open.
“A-an attack?”
“Yes, my lord. They say the caravan was attacked by bandits on its way back.”
“That’s impossible! They had five hundred guards and caravan porters! What bandits would be mad enough to attack them?”
Just as his horrified shout rang out—
“The world’s gone mad. Why should bandits be any different?”
A weary voice cut in. Jang Il turned toward it and blinked.
“M-Master of the Trading Company?”
There was no mistaking him. Even drenched in blood, with his clothes reduced to rags, Jang Il recognized him at once.
He was one of the three trading company masters who had joined the caravan—the big shot Jang Il had been waiting for these past two months.
“Glad I survived to see you again, Officer Jang.”
“W-what on earth happened? Where are the other two?”
“They came with us. But we’ll never have the chance to speak again.”
Jang Il followed the man’s pointing finger and felt the world go dark.
Several dozen bodies lay wrapped in straw mats. Two had been set apart from the rest. It was all too clear who they were.
“...Surely not.”
“Just what you think. They fought bravely to the end, but there was nothing we could do. We were simply outnumbered.”
“Outnumbered? There were that many bandits?”
“Bandits and river pirates, to be precise. Even in the confusion of the ambush, I could tell. Men with harpoons were swarming everywhere.”
“R-river pirates? How could they...?”
“Whether they’re in the mountains or on the Yangtze, thieves make their living by thieving, don’t they?”
The trading company master muttered wearily and leaned against a shattered cart.

“Everything went smoothly when we left Yichang two months ago. But as soon as we reached Chongqing, I had a feeling something was wrong. Sure enough, we’d barely set foot on Yuhua Mountain when they appeared.”
Despite its beautiful scenery, Yuhua Mountain was known as one of Chongqing’s rugged mountains.
The trading company master remembered the moment they’d first encountered their enemies, hemmed in by narrow paths and dense brush. He shuddered before he could stop himself.

“We thought nothing could stand in our way. Each company had brought only its best men, and we’d hired dozens of renowned wandering martial artists in case of trouble. But the moment the attackers appeared, I knew none of that mattered.”
“How many were there?”
“A thousand.”
“Pardon?”
“I said a thousand. That was only what I could count at a glance. There must have been more.”
For a moment, Jang Il thought he’d misheard.
A band of more than a thousand bandits? In the north, nomads or mounted bandits based on the grasslands sometimes joined forces and invaded with a large army. But not in Chongqing.
Something unprecedented had happened. Something that should never have happened.
“But haven’t things been getting strange around Chongqing lately?”
“Who told you that?”
“A traveling merchant I know. He said there’s been a bloodbath among martial artists, not just around Chongqing, but in Guangxi as well...”
Remembering the conversation he’d had with his elderly servant before leaving home, Jang Il felt his heart sink.
His cherished silk robe was damp with cold sweat, though he had no idea when he’d started sweating.
No way.
Chongqing was right next to Hubei. From Yichang, where he commanded a gate, it was three days by boat or five by land.
If—if all of this is true...
His hands and feet trembled. His breathing quickened.
He should’ve been on his feet, directing the soldiers and sounding the alarm, but his body wouldn’t move.
Whether he noticed Jang Il’s condition or not, the trading company master continued.
“We told them we’d pay the toll. Their answer was a volley of arrows.”
Someone died, and a fierce battle began.

The fighters trained by the trading companies and the hired wandering martial artists fought back. Even the caravan porters who had been hauling the carts joined in. But the river pirates and bandits, who’d spent their whole lives as raiders, cut them down without hesitation.
“It was less a battle than a slaughter. We had plenty of people, but half were caravan porters. The rest could only do so much.”
“But how? Weren’t most of those men slash-and-burn farmers or fishermen to begin with?”
“Probably. But there was something different about them. They kept charging at us like they were possessed.”
The trading company master had been speaking as calmly as he could, but now his voice began to shake.

“Even with their legs slashed or an arm gone, they kept coming. Knock one down, and three more came. Knock three down, and five more appeared. If we swallowed our fear and brought them down too, ten more were waiting. Again and again...”
The trading company master still remembered it clearly.
No—he would remember them until his dying breath.
They had charged like fiends bursting out of a hellscape.

“The battle ended decisively in just half a shichen—roughly an hour—and our side broke. Men started running in every direction. Surrounded by screams and death, I led my subordinates away, too. The caravan had failed, but we had to get out alive somehow.”
Nothing was more precious than life.
He had retreated with the other two trading company masters and the men they had left. By the time they emerged from Yuhua Mountain, their number had fallen from five hundred to half that.
“We kept running along the mountain foothills. For three whole days.”
“Th-three days?”
“We wanted to go down and ask the imperial troops or another Murim sect for help, but with those men watching, it was nearly impossible. Staying on the move was our best option.”
The enemy had been watching the main routes closely. The survivors, barely clinging to life, had made a break for Hubei along the shortest route and finally escaped Chongqing.
Or so they thought.
Then they came out of Yuhua Mountain and saw the ten merchant ships they’d left at the nearest dock burning.
“I was sure it was over. I couldn’t even bring myself to think about running anymore.”

The three-day pursuit had been brutal. From five hundred, they had fallen to half that. From that half, to fewer than a hundred. They thought of death as they watched their last hope—the merchant ships—sink amid dark red flames.
Behind them, the enemy shouted.
And just as their final battle was about to begin, people no one could have expected appeared.
“A middle-aged man. He had about ten people with him.”
“A middle-aged man...?”
