sentences.text: Jang Il, a junior military officer in Hubei Province, knew how to be satisfied with his life.
Some people who knew him would click their tongues and say he had no ambition, despite being born a man.
But Jang Il himself was proud of who he was.
I’ve done well enough.
Damn right I have.
He’d been born into a commoner family with next to nothing, yet he’d risen to become an officer.
His low rank meant the government paid him a pittance, but what mattered was that he was one of the seven gate commanders in Yichang, a major city in western Hubei Province.
And what kind of place was Yichang?
A port city on the Yangtze, which ran across Hubei Province.
Poets and scholars flocked there to admire its splendid scenery.
Countless people and goods passed through every day, and naturally, each gate collected hefty tolls.
There were also the little extras called bribes, which never found their way into reports to the higher-ups.
Wonder what big shots will come through today.
Jang Il rose early, eager to get ready for work.
He put on a silk robe with a lustrous sheen and belted on his finely decorated sword.
It stung a little that he couldn’t see himself in a mirror—they were far too expensive for him to buy—but his elderly servant offered some comfort.
“You truly have the bearing of a hero, my lord.”
“Ahem.
You think so, too?”
“Yes, my lord.
Whoever passes through the gate, none of them will dare raise their heads properly in the face of your authority.”
“Now, now.
What a silly thing to say.”
For all his protests, the corners of Jang Il’s mouth twitched upward.
The elderly servant laughed and waved a hand.
“When have you ever known me to flatter you?
But you’re wearing your best silk robe and even carrying your sword today.
Something important must be happening.”
“You’re always quick to catch on.
Some real big shots might be coming through.
A trading caravan that left for Chongqing about two months ago is due back around now.”
“Goodness.
But haven’t things been getting strange around Chongqing lately?”
“Who told you that?”
“A traveling merchant I know.
He said there’s been a bloodbath among martial artists, not just around Chongqing, but in Guangxi as well...”
“It’s all nonsense, so ignore it.
I’ve heard a little about Guangxi myself, but Chongqing only has a few disorganized bandits and river pirates.
This caravan is bound to bring in a fortune.”
Jang Il straightened his clothes and smiled with satisfaction.
Chongqing lay between Sichuan Province and Hubei Province.
It wasn’t quite a province in its own right, but its abundant resources and local specialties had countless trading companies eager to do business there.
The profits were high, and so was the competition.
The trading companies that won out were enormous.
Especially this caravan.
Three trading companies had joined forces.
Between their guards and caravan porters, they’d brought a staggering five hundred people.
They’d loaded more than a hundred carts onto ten merchant ships and set out about two months ago.
Jang Il couldn’t help looking forward to the little extras coming his way.
After everything it took to get this post, I ought to get something out of it.
The old saying “you reap what you sow” meant something entirely different to Jang Il.
He’d scattered a fortune in bribes to become a gate commander in Yichang.
In less than two years, he’d collected more than he’d spent, but he had no intention of stopping there.
As long as I keep collecting like this, that’s plenty.
No need to get greedy.
Just enough to buy a respectable estate.
One greed was soon forgotten in pursuit of another.
Proud to be a conscientious official who was only moderately corrupt and moderately lazy, Jang Il left home.
The moment he arrived at his post at the West Gate, he realized something was wrong.
What is this?
The air felt taut.
The soldiers who would usually be standing around yawning with their arms folded were drenched in sweat and running in every direction.
Bloodied stretchers and charred debris lay scattered about.
So did the three flags that had flown proudly when the caravan left for Chongqing two months ago.
“What on earth...”
“My lord!
Officer Jang!”
The sudden call snapped Jang Il out of his daze.
A familiar subordinate stood before him, pale as a sheet.
“What—what happened here?”
“Th-that is...”
“Tell me the truth, now!”
The subordinate flinched at his superior’s sharp shout, then stammered out an answer.
As Jang Il listened to his rambling account, his mouth fell open.
“A-an attack?”
“Yes, my lord.
They say the caravan was attacked by bandits on its way back.”
“That’s impossible!
They had five hundred guards and caravan porters!
What bandits would be mad enough to attack them?”
Just as his horrified shout rang out—
“The world’s gone mad.
Why should bandits be any different?”
A weary voice cut in.
Jang Il turned toward it and blinked.
“M-Master of the Trading Company?”
There was no mistaking him.
Even drenched in blood, with his clothes reduced to rags, Jang Il recognized him at once.
He was one of the three trading company masters who had joined the caravan—the big shot Jang Il had been waiting for these past two months.
“Glad I survived to see you again, Officer Jang.”
“W-what on earth happened?
Where are the other two?”
“They came with us.
But we’ll never have the chance to speak again.”
Jang Il followed the man’s pointing finger and felt the world go dark.
Several dozen bodies lay wrapped in straw mats.
Two had been set apart from the rest.
It was all too clear who they were.
“...Surely not.”
“Just what you think.
They fought bravely to the end, but there was nothing we could do.
We were simply outnumbered.”
“Outnumbered?
There were that many bandits?”
“Bandits and river pirates, to be precise.
Even in the confusion of the ambush, I could tell.
Men with harpoons were swarming everywhere.”
“R-river pirates?
How could they...?”
“Whether they’re in the mountains or on the Yangtze, thieves make their living by thieving, don’t they?”
The trading company master muttered wearily and leaned against a shattered cart.
“Everything went smoothly when we left Yichang two months ago.
But as soon as we reached Chongqing, I had a feeling something was wrong.
Sure enough, we’d barely set foot on Yuhua Mountain when they appeared.”
Despite its beautiful scenery, Yuhua Mountain was known as one of Chongqing’s rugged mountains.
The trading company master remembered the moment they’d first encountered their enemies, hemmed in by narrow paths and dense brush.
He shuddered before he could stop himself.
“We thought nothing could stand in our way.
Each company had brought only its best men, and we’d hired dozens of renowned wandering martial artists in case of trouble.
But the moment the attackers appeared, I knew none of that mattered.”
“How many were there?”
“A thousand.”
“Pardon?”
“I said a thousand.
That was only what I could count at a glance.
There must have been more.”
For a moment, Jang Il thought he’d misheard.
A band of more than a thousand bandits?
In the north, nomads or mounted bandits based on the grasslands sometimes joined forces and invaded with a large army.
But not in Chongqing.
Something unprecedented had happened.
Something that should never have happened.
“But haven’t things been getting strange around Chongqing lately?”
“Who told you that?”
“A traveling merchant I know.
He said there’s been a bloodbath among martial artists, not just around Chongqing, but in Guangxi as well...”
Remembering the conversation he’d had with his elderly servant before leaving home, Jang Il felt his heart sink.
His cherished silk robe was damp with cold sweat, though he had no idea when he’d started sweating.
No way.
Chongqing was right next to Hubei.
From Yichang, where he commanded a gate, it was three days by boat or five by land.
If—if all of this is true...
His hands and feet trembled.
His breathing quickened.
He should’ve been on his feet, directing the soldiers and sounding the alarm, but his body wouldn’t move.
Whether he noticed Jang Il’s condition or not, the trading company master continued.
“We told them we’d pay the toll.
Their answer was a volley of arrows.”
Someone died, and a fierce battle began.
The fighters trained by the trading companies and the hired wandering martial artists fought back.
Even the caravan porters who had been hauling the carts joined in.
But the river pirates and bandits, who’d spent their whole lives as raiders, cut them down without hesitation.
“It was less a battle than a slaughter.
We had plenty of people, but half were caravan porters.
The rest could only do so much.”
“But how?
Weren’t most of those men slash-and-burn farmers or fishermen to begin with?”
“Probably.
But there was something different about them.
They kept charging at us like they were possessed.”
The trading company master had been speaking as calmly as he could, but now his voice began to shake.
“Even with their legs slashed or an arm gone, they kept coming.
Knock one down, and three more came.
Knock three down, and five more appeared.
If we swallowed our fear and brought them down too, ten more were waiting.
Again and again...”
The trading company master still remembered it clearly.
No—he would remember them until his dying breath.
They had charged like fiends bursting out of a hellscape.
“The battle ended decisively in just half a shichen—roughly an hour—and our side broke.
Men started running in every direction.
Surrounded by screams and death, I led my subordinates away, too.
The caravan had failed, but we had to get out alive somehow.”
Nothing was more precious than life.
He had retreated with the other two trading company masters and the men they had left.
By the time they emerged from Yuhua Mountain, their number had fallen from five hundred to half that.
“We kept running along the mountain foothills.
For three whole days.”
“Th-three days?”
“We wanted to go down and ask the imperial troops or another Murim sect for help, but with those men watching, it was nearly impossible.
Staying on the move was our best option.”
The enemy had been watching the main routes closely.
The survivors, barely clinging to life, had made a break for Hubei along the shortest route and finally escaped Chongqing.
Or so they thought.
Then they came out of Yuhua Mountain and saw the ten merchant ships they’d left at the nearest dock burning.
“I was sure it was over.
I couldn’t even bring myself to think about running anymore.”
The three-day pursuit had been brutal.
From five hundred, they had fallen to half that.
From that half, to fewer than a hundred.
They thought of death as they watched their last hope—the merchant ships—sink amid dark red flames.
Behind them, the enemy shouted.
And just as their final battle was about to begin, people no one could have expected appeared.
“A middle-aged man.
He had about ten people with him.”
“A middle-aged man...?”
“Yes.
He walked toward us as if out for a stroll, pointed at the burning ships, and asked us this out of the blue.”
The trading company master steadied his breathing and continued.
“Which son of a bitch set those on fire?”

chapters.title: Chapter 855
paragraphs: “Which son of a bitch set the fire?”
A low, weighty voice.
Hyuk Mujin swept the area with a gaze sharp as a blade, then shuddered with a gasp.
“Damn. Just thinking about that moment makes me feel like I’m going to piss myself! As expected of Great Hero Je—”
“Shut your mouth and sit down before I beat you so badly you piss and shit yourself.”
“Yes, sir.”
“That mouth of his never takes a break. Was he like this in Nanman, too?”
At Jeok Cheongang’s weary question, Ju Hwaran answered cautiously.
“Yes. Hyuk Mujin has always been like that.”
“I wish I had a muzzle for him. It’s enough to drive me mad that I can’t get one out here.”
Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue and looked around, but no solution presented itself. They were traveling along a forest path surrounded by grass and trees.
They did encounter the occasional person, but what kind of lunatic would carry a muzzle fit for a human up a mountain?
“I have one. Would you like it?”
There was such a lunatic.
And he was right beside him.
“Why on earth are you carrying something like that?”
At Jeok Cheongang’s bewildered question, Namho lowered his voice.
“Doesn’t everyone have at least one person they’d like to put a muzzle on?”
“...You’re quite something yourself.”
“Anyway, if you need it, just say the word. I won’t give it to you outright, of course. I’ll lend it to you for a little while. I need to use it myself as soon as I get the chance.”
Namho glanced meaningfully over his shoulder. Not far away, by a stream, Taishan was staring into the water, looking close to tears.
“Taishan can’t find it. Taishan needs old, smart Namho’s help.”
“Hm.”
No matter how much you disliked someone, you couldn’t spit in the face of a smile.
Namho had been ready to scold him the moment their eyes met, but his voice softened a little.
“I’m not sure I like that first part... Fine. What do you need help with?”
“Taishan is looking for meat, but can’t see any. Namho is smart, unlike Taishan.”
“You’ve said nothing but true things today. But what were you sitting there waiting to catch? Carp? Crucian carp?”
“Neither.”
“Then what?”
“Five-spice pork.”
“Fuck...!”
Namho snatched up a rock and charged at Taishan like a mad bison, but he didn’t get far.
At a glance from Jeok Cheongang, Sama Pyo and Song Ilseom appeared like streaks of light and seized his arms from either side.
“Let go! Let go of me! You brats are still wet behind the ears!”
“Calm down, Elder Namho.”
“We don’t want to do this either.”
“I’m going to count to three. It would be in your best interest to release this old man before something irreversible happens. Now. One, two, two and a half. Two and three-quarters...”
Namho never made it to three. As he was dragged into the undergrowth, Hyuk Mujin watched him go and murmured sadly,
“That’s a shame. I’d grown quite attached to him.”
“What are you talking about? Anyone listening would think we were actually going to kill him.”
“Wait, we aren’t? I thought Great Hero Jeok had already given the order.”
What kind of man did this idiot take him for?
Flustered by Jeok Cheongang’s blazing stare, Hyuk Mujin began to ramble.
“I mean, a few days ago, you cut down all those bandits. Every last one of them.”
“What am I, a butcher? ‘Cut them down’? And they weren’t all bandits. There were river pirates, too.”
“Isn’t that the same thing?”
“They’re entirely different. Though that doesn’t change the fact that every one of them deserved to die.”
“Because they set the fire?”
“Of course... No. Because they harmed innocent people.”
Jeok Cheongang hurriedly corrected himself, but that only confirmed Hyuk Mujin’s suspicion.
It was because they set the fire. That’s why he killed them.
Strangely, of all the sins in the world, Jeok Cheongang considered arson the worst.

Perhaps that made sense. During the Great Faction War, he’d refused even Sword Saint Mae Jonghak’s request to join the orthodox faction. It was the Demonic Cult setting fires that had finally brought him out into the world.
The battle three days ago had been for exactly that reason.
Actually, it’s embarrassing to even call that a battle.
Hyuk Mujin revised his thought.
It hadn’t been a battle. It had been a massacre.
It was that one-sided, and that brutal.
Some three hundred bandits and river pirates had been wiped out in less than an hour.
Afterward, Hyuk Mujin and the others had left, barely listening to the trading company masters from Hubei thank them.
They’d taken the only merchant ship that had somehow survived the flames as payment for saving their lives.
Of course, they hadn’t asked for the other party’s consent. But anyway, that was what happened.
“Oh, come to think of it, those people must have reached Hubei by now, right?”
“Why are you suddenly changing the subject?”
“Those people. The ones we saved.”
“...Is that something a man who barely swung his sword a couple of times should say?”
“But I did swing it.”
The nerve of him.
Jeok Cheongang glared at Hyuk Mujin in disbelief, then shook his head.
From what he’d seen, every last member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion was out of his mind. If he thought too hard about them, the infirmities of old age he’d barely managed to cure might come back.
I suppose I should be grateful there’s at least one normal person among them.
Jeok Cheongang glanced to the side. There stood Ju Hwaran, the only person he could call sane in this madhouse.
The more I see her, the more I like her.
It had been seven days and nights since they’d left the Sichuan Tang Clan as though something were chasing them.
They’d traveled day and night, sticking to remote, rugged terrain to avoid attracting attention. Yet Ju Hwaran hadn’t complained once. She’d stayed cheerful throughout.
As the only woman in the group, she must have faced any number of difficulties.
She’s clearly kept up with her martial arts training, and her character is upright, too. The Escort King has himself one fine granddaughter.
Plenty of young people mistook recklessness for a virtue.
And not just street thugs. Even among the disciples of great sects hailed as young prodigies, fools were everywhere.
They relied on their natural talent instead of working hard, then strutted around trading on their sects’ prestige.
Jeok Cheongang had seen so many of them that he was sick of the type. It only made Ju Hwaran more admirable in his eyes.
Though he couldn’t claim he was entirely without an ulterior motive.

Even the ones swaggering around as Elders and Sect Leaders of the Nine Sects and One Gang now were a whole basket of no-good brats when they were young. Compared to them, Hwaran is more than Jin Taekyung deserves... No. What’s he lacking? He’s handsome, well-built, and there’s no need to mention his martial arts.
A fierce battle raged in his head.
He was already slurping noodle broth before anyone had even thought of offering him a rice cake when a voice startled him out of it.
“Great Hero Jeok, are you all right?”
“Hm? What?”
“You looked troubled, so I was wondering...”
“Ah. Ahem.”
Jeok Cheongang had nearly answered without thinking. He hurriedly cleared his throat instead.
The girl wasn’t merely young enough to be his granddaughter. She was young enough to be his great-granddaughter. He didn’t want her catching him indulging an old man’s foolish notions.
“It’s nothing. I was just thinking about how far we have left to Jiangsu.”
“Oh. At our current pace, we’ll arrive within five days. Even if something delays us, I’d expect it to take about seven days.”
“How can you be so sure?”
“I came through this area on an escort mission two years ago. I brought a map that’s been passed down from my grandfather’s time, too.”
“Ho. Impressive. Very impressive.”
“Thank you. But I’m not worthy of such high praise from you, Great Hero Jeok.”
They said she’d led the Escort Bureau for several years in place of her father, who had been bedridden until recently. Her answer was every bit as crisp as he’d expect.
Ju Hwaran seemed unsure what to do with the sudden praise, and Jeok Cheongang smiled fondly.
“You’ve thought everything through. So capable, unlike that brat.”
“Pardon? What do you mean...?”
“I was just talking to myself. Still, the more I hear you address me that way, the more stiff it sounds. From now on, you can just call me Grandpa—”
Jeok Cheongang glanced at Ju Hwaran and changed course.
Even he had to admit that Grandfather was too soon. Relationships had to begin slowly, one step at a time.
If he got ahead of himself and made Ju Hwaran wary, it would surely affect her relationship with his one and only Disciple, too.
“...No. Call me Old Master.”
“Really?”
The only people who called Jeok Cheongang that were those who had known his predecessors, or the heads of the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families.
Ju Hwaran’s eyes widened at the unexpected offer. Hyuk Mujin, who’d been listening, broke into a broad smile and chimed in.
“Thank you, Old Master. I thought the same thing—that the way I address you is too stiff...”
“Would you rather be hit by this old man’s fist, which is harder than a rock, or keep your mouth shut?”
“You may not call me that. Don’t even dream of it.”
Jeok Cheongang fixed Hyuk Mujin with a fierce glare. He had never been more emphatic.
“Come on. Why are you picking on the poor kid?”
The voice came from far away, yet sounded as clear as if the speaker stood right before them.
But Jeok Cheongang had known who it was before he heard a word.
A faint footstep and the sound of breathing—too subtle for even a Peak master with deep internal energy to hear. That alone had told him.
It wouldn’t have mattered if he weren’t known as the Fire King, or if he weren’t a Supreme Peak master.
A master always knew his one and only disciple.
“Hmph. Look at that slowpoke.”
Jeok Cheongang frowned out of habit, hiding his delight as best he could. He made sure his voice was gruff, too—a far cry from how he’d spoken to Ju Hwaran.
“What took you so long? Why are you only crawling back now? I’ve been waiting half a day because of you.”
“Half a day?”
Hyuk Mujin rushed toward Jin Taekyung shouting, “Captain!” Taekyung kicked him hard in the shin and gave a disbelieving laugh.
“That’s a bit much. Half a day? It’s been half an hour at most. Right?”
The Divine Physician followed behind him, carrying a bundle stuffed with needles and medicinal herbs. He answered with composure.
“I’ll refrain from commenting, Young Hero Jin.”
“Why?”
“Isn’t it obvious? There’s no point answering when there’s no reasoning with him anyway...”
“Wow. So you’re not called the Divine Physician just for your medical skills. You’ve got insight, too.”
“You’re too kind. It’s simply something anyone would learn from experience.”
“...What the fuck is wrong with you two?”
Jeok Cheongang eyed them both. Instead of laying into them, he clicked his tongue.

One way or another, that rude young brat was his one and only Disciple, whom he couldn’t bring himself to hate. And the old man right beside him was a physician who’d agreed to travel a long way to treat that young brat.
What more could he say?
All he could do was pretend nothing was wrong, hide his worry, and ask this:
How are you feeling?
Jin Taekyung heard Jeok Cheongang’s Sound Transmission and gave a quiet laugh as he nodded.

Jeok Cheongang couldn’t tell whether Taekyung truly felt all right or was only pretending. But if what the Divine Physician had said earlier was true, there had to have been at least some improvement.
He’s all right for now. I don’t know when he’ll hit a wall, but... I’ll do everything I can to find a way.
Noticing Jeok Cheongang had fallen silent, Jin Taekyung gave a faint, rueful smile. He stretched his stiff body and spoke.
“How much farther? Three days? Four?”
Ju Hwaran answered as though she’d been waiting for him to ask.
“About three days.”
“Three days... There’s still time before the first of the month, but it’s going to be close.”
Jin Taekyung looked somewhere to the east.
“Let’s cut that down to two days.”

The Escort King has himself one fine granddaughter.
Plenty of young people mistook recklessness for a virtue.
And not just street thugs.
Even among the disciples of great sects hailed as young prodigies, fools were everywhere.
They relied on their natural talent instead of working hard, then strutted around trading on their sects’ prestige.
Jeok Cheongang had seen so many of them that he was sick of the type.
It only made Ju Hwaran more admirable in his eyes.
Though he couldn’t claim he was entirely without an ulterior motive.
Even the ones swaggering around as Elders and Sect Leaders of the Nine Sects and One Gang now were a whole basket of no-good brats when they were young.
Compared to them, Hwaran is more than Jin Taekyung deserves...
No.
What’s he lacking?
He’s handsome, well-built, and there’s no need to mention his martial arts.
A fierce battle raged in his head.
He was already slurping noodle broth before anyone had even thought of offering him a rice cake when a voice startled him out of it.
“Great Hero Jeok, are you all right?”
“Hm?
What?”
“You looked troubled, so I was wondering...”
“Ah.
Ahem.”
Jeok Cheongang had nearly answered without thinking.
He hurriedly cleared his throat instead.
The girl wasn’t merely young enough to be his granddaughter.
She was young enough to be his great-granddaughter.
He didn’t want her catching him indulging an old man’s foolish notions.
“It’s nothing.
I was just thinking about how far we have left to Jiangsu.”
“Oh.
At our current pace, we’ll arrive within five days.
Even if something delays us, I’d expect it to take about seven days.”
“How can you be so sure?”
“I came through this area on an escort mission two years ago.
I brought a map that’s been passed down from my grandfather’s time, too.”
“Ho.
Impressive.
Very impressive.”
“Thank you.
But I’m not worthy of such high praise from you, Great Hero Jeok.”
They said she’d led the Escort Bureau for several years in place of her father, who had been bedridden until recently.
Her answer was every bit as crisp as he’d expect.
Ju Hwaran seemed unsure what to do with the sudden praise, and Jeok Cheongang smiled fondly.
“You’ve thought everything through.
So capable, unlike that brat.”
“Pardon?
What do you mean...?”
“I was just talking to myself.
Still, the more I hear you address me that way, the more stiff it sounds.
From now on, you can just call me Grandpa—”
Jeok Cheongang glanced at Ju Hwaran and changed course.
Even he had to admit that Grandfather was too soon.
Relationships had to begin slowly, one step at a time.
If he got ahead of himself and made Ju Hwaran wary, it would surely affect her relationship with his one and only Disciple, too.
Call me Old Master.”
“Really?”
The only people who called Jeok Cheongang that were those who had known his predecessors, or the heads of the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families.
Ju Hwaran’s eyes widened at the unexpected offer.
Hyuk Mujin, who’d been listening, broke into a broad smile and chimed in.
“Thank you, Old Master.
I thought the same thing—that the way I address you is too stiff...”
“Would you rather be hit by this old man’s fist, which is harder than a rock, or keep your mouth shut?”
“You may not call me that.
Don’t even dream of it.”
Jeok Cheongang fixed Hyuk Mujin with a fierce glare.
He had never been more emphatic.
“Come on.
Why are you picking on the poor kid?”
The voice came from far away, yet sounded as clear as if the speaker stood right before them.
But Jeok Cheongang had known who it was before he heard a word.
A faint footstep and the sound of breathing—too subtle for even a Peak master with deep internal energy to hear.
That alone had told him.
It wouldn’t have mattered if he weren’t known as the Fire King, or if he weren’t a Supreme Peak master.
A master always knew his one and only disciple.
“Hmph.
Look at that slowpoke.”
Jeok Cheongang frowned out of habit, hiding his delight as best he could.
He made sure his voice was gruff, too—a far cry from how he’d spoken to Ju Hwaran.
“What took you so long?
Why are you only crawling back now?
I’ve been waiting half a day because of you.”
“Half a day?”
Hyuk Mujin rushed toward Jin Taekyung shouting, “Captain!” Taekyung kicked him hard in the shin and gave a disbelieving laugh.
“That’s a bit much.
Half a day?
It’s been half an hour at most.
Right?”
The Divine Physician followed behind him, carrying a bundle stuffed with needles and medicinal herbs.
He answered with composure.
“I’ll refrain from commenting, Young Hero Jin.”
“Why?”
“Isn’t it obvious?
There’s no point answering when there’s no reasoning with him anyway...”
“Wow.
So you’re not called the Divine Physician just for your medical skills.
You’ve got insight, too.”
“You’re too kind.
It’s simply something anyone would learn from experience.”
“...What the fuck is wrong with you two?”
Jeok Cheongang eyed them both.
Instead of laying into them, he clicked his tongue.
One way or another, that rude young brat was his one and only Disciple, whom he couldn’t bring himself to hate.
And the old man right beside him was a physician who’d agreed to travel a long way to treat that young brat.
What more could he say?
All he could do was pretend nothing was wrong, hide his worry, and ask this:
How are you feeling?
Jin Taekyung heard Jeok Cheongang’s Sound Transmission and gave a quiet laugh as he nodded.
Jeok Cheongang couldn’t tell whether Taekyung truly felt all right or was only pretending.
But if what the Divine Physician had said earlier was true, there had to have been at least some improvement.
He’s all right for now.
I don’t know when he’ll hit a wall, but...
I’ll do everything I can to find a way.
Noticing Jeok Cheongang had fallen silent, Jin Taekyung gave a faint, rueful smile.
He stretched his stiff body and spoke.
“How much farther?
Three days?
Four?”
Ju Hwaran answered as though she’d been waiting for him to ask.
“About three days.”
“Three days...
There’s still time before the first of the month, but it’s going to be close.”
Jin Taekyung looked somewhere to the east.
“Let’s cut that down to two days.”

chapters.title: Chapter 856
paragraphs: Seven days and nights passed in the blink of an eye after we left the Sichuan Tang Clan.
The scenery and the people around us changed with every step.
But it was too soon to relax.
Despite my boast that we’d cut the remaining time down to two days, reality was less accommodating. The deeper we went to avoid drawing attention, the more time we lost.
“We’ll have to pick up the pace.”
“Even faster than this?”
“Yes. Faster than I thought we’d have to.”
“If we keep up this pace, we can arrive by the first of the month. We’re already pushing ourselves too hard.”
“I know. But do you think the Embroidered Uniform Guard is any different from us?”
“We’re not the only ones on the move. We have to push ourselves and get in their way before they reach their destination.”
Jeok Cheongang already knew I was right, so he said nothing.
Information was important. But perfect information didn’t exist.
If we’d picked up some information, then so had our opponents.
That was true even in the modern world, where information could be relayed by the minute or even the second. How much more so in Murim?
Wherever we went, we were still within the Great Nation’s territory. With eyes and ears everywhere, there had been countless variables from the start. There was only one way to minimize them.
Move as fast as possible. Run ourselves into the ground.
Of course, that meant enduring tremendous hardship.
We were trying to cross half the continent in a little over half a month. It was insane.
“Captain, we’re actually going to die at this rate.”
“Then we should rest.”
“Really?”
“Sure. In Jiangsu.”
“No, I’m not joking. I mean we’re going to die!”
“Mujin. Hyuk Mujin.”
“Yes?”
“If we don’t go, what do you think will happen?”
“If you want to rest, rest. I’m not being sarcastic or hinting at anything. If you think you can’t go on, drop out. It’ll be better for all of us.”
Hyuk Mujin said nothing after that.
No—neither did anyone else.
Instead of complaining, they held their tongues and kept moving.
We crossed rugged mountain ranges and forded winding rivers.
The vast continent’s climate and terrain varied a little from one region to the next.
The midday heat in Hubei was like a blast furnace, while the night wind in Anhui cut like a cold blade.
One day, after wind and rain had swept through, some of the party collapsed from exhaustion.
“Young Hero Jin, I understand how important this matter is, but... we can’t go on any longer.”
The Divine Physician had watched the others wear themselves down. I gave him a short answer.
“We’ll rest for fifteen minutes, then set out again.”
I carried Hyuk Mujin on my back, and Jeok Cheongang carried Ju Hwaran.
Both refused at first, but this time I wouldn’t budge. One look told me they were in no condition to say they were fine, even as a joke.
Of course they’re exhausted. We’ve been moving until their internal energy and stamina were spent.

And though his title was the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang was a man of cold disposition. For some reason, he felt sorry for Ju Hwaran, who was burning up from head to toe despite the Divine Physician’s treatment.
“Is this really necessary? We could—”
“If you’re about to suggest the two of us travel separately, I’ll refuse right now.”
“Why?”
“Because we have to make it through this together. If we can’t endure even this much, we’ll die before long anyway.”
This wasn’t for my sake. It was for all of us.
The war had already begun, and upheaval lurked on every side.
Catastrophes more terrible and vast than anything anyone had ever faced.
To survive the war against Dark Heaven, all of us had to grow stronger—not just me. A blade hammered and tempered countless times won’t break even when it strikes a rock.
Jeok Cheongang was one of the very few people who understood what I meant better than anyone.
He, too, had been remade through bone-deep effort and hardship. In the end, he’d become a peerless blade that cut through countless rocks blocking his way.
“We have to make it through this together...”
Jeok Cheongang slowly repeated my words, then gave a dry chuckle.
“You’ve grown up.”
“I’ve always been taller than you, Old Master. Then and now.”
Jeok Cheongang shook his head at my answer.
“You’re still an arrogant brat. Then and now.”
“Isn’t that part of my charm?”
“But no matter how I look at it, this is too much. You heartless little bastard.”
“Miss Ju wanted it. I respected her wishes. If she were in enough pain to actually die, I’d have stopped her myself.”
“Cut the crap. Anyway, your idea might be right, but I can be sure of one thing.”
“Yes? What?”
“This old man guarantees you’ll never find a partner as long as you live.”
“Where did that come from?”
“Enough. If you have the energy to flap your gums, take one more step.”
Jeok Cheongang dealt that brutal blow out of nowhere and darted away like the wind. As I watched him go, I noticed the world growing brighter and raised my head.
This is...
I gathered my internal energy and pushed off the ground. Stepping onto a branch of the nearest great tree, I sprang up above it. At last, I saw the light spreading in the distance.
It was the dawn light.
The eleventh dawn I’d seen since we’d left the Sichuan Tang Clan.
But what made the light of this new morning so welcome was something coming into view beyond the grass and streams that surrounded us.
“Ah.”
A faint exclamation rang in my ears.
Hyuk Mujin, still on my back, asked in a half-dead voice, “C-Captain. Where are we? What’s that?”
I laughed out loud.
Then I answered loudly enough for everyone below the tree to hear.
“Jiangsu.”
Empires are majestic and great.
But they can never last forever.
Not so long ago, by the continent’s standards, the empire founded by the nomads of the grasslands had been no different.
Each was a fine warrior and herdsman. They worshiped heaven and earth and were close companions to hawks and horses, but they were not good rulers.
A little over a hundred years.
That was all it took for the vast empire founded by the invaders from the grasslands to fall.

There had been a great conqueror who was both hero and devil, destined to remain a legend to the very end. There had also been a wise ruler who strengthened the empire from within and cared for his subjects and people.
But at the end of that age, all that remained were terrible famine, corruption, and countless red flags fluttering in the wind.
“You who hunger, rise up!”
An age of war began. People with blood-red flags and headscarves rose like wildfire on every side and swept across the continent.
The world called them the Red Turbans—bandits. They wanted to be called the Red Turban Army, but the world’s judgment was closer to the truth.
They were bandits.
Bandits who stole grain and valuables to fill their empty stomachs.
Bandits who wanted to steal this nation’s mountains and rivers, too.
“How can the blood of kings, nobles, generals, and ministers be any different from anyone else’s?”
They might have been shabby on the outside, but did that mean there was nothing great within them?
Steal a handful of millet and you’re a bandit. Steal a continent and you become the Son of Heaven.
Just as one hero had done at the end of that long age of war, when he finally seized all under heaven.
“My king, please ascend the imperial throne!”
And so a new heaven opened.
Born the son of a poor farmer, he had wandered the land as a mendicant monk. Now he held all under heaven in his hands and stood above everyone, with countless officials and commoners beneath him.
But even after many years had passed and one of his children inherited the throne, nothing changed.
At least, not for one boy living in Jiangsu.
“Hey, you beggar brat!”
Beggar brat.
It was one of the things he’d heard most often in his life. Even now, decades later, that moment was etched clearly into his mind.
It appeared without fail whenever he had a nightmare like this one.
Hong Jin woke with a start and blinked. Then he respectfully bowed his head to the boy who had been watching him in silence.
“I dared to dream in Your Highness’s presence. Please forgive your unfaithful servant.”
The boy, Prince Shangshan Zhu Bao, replied.
“Forgive you? Don’t be absurd.”
His composure and dignified voice were hard to believe in someone not yet in his midteens.
The young prince, much taller and more solidly built than most boys his age, continued speaking to his servant.
“If anyone should apologize, it’s me, not you. I’ve put a loyal subject through so much hardship.”
“Hardship? I beg Your Highness to take back those words.”
“No. This is all because of my own shortcomings.”
“Your Highness...”
“But set aside your worries. What you fear will never happen.”
Hong Jin answered by bringing his hands together and bowing deeply.
But as he stared at the floor of the slowly moving carriage, his gaze held both pride in the young prince and a hint of bitterness.
I earnestly pray it will be so as well, Your Highness... But your elder brother will not see it that way.
Hong Jin forced down the voice rising deep in his heart.
His master, Prince Shangshan, had been an intelligent, mature boy from a young age. But he was far too young to understand the cruelty of the world.
Even now, surrounded by the Embroidered Uniform Guard and bound for the Imperial Capital as though he were a prisoner under escort, he still had unwavering faith in his only blood relative.
Hong Jin did not.
You already have all under heaven. What more could you possibly want, Emperor?
With that question, which would reach no one, Hong Jin closed his eyes.
In the pitch-darkness, memories surfaced. Sounds returned.
The days when the blood never dried. The days of purges, when hundreds died with their limbs torn from their bodies and thousands were beheaded, their heads put on display.
And the late Emperor’s final words.
“Bao. I entrust that child to you.”
Thump.
A small jolt ran through the carriage. Hong Jin opened his eyes, turned, and saw someone’s profile through a gap in the window.
“What’s going on?”
At Hong Jin’s low question, the man beside the carriage replied. He wore shabby martial robes that hardly suited the name Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“None of your business.”
His voice was blunt, devoid of emotion. But Hong Jin sensed a cold blade beneath it.
A feeling both strange and familiar.
Hong Jin had once served as the late Emperor’s hands and feet, just as the Embroidered Uniform Guard did now. The man’s voice brought back a sensation he hadn’t felt in over a decade.
Along with a hint of puzzlement.
Why have we stopped?
This covert procession had already entered Jiangsu, and the Embroidered Uniform Guard had no reason to stop. They were people who would gladly give their lives to carry out the Emperor’s orders.
Something’s going on.
Hong Jin quietly sharpened his senses. He might not have mastered martial arts to the point of founding his own school, but he had learned them.
Fortunately, the guards seemed to decide the matter didn’t warrant Sound Transmission. Their conversation drifted through the gap in the window.
“According to the scouts, there’s an unidentified corpse about three hundred zhang ahead...”
“They didn’t get close in case it was a trap, but they couldn’t see any obvious wounds...”
“It could be an attempt to split up our forces. We’ll keep moving. Stay close to the carriage.”
The murmuring conversation abruptly stopped. After a brief pause, the carriage started moving again.
Clip-clop. Clip-clop.
As he listened to the quiet sound of hooves, Hong Jin thought,
An unidentified corpse.
It wasn’t so strange. The continent was vast, and people wandered its roads begging for food. Even Jiangsu, so close to the Imperial Capital, was no exception.
Why did one man’s name suddenly come to mind at this very moment?
And why did an inexplicable hope well up in one corner of his heart?
Could it be...
Hong Jin had just lifted his head when—
“Didn’t you say it was a corpse...?”
One of the Embroidered Uniform Guard had muttered the words. Then a voice Hong Jin recognized reached his ears.
“Captain. I swear I wasn’t dozing off. I was just lying down for a second... Huh? Who are you?”
At that moment, Hong Jin burst out laughing, briefly forgetting that the young prince was right in front of him.

Stay close to the carriage.”
The murmuring conversation abruptly stopped.
After a brief pause, the carriage started moving again.
Clip-clop.
Clip-clop.
As he listened to the quiet sound of hooves, Hong Jin thought,
An unidentified corpse.
It wasn’t so strange.
The continent was vast, and people wandered its roads begging for food.
Even Jiangsu, so close to the Imperial Capital, was no exception.
Why did one man’s name suddenly come to mind at this very moment?
And why did an inexplicable hope well up in one corner of his heart?
Could it be...
Hong Jin had just lifted his head when—
“Didn’t you say it was a corpse...?”
One of the Embroidered Uniform Guard had muttered the words.
Then a voice Hong Jin recognized reached his ears.
“Captain.
I swear I wasn’t dozing off.
I was just lying down for a second...
Huh?
Who are you?”
At that moment, Hong Jin burst out laughing, briefly forgetting that the young prince was right in front of him.

chapters.title: Chapter 857
paragraphs: “What? Where’d everyone go? Hey, mister. Have you seen anyone around here?”
His hair was matted with grease, and his face was streaked with grime.
As the young man got to his feet and babbled, the man he’d called “mister” spoke.
“What happened? He doesn’t look dead to me.”
“I-I’m sorry. He was sleeping so soundly he looked dead, and I mistook him for—”
“That’s enough. We’ll discuss it when we return to the palace.”
The Embroidered Uniform Guard martial artist who had reported the scouts’ findings went rigid.
He knew what kind of man his superior was. He’d served under him for nearly three years. He also knew how seriously the man took this mission.
If he was lucky, he’d be demoted. If things went badly, he could be stripped of his position altogether.
Damn it.
He bit down on his lip and struggled to suppress his anger. He couldn’t deny that he felt wronged, but a mistake was still a mistake.
He couldn’t put spilled water back where it came from, but he could at least wipe it up.
No—he had to. If only to lessen the punishment coming his way.
“...I’ll take care of it.”
He spoke in a subdued voice and stepped toward the young man, who still looked half asleep.
The fellow was some beggar who could’ve wandered in from anywhere. If he resisted, one stroke of the sword would be enough.
At least, that was what the martial artist thought.
“What are you doing?”
Thud.
At his superior’s sudden call, he stopped dead. The man looked down at him with calm, cold eyes, and he stammered out a reply.
“I—it can’t be left like this, so I thought I’d handle it myself...”
“Handle it?”
“Y-Yes.”
“How?”
Pardon?
“I asked how you intend to handle it.”
“Well... given the situation, shouldn’t we use force if necessary to eliminate the threat?”
The man was silent for a moment.
“How many years have you served?”
“I’ve served you for almost three years, Commander Jeong. And...”
The martial artist hesitated, watching his superior’s expression, then added, “As my father advised me, I believe I’ve always done my best to follow your orders.”
There was a little unease in his voice, and far more resentment.
His superior had barely given him a second look in nearly three years. Worse, he treated him as though being the son of a prestigious family meant nothing.
How much did my family spend to get me into the Embroidered Uniform Guard?
Gold, silver, and influence could reach anywhere—even the Embroidered Uniform Guard, which answered directly to the Emperor.
A rigorous screening meant that even a fortune could buy him no more than a low-ranking position. Still, plenty of people would have given anything to get that far.
He had no intention of backing down. Mentioning his father had been a warning: a reminder to his difficult, strict superior of the family standing behind him.
Which made the man’s next words all the harder to believe.
“Three years. That’s long enough.”
Pardon?
“Hand over your badge right now and go where you belong. This will conclude your punishment for the mistake you made earlier.”
“What? Do you still have something to say?”
The martial artist stared at him, eyes wide, then burst out, “What? How can you do something so outrageous? Have you forgotten who I am—”
“I remember perfectly. Otherwise, I wouldn’t have kept you under me for three years.”
The man cut him off and continued in the same calm voice.
“But what people remember isn’t you. It’s the prestige of the family behind you. If you don’t want to make the same mistake again, take that to heart.”
“Are you done?”
“No, but there’s no point saying the rest. Especially to someone who can’t even tell whom he’s dealing with.”
“What the hell are you—”
He was about to shout when a voice reached his ear.
“Excuse me. Sorry to interrupt, but could I have some water first? I’ve been thirsty for a while.”
The voice hadn’t come from a distance.
It was right behind him—close enough for him to catch the sweetish scent on the speaker’s breath.
How did he—?!
Every hair on his body stood on end. He spun around like lightning and drew the sword at his waist.
Shing—whoosh!
The treasured sword passed down through his family for generations flashed with five-colored light as it split the figure behind him clean in half.
Or so he thought.
Just as the blade was about to bite into the top of the young man’s head, two hands filthy with streaming grime moved in a flash.
Clang!
The young man brought his palms together with a deafening crash. A gasp escaped the martial artist.
“Empty-Hand Seizes the Blade...?”
It was a technique a master might show someone a level or two beneath him.
The martial artist had reached the Supreme First Rate realm thanks to his family’s unstinting support. He understood at once what it meant and stared in shock at the man he’d taken for a mere beggar.
“A Peak master!”
At that horrified cry, the mysterious Peak master answered, “What the fuck are you talking about? I get shit all the time for being the guy who can’t even use Sword Energy.”
“Y-You! Who are you? State your identity!”
“Fuck off. Give me water, not a sword.”
Whoosh—thud!
It happened in an instant.

The young man swept aside the sword caught between his palms and drove his hard knee into the martial artist’s face. As the man crumpled like a rotten log, the young man found a small flask in his robes and drank it down in one go.
Gulp, gulp.
“Ahhh. Now I feel alive.”
He looked as though he hadn’t had a drop of water in days.
Commander Jeong watched him empty the flask and shake it for the last drops before speaking.
“I suspected as much when I first saw you. You’re quite skilled.”
The young man stared into the empty flask as though liquor might appear if he waited long enough. Then he asked, “Do you mean that?”
“Of course. You don’t seem to have reached the level of injuring others with Sword Energy, but the movement you just showed was extremely efficient and impressive.”
“Thanks. Hearing that from someone way more skilled than me almost brings a tear to my eye. Though I could do without you talking down to me.”
“You misunderstand. I wasn’t mocking you.”
“I know. I didn’t misunderstand. I really do feel like I’m about to cry.”

“I’ve been through so much fucking shit, taken every insult anyone could throw at me. I train my ass off, and all I ever hear is, ‘Why can’t you use Sword Energy?’ and ‘How can you call yourself a proper person if you can’t even do that?’ And now they’ve gone and left me on the side of the road, too... Ahem. Hic!”
Commander Jeong fell silent.
The young man’s complaints had poured out as though he’d been waiting for the chance, and now tears were streaming down his face. Everyone there had the same question.
What the hell is that guy?
He looked exactly like a beggar. Apparently, he was a lunatic.
The problem was that the lunatic was skilled. He was only Supreme First Rate, yet he moved like a Peak master.
And they were in the middle of an operation.
The Embroidered Uniform Guard martial artists lined up behind Commander Jeong exchanged bewildered looks.
What are we supposed to do in a situation like this?
I don’t know. Captain Hong might know.
I don’t know, either.
How can you not know, Captain Hong? You’re our Captain.
Does a Captain have to be some kind of god? Still, Senior Officer Gal should know. He’s been around much longer than I have.
No. I don’t know, either...
Pardon?
Their gazes wandered, and their mouths went dry.
When had the famed Embroidered Uniform Guard ever dealt with anything like this? The lunatic had sat down in the road and was sobbing at the top of his lungs. None of them knew what to do with him.
None of them except one.
Clip-clop. Clip-clop.
Commander Jeong slowly rode forward and looked down at the young man with his usual calm gaze.
“Are you done crying?”
The young man answered in a tear-choked voice.
“I’ve still got a little left.”
“That doesn’t matter. You’re delaying us. Move aside.”
“Mm.”
The young man sniffled.
“That might be difficult.”
“Why?”
“Moving aside would be easy enough, but the person I serve would be furious.”
“I thought you said you’d been abandoned.”
“Sometimes I get left behind when I’m with that person. Anyway, I don’t know why I ended up here, but they’ll be back soon.”
Brush, brush.
The young man stood and dusted off his backside.
“Believe it or not, I’m his right-hand man. Though I might just be his little toe.”
“I see.”
Commander Jeong gave a slight nod.
“Do you have an identity tag?”
“An identity tag? Is that something you boil in soup?”
“So you’re a rogue of the martial world. You treat the strict laws established by the Son of Heaven as nonsense.”
“Something like that. Why ask all of a sudden?”
“It’s merely a check. I can’t harm a citizen of the Great Nation who carries an identity tag because I judged him wrongly.”
“Hm. You talk like you belong to the authorities.”
“Something like that, but not quite.”
“That’s vague. Care to give me an example?”
“You don’t need to know.”
“Oh.”
At the calm, cold answer, the young man shrugged and dropped something he’d been holding.
Tap.
A faint sound, and a copper badge flashed as it caught the light. Three characters were engraved on its dirt-streaked surface.
Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“Whoops. Dropped it by accident. I was going to keep it as a souvenir.”
His voice was exaggerated, but his gaze, fixed on Commander Jeong, had settled into a deep stillness.
“I was only looking for the flask, but this weird thing came out with it.”
“You’ve got sticky fingers for a rogue of the martial world.”
“Let’s call it self-defense. If it had been the person I serve, this wouldn’t have ended with just that.”
Commander Jeong raised a hand instead of answering.
The Embroidered Uniform Guard drew their weapons and surrounded the young man in a wave of steel.
“Before I kill you, I’ll ask one thing.”
“If you have time, ask as many as you like. I’d like to live a little longer, if possible.”
Something flickered in Commander Jeong’s eyes.
This unexpected encounter was as good as over. At his signal, the young man would die in an instant, and they would continue on their way as though nothing had happened.
And yet...
He has no intention of backing down.
The young man feared death, but he would not retreat. Commander Jeong saw the spirit of a martial artist in him.
“What is your name?”
“Hyuk Mujin.”
Commander Jeong nodded to Hyuk Mujin.
“Who’s behind this?”
None of this was a coincidence.
Someone whose identity they didn’t know had been waiting for them from the start. They had surely placed people at every chokepoint the procession had to pass through.
Commander Jeong needed to learn who it was. The answer came from somewhere he never expected.
“Being called the one behind it sounds a little grand, but now that I hear it, I kind of like it. Makes me feel like a Constellation.”
There had been no sound. No trace of a presence.
Yet the shadow of a young man had appeared among them, stretching down from a tree above.
“We finally meet. How’ve you been?”
“Do you... know me?”
At Commander Jeong’s stiff question, the young man laughed.
“How the fuck would I know you, you son of a bitch?”

chapters.title: Chapter 858
paragraphs: Times like this, I really missed the System.
If it weren’t for that damn update, a holographic window would’ve appeared by now with its signature clear chime.
Ding.
System Quest Saving Prince Shangshan successfully completed! Quest completion rewards have been granted! You have gained a large amount of EXP!
Something like that.
But unlike the scene I’d just imagined, reality was quiet. The cold killing intent pouring from dozens of Embroidered Uniform Guard members pricked my entire body like needles.
“That’s enough. Rein it in and put it away. Keep this up and you’ll put me in a bad mood.”
I tossed out a few words, then pushed off a branch and dropped toward the ground.
No—I walked down through empty air, stepping on it as if it were a staircase.
“Stepping on Empty Air...!”
Someone’s gasp reached my ears. I could almost feel the Embroidered Uniform Guard’s blade-sharp aura waver.
It burns through internal energy like crazy, but nothing beats it for this.
No matter how hostile someone was, after seeing something like that, they wouldn’t dare bare their teeth at me.
Stepping on Empty Air was a technique exclusive to Supreme Peak masters.
Tap.
I landed lightly on the ground. Waiting for me there was a beast howling miserably.
“Waaah, Captain!”
“Stop. Don’t come over here. Shut up.”
“Where have you been all this time?! I was so scared!”
I’d gone to all that trouble to set the mood, and this bastard—
I let out a deep sigh and pushed Hyuk Mujin away as he kept trying to hug me.
“Ah, quit whining. I didn’t leave you behind.”
“What?”
“I just took a nap up there. I was tired.”
We’d been on a forced march for over ten days.
Even with three jiazi of internal energy and a body beyond human limits, I couldn’t beat the need for sleep. The fact that I’d held out this long was practically a miracle.
Scouting and standing night watch in case something happened. Checking on the others and looking after them. And on top of that, the mental strain.
If the Divine Physician hadn’t tried to stop me and Jeok Cheongang hadn’t helped, I might have collapsed before we ever reached Jiangsu.
I wasn’t exactly in good shape, either. I’d been sleeping for half a shichen every three days.
After going through all that hell, it was only natural that sleep hit me the moment we reached our destination and I was sure we’d arrived ahead of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“...So you slept? In a tree?”
“Yeah. If I slept on the road, my mouth would get crooked. And I might get attacked while I was out cold.”
“What about me?”
“You? What about you?”
“I’m asking why you threw me down in the middle of the road while you went somewhere safe to sleep by yourself.”
“Someone had to keep watch on the road. And I didn’t throw you.”
“Then what did you do?”
“I set you down. Carefully.”
I’d actually more or less tossed him down. I was that tired.
Hyuk Mujin’s mouth fell open at my slightly dishonest answer.
“So it doesn’t matter if my mouth goes crooked?”
“You’re the kind of man who speaks the truth even with a crooked mouth. That’s Hyuk Mujin.”
“You said we could be attacked!”
“And I’d wake up when I heard it. Like I did just now.”
“I almost died! If you’d woken up moments later, I’d have been a dead man!”
“But I woke up moments earlier. You’re alive.”
“My God. Captain, are you even human?”
I wasn’t sure what gave the bastard who’d been snoring on my back the right to say that, but I decided to show him a little mercy and let it slide.
We’d been pushing ourselves hard, and besides...
The way he’d looked a little while ago had been pretty impressive.
“Good job.”
At my sudden praise, Hyuk Mujin furrowed his brow.
“What?”
“I said you did a good job. Holding on even in a situation like that.”
“But don’t do that again. If you think you can’t win, take a step back and think of another way.”
I patted Hyuk Mujin on the shoulder, then slowly turned around and added,
“Right, Your Excellency from the Embroidered Uniform Guard?”
Our eyes met in midair.
His eyes were impassive, showing no particular emotion. Unlike the others, the man at the head of the procession hadn’t so much as blinked at my appearance. He spoke.
“You know that, and yet you blocked our way. Reckless, to say the least.”
“Mister, watch your mouth. I’ve still got plenty of hair.”
“I don’t know what nonsense you’re talking about, but you are standing against the Embroidered Uniform Guard, who are carrying out the Emperor’s command. Do you understand that?”
“Of course I do.”
“I see. So you admit to treason.”
Treason?
Could it really be called that?
After a moment’s thought, I decided I ought to take back what I’d said.
“Uh. Then I retract what I said earlier.”
“I was walking along, got tired, and took a nap. And then, by coincidence, you happened to pass by. How’s that?”
Hyuk Mujin, who’d been looking at me as though my earlier praise had touched him a little, answered quickly.
“Sounds fine to me.”
“Right?”
“Yes. It’s convincing. Plenty of people sleep rough while traveling.”
“You know what you’re talking about. What can they do if it was a coincidence?”
“Exactly. Jiangsu isn’t their land.”
“Wait. Isn’t it, though? Jiangsu or anywhere else, it’s all part of the Great Nation.”
“Huh. Does it work like that?”
“Doesn’t it? That’s what I understand.”
“Captain, since when do you know things like that?”
“You little shit.”
“Sorry. Anyway, I’ll remember that and ask Old Man Nam later... Hey, where is everybody?”
Just as I was about to answer, the man spoke first.
“What is the meaning of this?”
“Oh, sorry. We got sidetracked for a second. Anyway, now that you mention it, Jiangsu belongs to you lot too, right?”
“All the mountains and rivers under heaven are ruled by His Imperial Majesty, whose authority is—no, why am I even answering this?”
“It’s nice to help each other out.”
“Enough!”
Our frantic conversation seemed to have rattled him.
I narrowed my eyes at the man, whose aura had grown as cold as frost.

“You there, Your Excellency from the Embroidered Uniform Guard. You said you were Thousand Captain Jeong, right? Why be so stiff about this? Frankly, neither of us stands to gain anything by fighting here.”
Shing.
A cold blade appeared in place of an answer. Thousand Captain Jeong drew the enormous saber from his back and spoke in a rigid voice.
“It makes no difference who you are. The Embroidered Uniform Guard obeys His Imperial Majesty. If you oppose his command and stand in our way, you will die.”
Fwoooooosh.
An invisible force spread out from him. I licked my dry lips as I felt his aura—pure and heavy.
Well, look at that...
I’d suspected it from the moment I first saw him, but the man called Thousand Captain Jeong was a formidable master.
No—by ordinary standards, even “formidable” was an understatement. His skill was enough to shatter a prejudice I’d held deep inside.
He doesn’t seem to have crossed the Supreme Peak threshold yet, but he’s at least at the very top of Peak.
The authorities and Murim were always close and yet far apart.
Murim was one forest within the Great Nation’s borders, but that forest was full of beasts like dragons and tigers.
And yet, even among those serving the authorities, I’d rarely seen a proper master.
Common soldiers were Third Rate or Second Rate, while martial officers were First Rate at best. Peak masters were rare among those in the military.
And most of those had belonged to Murim before.

The former Captain of the Guards to the City Lord of Sichuan Province had been a famous wandering martial artist, practically a personal bodyguard. Li Feng, Assistant Military Commissioner of Shanxi Province, was a former lay disciple of Huashan who’d joined the military after passing the military examination.
But...
Where’d a master of his caliber come from?
My experience might not have been all that broad, but as a Supreme Peak master, I could get a rough measure of someone’s ability at a glance.
And Thousand Captain Jeong bore not the slightest trace of a Murim martial artist. From head to toe, he looked every inch a general.
Even his internal energy is pure.
What was more surprising was that the other Embroidered Uniform Guard members were no exception.
They ranged from young men who looked to be in their twenties to middle-aged men around forty. They varied in skill, but it wasn’t hard to tell that most of them were Peak masters.
Dozens of Peak masters...
A force to match a mid-sized sect—or surpass one.
Whether they lived up to their reputation as the Son of Heaven’s hands and feet, or had been trained by someone other than the Son of Heaven, was a question for later.
I had no intention of letting this standoff continue when neither side stood to gain anything.
“Impressive aura, but you’d better put away those ugly weapons before someone gets hurt.”
The instant I stepped forward after warning them—
Whoosh!
A shaft of light shot straight at my face with a powerful crack of air. I caught it as gently as if I were cradling it, then sent it flying back the way it had come.
Thud! Boom!
Instead of a final scream, a tremor rolled through the ground.
The archer, who’d leapt from the saddle of his fallen steed, stared at me in disbelief. An arrow was lodged in the center of the horse’s forehead.
“I told you to put away what you were holding.”
“You’re the reason it died, you animal-abusing bastard.”
Hyuk Mujin, scratching his grime-covered body as if he’d known this was coming, said, “Why is it his fault? You’re the one who killed it, Captain.”
“If we’re getting technical, sure. But Mujin.”
“Yes?”
“I can kill you too.”
“I’m sorry. I spoke out of turn.”
“All right, got it.”
It was a peaceful conversation, as usual. But the tension around us had already grown so taut it felt ready to burst.
Snort. Snort.
Dozens of horses breathed heavily. The hands gripping their reins with all their strength had gone white, and the aura pouring from their riders wavered but didn’t subside.
At their head stood Thousand Captain Jeong.
“You’re crossing a river that should never be crossed.”
“I haven’t crossed it yet. But setting that aside, you all seem pretty confident. No matter how good you are, you won’t come out of a fight with me looking pretty.”

I wasn’t the one who gave that answer.

Step.
Beneath my lowered gaze, someone’s foot came into view—much larger than it had been in the last glimpse I remembered.
With it came a voice that had grown more mature, too. No longer the voice of a little child.
“It’s been a long time, Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
Prince Shangshan Zhu Bao.
The bloodline of a dragon, grown so much taller, helped me to my feet.

This is...
A secret letter.
The moment that secretive word pierced my mind, Prince Shangshan leaned close to my ear and whispered,
“Please give me your autograph.”
No, Your Highness. What the fuck.

sentences.text: Times like this, I really missed the System.
If it weren’t for that damn update, a holographic window would’ve appeared by now with its signature clear chime.
Ding.
System Quest Saving Prince Shangshan successfully completed!
Quest completion rewards have been granted!
You have gained a large amount of EXP!
Something like that.
But unlike the scene I’d just imagined, reality was quiet.
The cold killing intent pouring from dozens of Embroidered Uniform Guard members pricked my entire body like needles.
“That’s enough.
Rein it in and put it away.
Keep this up and you’ll put me in a bad mood.”
I tossed out a few words, then pushed off a branch and dropped toward the ground.
No—I walked down through empty air, stepping on it as if it were a staircase.
“Stepping on Empty Air...!”
Someone’s gasp reached my ears.
I could almost feel the Embroidered Uniform Guard’s blade-sharp aura waver.
It burns through internal energy like crazy, but nothing beats it for this.
No matter how hostile someone was, after seeing something like that, they wouldn’t dare bare their teeth at me.
Stepping on Empty Air was a technique exclusive to Supreme Peak masters.
Tap.
I landed lightly on the ground.
Waiting for me there was a beast howling miserably.
“Waaah, Captain!”
“Stop.
Don’t come over here.
Shut up.”
“Where have you been all this time?!
I was so scared!”
I’d gone to all that trouble to set the mood, and this bastard—
I let out a deep sigh and pushed Hyuk Mujin away as he kept trying to hug me.
“Ah, quit whining.
I didn’t leave you behind.”
“What?”
“I just took a nap up there.
I was tired.”
We’d been on a forced march for over ten days.
Even with three jiazi of internal energy and a body beyond human limits, I couldn’t beat the need for sleep.
The fact that I’d held out this long was practically a miracle.
Scouting and standing night watch in case something happened.
Checking on the others and looking after them.
And on top of that, the mental strain.
If the Divine Physician hadn’t tried to stop me and Jeok Cheongang hadn’t helped, I might have collapsed before we ever reached Jiangsu.
I wasn’t exactly in good shape, either.
I’d been sleeping for half a shichen every three days.
After going through all that hell, it was only natural that sleep hit me the moment we reached our destination and I was sure we’d arrived ahead of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“...So you slept?
In a tree?”
“Yeah.
If I slept on the road, my mouth would get crooked.
And I might get attacked while I was out cold.”
“What about me?”
“You?
What about you?”
“I’m asking why you threw me down in the middle of the road while you went somewhere safe to sleep by yourself.”
“Someone had to keep watch on the road.
And I didn’t throw you.”
“Then what did you do?”
“I set you down.
Carefully.”
I’d actually more or less tossed him down.
I was that tired.
Hyuk Mujin’s mouth fell open at my slightly dishonest answer.
“So it doesn’t matter if my mouth goes crooked?”
“You’re the kind of man who speaks the truth even with a crooked mouth.
That’s Hyuk Mujin.”
“You said we could be attacked!”
“And I’d wake up when I heard it.
Like I did just now.”
“I almost died!
If you’d woken up moments later, I’d have been a dead man!”
“But I woke up moments earlier.
You’re alive.”
“My God.
Captain, are you even human?”
I wasn’t sure what gave the bastard who’d been snoring on my back the right to say that, but I decided to show him a little mercy and let it slide.
We’d been pushing ourselves hard, and besides...
The way he’d looked a little while ago had been pretty impressive.
“Good job.”
At my sudden praise, Hyuk Mujin furrowed his brow.
“What?”
“I said you did a good job.
Holding on even in a situation like that.”
“But don’t do that again.
If you think you can’t win, take a step back and think of another way.”
I patted Hyuk Mujin on the shoulder, then slowly turned around and added,
“Right, Your Excellency from the Embroidered Uniform Guard?”
Our eyes met in midair.
His eyes were impassive, showing no particular emotion.
Unlike the others, the man at the head of the procession hadn’t so much as blinked at my appearance.
He spoke.
“You know that, and yet you blocked our way.
Reckless, to say the least.”
“Mister, watch your mouth.
I’ve still got plenty of hair.”
“I don’t know what nonsense you’re talking about, but you are standing against the Embroidered Uniform Guard, who are carrying out the Emperor’s command.
Do you understand that?”
“Of course I do.”
“I see.
So you admit to treason.”
Treason?
Could it really be called that?
After a moment’s thought, I decided I ought to take back what I’d said.
“Uh.
Then I retract what I said earlier.”
“I was walking along, got tired, and took a nap.
And then, by coincidence, you happened to pass by.
How’s that?”
Hyuk Mujin, who’d been looking at me as though my earlier praise had touched him a little, answered quickly.
“Sounds fine to me.”
“Right?”
“Yes.
It’s convincing.
Plenty of people sleep rough while traveling.”
“You know what you’re talking about.
What can they do if it was a coincidence?”
“Exactly.
Jiangsu isn’t their land.”
“Wait.
Isn’t it, though?
Jiangsu or anywhere else, it’s all part of the Great Nation.”
“Huh.
Does it work like that?”
“Doesn’t it?
That’s what I understand.”
“Captain, since when do you know things like that?”
“You little shit.”

Anyway, I’ll remember that and ask Old Man Nam later...
Hey, where is everybody?”
