paragraphs: A fire rising from a dense bed of reeds was not easily stopped, even by fierce wind and rain.
Neither were the rumors that had suddenly begun sweeping through the Imperial Capital.
“Have you heard? His Highness, Prince Shangshan, is in the imperial palace right now...”
“They say the Emperor finally has an heir.”
“I heard they’ll hold a great banquet soon. That must be why His Highness, Prince Shangshan, returned after more than ten years.”
“But an heir? Does that mean Her Majesty the Empress is pregnant?”
“Who knows for sure? Jang next door told me it’s a new concubine the Emperor recently took...”
“Jang next door? The butcher?”
“That’s the one. You know him too?”
“Of course. That man knows how to slaughter livestock. But where on earth did he hear it?”
“From someone... what was his name? Oh, right. Wu, who runs the shop across the street.”
“Then who did Wu hear it from?”
“Li the woodcutter.”
Even the Embroidered Uniform Guard, said to be capable of catching a bird in flight and dragging it off to prison, could scarcely silence so many mouths.
The rumors spread so quickly that the imperial palace’s towering walls might as well not have been there. In a single night, the Embroidered Uniform Guard dragged away hundreds of people.
“If you want to live, tell us everything. Which bastard has been spreading this nonsense?”
“Eek! I’ll tell you! I’ll tell you everything!”
Everyone knew what happened when the Embroidered Uniform Guard took someone away. You were as good as dead. Even the highest officials could be cut down like weeds.

The prisoners knew that reputation well. Before the guards even brought out the instruments of torture, they told them everything they knew. Yet for all the ease of the interrogations, the Guard learned nothing useful.
“What did they say?”
“All of them say the same thing. They heard it from ordinary neighbors with no ties to the imperial palace, street vendors, or strangers they met at inns and pleasure houses.”
“Damn it.”

Countless names had come up during the interrogations, but every lead was an empty shell. The people the prisoners named were utterly ordinary, and the source of the rumors spreading across the capital remained a mystery.
It was like being ordered to find a vein of gold in an exhausted mine.
But they were the Embroidered Uniform Guard. In this vast realm, they owed absolute loyalty to one person alone: the Emperor. Whatever the circumstances, they had to produce results.
“Begin the interrogation in earnest.”
“Pardon?”
“Use whatever methods you need. Find the culprits as quickly as possible.”
“B-but those people...”
“They’ve thrown the Great Nation into turmoil with baseless rumors and sullied His Majesty’s name. Are they subjects of this country, or traitors?”
The officers fell silent at their superior’s command. They knew the prisoners trembling in their cells were nothing more than ignorant commoners.
Just as no storeroom was so clean that shaking it wouldn’t stir up dust, countless high officials had passed through the Guard’s prison, each with a crime or two to their name, great or small.
But these people were ordinary subjects. When the wind blew, they bent; when it rained, they got wet.
And now the officers were to torture them. They had to send their superiors results, even if it meant killing those people horribly or leaving them half-crippled.
The officers took pride in punishing corrupt and disloyal people in power to set the Great Nation in order. This left them uneasy.
But...
“Answer me!”
At their superior’s renewed roar, they realized they had nowhere left to retreat. Military discipline was strict, especially in an institution as powerful as the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“We obey the Thousand Captain’s orders.”
They answered reluctantly and were about to return to the cells when a quiet voice stopped them.
“Everyone, halt.”
A middle-aged man appeared and swept his gaze over them. His golden armor was spotless, his bearing imposing. The Thousand Captain recognized him at once, his eyes widening.
“Thousand Captain Jeong?”
Jeong Hogun gave a curt nod.
“It’s been a while, Thousand Captain Hong. How are the interrogations of last night’s prisoners going?”
“We’ll have proper results soon. But what do you mean, halt?”
“Just what I said. Stop. There’s nothing more to uncover.”
The Thousand Captain, who had been roaring at his subordinates moments ago, frowned at Jeong Hogun’s firm reply.
“You’re interfering more than usual today. Are you planning to overstep your authority?”
“Of course not.”
“Then what is this? No matter how much the Guard Commander favors you, this is clearly—”
“An imperial order.”
“What?”

“I said it’s an imperial order. The moment you receive it, you are to stop interrogating or torturing the prisoners brought in last night and release every one of them within half an hour. His Majesty commands it.”
“What are you all waiting for? Obey the imperial order.”
Jeong Hogun’s sudden arrival settled the matter in an instant.

The Embroidered Uniform Guard officers knelt and formally received the imperial command, then streamed away like the tide to release the hundreds of prisoners. Their superior, the Thousand Captain, asked Jeong Hogun with a stony expression,
“What’s going on? And what about our report?”
“Forget the whole matter. That is His Majesty’s will.”
Jeong Hogun’s voice was as flat and unreadable as ever.
“I’ll get straight to the point. The rumors are true.”
“What?”
“I said they’re all true. The imperial court will make an official announcement soon. The Embroidered Uniform Guard will be responsible for the task.”

“His Majesty has a good idea where the rumors came from, but he says there’s no point trying to establish the exact facts. Whoever planned and spread them so thoroughly will have left almost no evidence.”
“T-then...”

“A banquet will soon be held at the imperial palace to celebrate. His Highness, Prince Shangshan, will attend, as will every civil and military official. Until you receive further orders, see to security inside and outside the palace.”

The matter of the Emperor’s heir had been a closely guarded secret known to only a handful of people. The Thousand Captain had known of Prince Shangshan’s return, but nothing of this. His face hardened like stone.
“You mean to confirm all of it—and announce it to the people? Now?”
“Exactly.”
“Do you understand what that means, Thousand Captain Jeong? Or are you pretending you don’t?”
“I understand well enough. Including something else you’re overlooking.”
“Something I’m overlooking? What are you—”
“What a mere military officer like me can guess, surely His Majesty the Emperor knows.”
“Follow the order.”
Jeong Hogun left the speechless Thousand Captain behind. As he passed the dark cells and the people emerging from them one by one, he thought:
This is where it begins.
He could feel it: a great storm that would soon sweep through this splendid city called the Imperial Capital—no, through the whole realm.
The imperial court’s formal announcement would be the first arrow, signaling everything to come.
Many people will gather. Many words will be exchanged.

The people drawn into this now would not be ordinary folk like those filling the cells. The so-called educated classes would take notice. Those with power, who could grasp what was happening and act on it, would begin to move.
And in the process...
At last, we’ll know friend from foe.

Until war began, there was no telling who was an enemy and who was an ally. But when everyone drew their weapons and the fighting began in earnest, with no retreat possible, the truth would finally show itself.
Whatever form it took.
What choice will that bastard make in this war?
Jeong Hogun thought of a young man he could never quite figure out.
A reckless young ruffian of the martial world who had thrown himself into the eye of the storm.
“As daring as ever. Just like a little over ten years ago.”
Hong Jin broke a long silence with those words, and I nodded quietly. I felt the same way.
This is more than I expected.

As soon as Ma Sanbao received the information I’d given him after my visit to Qianqing Palace, he acted. He sent trusted subordinates across the Imperial Capital to spread rumors about Prince Shangshan’s whereabouts and everything concerning the Emperor’s heir—which we still hadn’t confirmed for certain.
But what the Emperor did next caught me completely off guard.
I can’t believe he admitted it right away.
Even celebrities caught red-handed by Daspatch usually spend a day or two keeping quiet and denying the dating rumors. The Emperor had gone beyond admitting the rumors and announced them outright.
All in less than a day.
He sure is quick to act, but what on earth is he up to?

The more widely this became known, the worse it was for the Emperor. Unless the thing on his shoulders was purely decorative, anyone with a drop of ink on their hands and a working brain would come to roughly the same conclusion.
—Huh? The Emperor secretly brought Prince Shangshan into the palace?
—Huh? There’s an Emperor Junior, and he hid that until he got caught?
—Huh? Now I’m pissed.
Those thoughts led to one conclusion:
—The Emperor might get rid of Prince Shangshan!
It would be one thing if he had a good reputation to begin with. But wasn’t the current Son of Heaven the one who’d come to the throne after unleashing a river of blood?
A first-time offender might get probation for a minor crime. Nobody was going to trust a murderer with a record.
They might pretend not to notice because they’re afraid of him, though.

In Go terms, the Emperor had made a terrible move. For us, though, it meant we could breathe a little easier. We’d tried to buy time so he couldn’t recklessly threaten Prince Shangshan, and now that protection seemed firmer.
“Isn’t this a decent situation? Whatever else, the imperial court has acknowledged everything in its own name. For now, the threats surrounding His Highness, Prince Shangshan, will disappear.”
Hyuk Mujin had spoken cautiously, watching for their reactions. Hong Jin nodded.
“You’re not wrong. But we always have to consider the worst.”
“The worst...?”
“Young Master Jin, you can probably guess. You’ve experienced for yourself what the current Emperor is like.”
At their gaze, I smacked my lips and slowly began.
“Personally, I see two possibilities. One good, one bad. Which do you want first?”
“Hmm. I think I’d rather hear the bad one first.”
“Mujin.”
“Yes?”
“Read the room.”
“Yes.”
Hong Jin looked sympathetically at Hyuk Mujin, who had quietly shut his mouth, then spoke.
“The good one first.”
The good possibility.
I sorted through my thoughts once more, then slowly parted my lips.
“First: now that he’s made it public, the Emperor will find it hard to lay a hand on his only younger brother, and he’ll send him back safely after the banquet.”
“I like that one, but... what’s the bad one?”
“Second, now that things have come to this, he decides he can take being cursed out one more time and kills off every remaining dissident.”
Hong Jin fell silent. After a long while, he murmured, his expression dark.
“This banquet... could become a Hongmen Banquet.”

chapters.title: Chapter 881
paragraphs: They say rats hear what you say at night, and birds hear what you say by day.
But the guests who had gathered in a secret room early that morning at someone’s invitation weren’t the least bit troubled by such an old, tired saying.
Rats could be trampled to death. Birds could be shot down.
The only ones they worried about were the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
Little more than the Emperor’s watchdogs, the Guard wore golden armor as yellow as a mongrel’s coat. Their specialty was combing every corner as if hunting for lice.
They sniffed out a target, tracked it down, sank their foul-smelling teeth into its neck, then ran back to their master, wagging their tails.
With so many eyes and ears throughout the Imperial Capital, though, even moving in the strictest secrecy left them uneasy, like a fish bone caught in the throat.
Perhaps that was why.
Though a dozen or so people had gathered in one place, an uncomfortable silence lingered in the secret room for some time.
Then, with a faint noise, the last person they were waiting for appeared.
Creeeak.
The old hatch overhead opened, and dim light spilled in. Their eyes, accustomed to the darkness, narrowed reflexively, but they didn’t let down their guard.
They weren’t sure the unfamiliar man who had just stepped into the room was the ally they knew so well.
The newcomer immediately understood what their looks meant.
“Ah, my apologies. I was in such a hurry to get here that I forgot for a moment.”
Krrk. Crack.
“Hmm.”
A low groan rose from them all at once. The dozen or so guests watched the changes around the man with grave expressions.
Shhhk.
His features rippled like a wave.
His long philtrum shortened, his unusually prominent bulbous nose grew sharp, and an odd light appeared in his once-dull, unfocused eyes.
That alone was astonishing enough, but the changes didn’t stop there.
Crack.
With the sound of hundreds of bones shifting out of place, his body shrank and stretched, again and again.
The transformation happened in an instant. A moment later, not a trace of the man they’d just seen remained.
In his place stood a handsome, lean man in his thirties or forties.
At last, the guests recognized the face before them and relaxed.
“Your skill is as wondrous as ever.”
“We ought to be used to it by now, but we still tense up every time. Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma, your talent truly is remarkable.”
At the admiring remarks from all around, Ma Sanbao, the East Depot’s Brush-Holding Eunuch, smiled faintly.
“It’s just a parlor trick I happened to pick up.”
Having modestly brushed off his astonishing disguise technique and Bone-Shrinking Technique, Ma Sanbao continued.
“More importantly, it seems everyone arrived at the appointed time. I hope the journey here wasn’t too inconvenient.”
The guests answered in more relaxed voices.
“It wasn’t as bad as I expected. Your loyal subordinates helped us, and we took far greater care with our disguises.”
“Of course, this ghastly thing is unpleasant and stifling, but what wouldn’t we endure to evade those Embroidered Uniform Guard bastards?”
Someone pointed to the human-skin mask stretched over his face. The others nodded in agreement.
That was right.
What mattered wasn’t whether this skin belonged to a person or an animal.

Their only goal was to overthrow the man sitting on the throne now—the Emperor who had brutally slaughtered countless longtime friends and comrades who shared their cause, then turned that fearsome blade on them.
“We can’t let ourselves be crushed so easily again. Not if I want to save my family and my people.”
“What can we do? There’s no taking back water once it’s spilled. We were all at fault for underestimating the Emperor—or rather, the Fourth Prince.”
“Indeed. But that doesn’t mean we have to scoop up water that’s already dirty.”
“Couldn’t agree more. We can refill the vessel as it empties, and replace the cracked one that reeks of blood with a new one.”
For a while, they spoke in measured voices.

They had ridden the tiger and were now clinging to its back. Only two choices remained: let fear drive them to climb down and be eaten alive, or hold on with all their might until the tiger exhausted itself—and plunge a dagger into the back of its neck.
Everyone gathered here had chosen the latter.
For survival, in the narrowest sense. And for a great and glorious future, in the broadest.
Thus, their fervent hopes and wishes came together, and at last they drew up a pledge bearing all their signatures.
They would wait for the time to defy heaven.
Fortunately, they didn’t have long to wait.
More than a decade had passed since the day the Imperial Capital ran red with blood.

White frost had settled on the heads of the old ministers who had barely survived, but the faction they’d secretly built with painstaking effort had grown stronger and larger. The child who had left for the frontier bundled in swaddling clothes had returned as a boy. And an ominous air was slowly gathering over the Imperial Capital.
“Now everyone is watching the Emperor. The civil and military officials, and even the ignorant common folk.”
“We only meant to buy ourselves a little time by spreading the rumors, but instead of denying them, he announced them to the whole world.”
“For once, that cunning Emperor has made a blunder. Now that he’s made the announcement, the flames will grow beyond anyone’s control.”
“Scandalous stories about the Emperor keep surfacing everywhere. It’s hard to guess what he’s planning.”
“Ten years can change even mountains and rivers, but people don’t change easily. Just look at me. I was already past seventy back then, and I’m still going strong.”
“What do you mean...?”
“The Emperor is the same. This is one of his schemes. Perhaps he means to unleash another storm of blood.”
At the aged voice of a man whose finely made human-skin mask made him look middle-aged, the others let out low groans.
Was it because they hadn’t expected it at all?
No. His words had laid bare the truth they were all trying to ignore.
They too had stumbled and rolled through the filth of politics and lived to tell the tale.
They knew firsthand just how ruthless and daring the Emperor was.
Still, it was hard to shake the question: would he really go that far?
“Isn’t that an overstatement? If the Emperor really intends to do that, rebellions might break out throughout the realm. No—they certainly will.”
At that, the old minister disguised as a middle-aged man burst into a hearty laugh.
“Your own home, with all its furnishings and storehouses, is about to go up in flames. Why worry about a fire approaching from a thousand li away?”
“Stop saying foolish things and face reality. Like Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma.”
Every head turned toward him at once. Ma Sanbao, who had been listening quietly to the conversation, broke his long silence.
“It’s just as I’d expect from the man who nurtured the pillars of the Hanlin Academy. Your mind is as sharp as ever, even past eighty.”
“Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma. Then...”
“I agree with His Excellency the Grand Academician.”
“This is not merely my personal judgment. It is my judgment as the East Depot’s Brush-Holding Eunuch.”
The others fell silent for a moment. Ma Sanbao had invoked his title as Brush-Holding Eunuch, and that could mean only one thing.
“Then a storm of blood will sweep through the court.”
“It will.”
Even as someone groaned, Ma Sanbao continued in an unwavering voice.
“But it’s already clear whose blood will be caught up in that storm. It’s almost upon us, and both sides will have to throw everything they have into the clash.”
“Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma. Forgive me for asking, but can we really stand against the Emperor? From what we’ve learned so far, their forces are far greater than we expected...”
The man regretted speaking almost at once.
Ma Sanbao’s gaze had shot toward him, cold and keen as a blade, making his heart sink.
“I—no, forgive me. I misspoke.”
He forced out the apology in a voice that would barely come. Ma Sanbao withdrew his gaze as if nothing had happened and replied calmly.
“That was unusually careless of you.”
“We’ve trusted one another and boarded the same boat. We all have to row together if we’re going to get anywhere. Isn’t that right?”
“Let me apologize once more. I’m truly sorry.”
For a moment, Ma Sanbao’s response had chilled the air in the room. But he was also the one who warmed it again.
“Don’t worry. We have the justification and the strength to bring the Emperor down.”
“What do you mean...?”
“I can’t tell you everything, but we’ve made ample preparations for this great undertaking. Please understand that I can’t say more than that.”
When Ma Sanbao put it that way, the others quietly folded away the questions lingering on their tongues and tucked them into a corner of their hearts.
The fewer people who knew a secret, the better.
Besides, though each of them had contributed some measure of influence and power, Ma Sanbao was one of the key figures in this plan.
Much like a certain old minister: the Grand Academician of the Hanlin Academy, the cradle of the realm’s talent, who still held sway over the court even after retiring from office.
“By the way, how is that person doing?”
Ma Sanbao immediately understood the meaning behind the sudden question and answered.
“That person is still safe.”
“I’m worried. The Emperor must be watching for an opportunity every chance he gets.”
“But he won’t get what he wants. I’ll say this with confidence: for now, even the Emperor won’t find it easy to lay a hand on that person.”
“The whole Imperial Capital is boiling like a pot left over a fire. Before long, it’ll spill over in every direction.”
“When do you think that will happen, Your Excellency?”
The old minister answered without the slightest hesitation.
“The banquet. The one where the Emperor acknowledged the rumors and made his announcement.”
“I think so too.”
“It’ll be a Hongmen Banquet. Blades will cross, and lives will hang in the balance.”
“It won’t be the same as Hongmen. Xiang Yu was foolish enough to let Liu Bang live, but the Emperor won’t do that.”
The old minister quietly nodded, lost in thought. Then he suddenly spoke.
“What about that young martial artist? What do you think he’ll do?”
“He’ll help us. Just as we expected.”
“I’ve heard he possesses martial arts far beyond what you’d expect for his age. But there are several masters around the Emperor who are just as strong. Do you think he’ll be much help?”
“Who knows?”
Ma Sanbao continued with a faint smile.
“But if his master is there, that changes things.”

His long philtrum shortened, his unusually prominent bulbous nose grew sharp, and an odd light appeared in his once-dull, unfocused eyes.
That alone was astonishing enough, but the changes didn’t stop there.
Crack.
With the sound of hundreds of bones shifting out of place, his body shrank and stretched, again and again.
The transformation happened in an instant.
A moment later, not a trace of the man they’d just seen remained.
In his place stood a handsome, lean man in his thirties or forties.
At last, the guests recognized the face before them and relaxed.
“Your skill is as wondrous as ever.”
“We ought to be used to it by now, but we still tense up every time.
Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma, your talent truly is remarkable.”
At the admiring remarks from all around, Ma Sanbao, the East Depot’s Brush-Holding Eunuch, smiled faintly.
“It’s just a parlor trick I happened to pick up.”
Having modestly brushed off his astonishing disguise technique and Bone-Shrinking Technique, Ma Sanbao continued.
“More importantly, it seems everyone arrived at the appointed time.
I hope the journey here wasn’t too inconvenient.”
The guests answered in more relaxed voices.
“It wasn’t as bad as I expected.
Your loyal subordinates helped us, and we took far greater care with our disguises.”
“Of course, this ghastly thing is unpleasant and stifling, but what wouldn’t we endure to evade those Embroidered Uniform Guard bastards?”
Someone pointed to the human-skin mask stretched over his face.
The others nodded in agreement.
That was right.
What mattered wasn’t whether this skin belonged to a person or an animal.

Their only goal was to overthrow the man sitting on the throne now—the Emperor who had brutally slaughtered countless longtime friends and comrades who shared their cause, then turned that fearsome blade on them.
“We can’t let ourselves be crushed so easily again.
Not if I want to save my family and my people.”
“What can we do?
There’s no taking back water once it’s spilled.
We were all at fault for underestimating the Emperor—or rather, the Fourth Prince.”
“Indeed.
But that doesn’t mean we have to scoop up water that’s already dirty.”
“Couldn’t agree more.
We can refill the vessel as it empties, and replace the cracked one that reeks of blood with a new one.”
For a while, they spoke in measured voices.
They had ridden the tiger and were now clinging to its back.
Only two choices remained: let fear drive them to climb down and be eaten alive, or hold on with all their might until the tiger exhausted itself—and plunge a dagger into the back of its neck.
Everyone gathered here had chosen the latter.
For survival, in the narrowest sense.
And for a great and glorious future, in the broadest.
Thus, their fervent hopes and wishes came together, and at last they drew up a pledge bearing all their signatures.
They would wait for the time to defy heaven.
Fortunately, they didn’t have long to wait.
More than a decade had passed since the day the Imperial Capital ran red with blood.
White frost had settled on the heads of the old ministers who had barely survived, but the faction they’d secretly built with painstaking effort had grown stronger and larger.
The child who had left for the frontier bundled in swaddling clothes had returned as a boy.
And an ominous air was slowly gathering over the Imperial Capital.
“Now everyone is watching the Emperor.
The civil and military officials, and even the ignorant common folk.”
“We only meant to buy ourselves a little time by spreading the rumors, but instead of denying them, he announced them to the whole world.”
“For once, that cunning Emperor has made a blunder.
Now that he’s made the announcement, the flames will grow beyond anyone’s control.”
“Scandalous stories about the Emperor keep surfacing everywhere.
It’s hard to guess what he’s planning.”
“Ten years can change even mountains and rivers, but people don’t change easily.
Just look at me.
I was already past seventy back then, and I’m still going strong.”
“What do you mean...?”
“The Emperor is the same.
This is one of his schemes.
Perhaps he means to unleash another storm of blood.”
At the aged voice of a man whose finely made human-skin mask made him look middle-aged, the others let out low groans.
Was it because they hadn’t expected it at all?
No.
His words had laid bare the truth they were all trying to ignore.
They too had stumbled and rolled through the filth of politics and lived to tell the tale.
They knew firsthand just how ruthless and daring the Emperor was.
Still, it was hard to shake the question: would he really go that far?
“Isn’t that an overstatement?
If the Emperor really intends to do that, rebellions might break out throughout the realm.
No—they certainly will.”
At that, the old minister disguised as a middle-aged man burst into a hearty laugh.
“Your own home, with all its furnishings and storehouses, is about to go up in flames.
Why worry about a fire approaching from a thousand li away?”
“Stop saying foolish things and face reality.
Like Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma.”
Every head turned toward him at once.
Ma Sanbao, who had been listening quietly to the conversation, broke his long silence.
“It’s just as I’d expect from the man who nurtured the pillars of the Hanlin Academy.
Your mind is as sharp as ever, even past eighty.”
“Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma.
Then...”
“I agree with His Excellency the Grand Academician.”
“This is not merely my personal judgment.
It is my judgment as the East Depot’s Brush-Holding Eunuch.”
The others fell silent for a moment.
Ma Sanbao had invoked his title as Brush-Holding Eunuch, and that could mean only one thing.
“Then a storm of blood will sweep through the court.”
“It will.”
Even as someone groaned, Ma Sanbao continued in an unwavering voice.
“But it’s already clear whose blood will be caught up in that storm.
It’s almost upon us, and both sides will have to throw everything they have into the clash.”
“Brush-Holding Eunuch Ma.
Forgive me for asking, but can we really stand against the Emperor?
From what we’ve learned so far, their forces are far greater than we expected...”
The man regretted speaking almost at once.
Ma Sanbao’s gaze had shot toward him, cold and keen as a blade, making his heart sink.
“I—no, forgive me.
I misspoke.”
He forced out the apology in a voice that would barely come.
Ma Sanbao withdrew his gaze as if nothing had happened and replied calmly.
“That was unusually careless of you.”
“We’ve trusted one another and boarded the same boat.
We all have to row together if we’re going to get anywhere.
Isn’t that right?”
“Let me apologize once more.
I’m truly sorry.”
For a moment, Ma Sanbao’s response had chilled the air in the room.
But he was also the one who warmed it again.
“Don’t worry.
We have the justification and the strength to bring the Emperor down.”
“What do you mean...?”
“I can’t tell you everything, but we’ve made ample preparations for this great undertaking.
Please understand that I can’t say more than that.”
When Ma Sanbao put it that way, the others quietly folded away the questions lingering on their tongues and tucked them into a corner of their hearts.
The fewer people who knew a secret, the better.
Besides, though each of them had contributed some measure of influence and power, Ma Sanbao was one of the key figures in this plan.
Much like a certain old minister: the Grand Academician of the Hanlin Academy, the cradle of the realm’s talent, who still held sway over the court even after retiring from office.
“By the way, how is that person doing?”
Ma Sanbao immediately understood the meaning behind the sudden question and answered.
“That person is still safe.”
“I’m worried.
The Emperor must be watching for an opportunity every chance he gets.”
“But he won’t get what he wants.
I’ll say this with confidence: for now, even the Emperor won’t find it easy to lay a hand on that person.”
“The whole Imperial Capital is boiling like a pot left over a fire.
Before long, it’ll spill over in every direction.”
“When do you think that will happen, Your Excellency?”
The old minister answered without the slightest hesitation.
“The banquet.
The one where the Emperor acknowledged the rumors and made his announcement.”
“I think so too.”
“It’ll be a Hongmen Banquet.
Blades will cross, and lives will hang in the balance.”
“It won’t be the same as Hongmen.
Xiang Yu was foolish enough to let Liu Bang live, but the Emperor won’t do that.”
The old minister quietly nodded, lost in thought.
Then he suddenly spoke.
“What about that young martial artist?
What do you think he’ll do?”
“He’ll help us.
Just as we expected.”
“I’ve heard he possesses martial arts far beyond what you’d expect for his age.
But there are several masters around the Emperor who are just as strong.
Do you think he’ll be much help?”
“Who knows?”
Ma Sanbao continued with a faint smile.
“But if his master is there, that changes things.”

chapters.title: Chapter 882
paragraphs: From the day the imperial proclamation went up in the streets, the area around the palace was busier than ever.
People came for all sorts of reasons.

Commoners lingered outside the palace, hoping to catch even a glimpse of the ill-fated young prince they’d heard about only in rumors. Confucian scholars who fancied themselves men of loyalty and righteousness shouted at the top of their lungs, demanding to know why Prince Shangshan had been summoned in secret at a time like this. And poets and writers hoping to land themselves a position took the opportunity to compose and recite poems for the Emperor, who had finally secured an heir.
“How long are we supposed to wait? We can’t see a damn thing from here, Prince Shangshan or no Prince Shangshan.”
“You fool. Did you think His Highness would come out and say, ‘Oh, you’re here,’ just because we’re waiting? We’re only here on the off chance he might.”
“Fair enough. But why are those high-and-mighty people so desperate to tear each other apart?”
“Perhaps they disagree.”
The commoners murmured as they watched two groups of scholars argue, their faces flushed red.
“What? The Emperor having an heir is the Great Nation’s good fortune and a joy to all its people? It’s toadies like you who are ruining this country!”
“Shut your mouth! How dare you speak like that before His Majesty... Right outside the imperial palace!”
“How is it nonsense? You vermin can see perfectly well what’s happening, yet you pretend you can’t!”
“What did you say? Vermin? I’ve heard enough from you, you backwater scholar!”
“You bootlicking son of a bitch! Which academy are you from?”
“So what if you know? What are you going to do about it?”
“You son of a—Everyone! Words won’t settle this! Let’s drive those toadies out of the Imperial Capital!”
“Yeah!”
Hundreds of scholars hurling fists and inkstones at one another made quite a spectacle.
“Hit them! Hit them!”
“Grab that one first!”
Shouts and screams rang out from every direction. Someone watched the scene with their mouth hanging open, then muttered, “The greatest contest since the founding of the nation.”
But the fierce brawl ended as suddenly as it had begun.
And it wasn’t the imperial guards watching the fight from up close with keen interest who stopped them.
Thud.
Amid the chaos, a scholar backing away with a brush gripped like a dagger felt something touch his back.
Have I already been driven up against a wall?
That couldn’t be right.
The main road in front of the imperial palace was so wide that a hundred grown men could walk abreast without their shoulders touching. Besides, there was nothing nearby that could be called a wall.
And it doesn’t even feel completely hard.
So what was it?
The scholar started to turn around cautiously. At that very moment—
“You rat!”
“Gah!”
“I’ve finally got you—!”
One of the poets and writers, a pair of inkstones in his hands as he raced through the battlefield, charged toward the scholar—and suddenly froze. His mouth slowly fell open as he lifted his head.
Not toward the scholar’s face, only a few paces away, but far above it.
A dazed voice escaped his lips. At the same time, a huge shadow fell over him.
Step.
A particularly heavy footstep sounded, and something pushed the scholar forward. He gulped, turned around, and finally understood.
What stood behind him had never been a wall.
It was a monstrous man, tall as a wall and hard as a boulder.
The air, hot with the brawl only moments ago, froze. Everyone gathered along the road outside the imperial palace stared, mouths agape, at the giant who had appeared among them.
What kind of monster is that...?
A shock flashed through everyone’s minds like a bolt of lightning.
The fierce disagreement of moments before was forgotten. They could only stare at a giant unlike any they had seen before—or would ever see again.
Even at a glance, he stood well over nine feet tall.
His limbs were like pillars; a single swing looked as if it could raise a gale. Muscles covered his body like armor, enough to make their knees go weak just looking at him.
And what about the head perched on his thick neck like a great boulder?
Never mind that it was as big as a well-grown pumpkin. Every time those enormous eyes blinked, people felt as though it took years off their lives.
The scholars who, only moments ago, had dared to demand an explanation from the Emperor were especially beside themselves.
Could he be an Embroidered Uniform Guard?
No. The Guard recruits from among ordinary people. That thing isn’t human.
A secret weapon! The Emperor raised him to wipe out his opposition!
To hell with loyalty and righteousness. At the sight of that terrifying giant, their hands and feet trembled and their heads went numb.

If they were formally sentenced to drink poison or be beheaded, at least people would call it an honorable death. But if they took even one slap from that hand larger than a pot lid, they’d die like dogs.
And yet...
“Y-You think we’ll back down just because of that?!”

The scholar who would go down as the first person to discover the giant—and probably the first person to die at his hands—in the annals of the Great Nation’s scholarly world, barely managed to force out a voice that wouldn’t come.
“J-Justice still lives! Even if you kill everyone here, the whole world will learn of your wicked plot!”
He was speaking to the giant before him and to the Emperor.
How many years had he spent committing the words of ancient sages to heart, beginning with the Four Books and Three Classics?
There was right and wrong in all things, and a nation could stand only if it upheld the Three Bonds and Five Relationships. The scholar bit his lip until it bled.
I’d rather die here than spend the rest of my life cowering beneath the Emperor’s power!
If he died protecting Prince Shangshan and the world for a great cause, it would be worth it.
His body trembled like an aspen, but his resolve was like bamboo: it would break before it bent. He forced down his fear and looked up at the giant.
Then he noticed that hundreds of Imperial Guards had surrounded them and knew death was coming.
Until the guards’ commander shouted in a trembling voice.
“W-Who are you?!”
“Id-Identify yourself at once!”
The scholar and everyone else watching blinked.
What the hell?
Weren’t they on the same side?
Then what’s that monster?
And then—
The giant, who had stood there like an iron wall without saying a word, finally spoke.
His voice was as innocent as a child’s.
“I am Taishan—no, Geosan. I don’t want to get in trouble. I don’t know what I did wrong, but I’m sorry.”
“I just heard a noise and came to watch. Can I go on my way?”
In an instant, the atmosphere, drawn taut as a bowstring, collapsed.
He came to watch? Just to watch?
He’s sorry? He doesn’t want to get in trouble? He apologizes that easily?
And what’s with the way he talks?
Everyone was at a loss for words as the giant blinked slowly, like a young calf.
“Y-You little bastard, I finally found you! Hey! Stand right there! You’re built like a damn mountain, so why the hell do you vanish like a squirrel the moment I look away?”

The voice rang through the hushed crowd. A dark-skinned old man who barely reached five feet shoved his way through and ran over. He gave the giant’s thigh a sharp smack, then noticed all the eyes fixed on him and froze like a statue.
In the awkward silence, the commander of the guards looked back and forth between the young giant and the old dwarf, his eyes gone cold.
“Who exactly are you, old man?”
After a brief silence, the old dwarf answered, “An ordinary traveler passing by. Nothing more.”
“You look awfully suspicious. Do you two know each other?”
“Sadly, yes.”
“Then what’s your relationship?”
“I’ve no idea what that idiot thinks of me, but whenever he falls asleep, I try to strangle him. Unfortunately, I’ve failed every time.”
The commander of the Imperial Guards looked at the giant’s neck, thicker than a bull’s, and murmured in understanding.
“You sound even more suspicious now.”
“I hear that a lot. It’s because of the big fellow next to me.”
“Have you ever been arrested by the local authorities because of him?”
“Not once.”
“Then let’s make this your first time. Guards!”
Clang!
Sharp spears and swords flashed in the tightly clenched hands of the guards. The old man let out a deep sigh at their menacing show of force, then spoke.
“Could you wait just a moment?”
The commander’s expression and voice hardened.
“Not a chance. Hand over your identity tag before blood is spilled.”
“My companion has it, so that’s a bit difficult.”
“Then you’ll learn what a truly difficult situation is. And what companion? Is there another accomplice?”
“He’s not an accomplice... Hey, don’t just stand there. Hurry up and call your wet nurse.”
“Wait! Don’t try anything!”
The guards nearby sensed trouble and hurried to stop him, but they were too late to prevent the giant’s shout.
“Fiiive-spiiice poooork!”
The people filling the road outside the imperial palace were startled once by the tremendous shout that battered their ears, then again by the strange words it contained.
Why is he suddenly asking for five-spice pork?
Is he actually crazy?
Even the commander of the Imperial Guards was momentarily confused.
Why was he shouting about five-spice pork out of nowhere? Was the name of those suspicious men’s accomplice Five-Spice Pork? Or had something gone wrong with his ears?
It was none of those things.
The giant had shouted because he wanted five-spice pork right then and there. And his companions had been through this sort of thing so often they were sick of it.
Put simply, they knew better than anyone that there was only one man in the world crazy enough to call for five-spice pork that loudly and desperately outside the imperial palace.
They also knew he was their companion, who had vanished the moment they looked away.
“Tai... no, Geosan!”
At the urgent shout, the crowd parted like a receding tide.
The people who had thought nothing could surprise them anymore found themselves rubbing their eyes again.
A carriage pulled by two horses was racing toward them at a mad pace.
“Whoa! Whoaaaa!”
“Move! Get out of the way!”
The street erupted into chaos. The carriage barely managed to stop when it reached the tense Imperial Guards.
A young man jumped lightly down from it and hurriedly felt over the giant’s body.
“Are you all right? Are you hurt anywhere?”
“Hehe, I’m fine. Everything’s good except I’m hungry.”
The giant answered with a broad grin like a five-year-old’s. The onlookers shuddered again, but the commander did not.
He watched people spill out of the little carriage.
What kind of group is this?
There were seven of them in all.
A pretty girl with noticeable freckles, and a young man beside her whose face was as stiff as a log.

A giant who looked like a walking natural disaster, and a young man who handled that mountain of muscle as if it were a delicate piece of porcelain. An old man smiling placidly like an immortal amid all the chaos, and a short, dark-skinned old man beside him muttering curses.
And finally...
Is that a monk?
For some reason, even his eyebrows had been shaved clean off. He was a mean-looking, disreputable monk.
What the hell is going on?
The commander guarded one of the imperial palace’s twelve gates and had seen all kinds of things, but he swore he had never seen anything like this.
As he hesitated in confusion, the mean-looking monk, who had been the last to climb down from the carriage, approached and held something out.
“What is this?” the commander asked.
“What is this? You son of a—”
“Ah. That slipped out.”
As if trying to hold back his anger, the disreputable monk took a deep breath and continued.
“We’re the circus troupe performing at the banquet. That’s our official letter of introduction.”
“A circus troupe?”
“That’s right. To liven things up, some bigwig or other invited us.”
The commander hurriedly unfolded the letter in his hand. His eyes widened when he saw the seal of a high official—someone far beyond his station to question.
“This is...”
“You’ve seen it, so you know. Open the gate already.”
He might only be a junior officer, but he was a hundred-man commander in the imperial guard, responsible for protecting the capital. To be spoken to like that by a troupe of traveling performers—
But whoever backed the troupe was beyond his ability to deal with. He swallowed his anger and ordered his men to open the gate, committing the troupe’s name on the letter to memory.
The Blazing Flame Troupe? Even the name sounds tacky.
Of course, it never crossed his mind that the monk would have beaten him half to death if he’d said that aloud.

Was the name of those suspicious men’s accomplice Five-Spice Pork?
Or had something gone wrong with his ears?
It was none of those things.
The giant had shouted because he wanted five-spice pork right then and there.
And his companions had been through this sort of thing so often they were sick of it.
Put simply, they knew better than anyone that there was only one man in the world crazy enough to call for five-spice pork that loudly and desperately outside the imperial palace.
They also knew he was their companion, who had vanished the moment they looked away.
“Tai... no, Geosan!”
At the urgent shout, the crowd parted like a receding tide.
The people who had thought nothing could surprise them anymore found themselves rubbing their eyes again.
A carriage pulled by two horses was racing toward them at a mad pace.
“Whoa!
Whoaaaa!”
“Move!
Get out of the way!”
The street erupted into chaos.
The carriage barely managed to stop when it reached the tense Imperial Guards.
A young man jumped lightly down from it and hurriedly felt over the giant’s body.
“Are you all right?
Are you hurt anywhere?”
“Hehe, I’m fine.
Everything’s good except I’m hungry.”
The giant answered with a broad grin like a five-year-old’s.
The onlookers shuddered again, but the commander did not.
He watched people spill out of the little carriage.
What kind of group is this?
There were seven of them in all.
A pretty girl with noticeable freckles, and a young man beside her whose face was as stiff as a log.
A giant who looked like a walking natural disaster, and a young man who handled that mountain of muscle as if it were a delicate piece of porcelain.
An old man smiling placidly like an immortal amid all the chaos, and a short, dark-skinned old man beside him muttering curses.
And finally...
Is that a monk?
For some reason, even his eyebrows had been shaved clean off.
He was a mean-looking, disreputable monk.
What the hell is going on?
The commander guarded one of the imperial palace’s twelve gates and had seen all kinds of things, but he swore he had never seen anything like this.
As he hesitated in confusion, the mean-looking monk, who had been the last to climb down from the carriage, approached and held something out.
“What is this?” the commander asked.
“What is this?
You son of a—”
“Ah.
That slipped out.”
As if trying to hold back his anger, the disreputable monk took a deep breath and continued.
“We’re the circus troupe performing at the banquet.
That’s our official letter of introduction.”
“A circus troupe?”
“That’s right.
To liven things up, some bigwig or other invited us.”
The commander hurriedly unfolded the letter in his hand.
His eyes widened when he saw the seal of a high official—someone far beyond his station to question.
“This is...”
“You’ve seen it, so you know.
Open the gate already.”
He might only be a junior officer, but he was a hundred-man commander in the imperial guard, responsible for protecting the capital.
To be spoken to like that by a troupe of traveling performers—
But whoever backed the troupe was beyond his ability to deal with.
He swallowed his anger and ordered his men to open the gate, committing the troupe’s name on the letter to memory.
The Blazing Flame Troupe?
Even the name sounds tacky.
Of course, it never crossed his mind that the monk would have beaten him half to death if he’d said that aloud.

chapters.title: Chapter 883
paragraphs: It was only natural for the imperial palace to be heavily guarded.
But since the current Son of Heaven had taken the throne, its defenses had grown into an impregnable fortress beyond anything the past could compare to.
Ten times as many guards. Security that shut outsiders out completely.
Even a well-known court official couldn’t enter or leave without an authorized pass.
Some gossips had dared to call the palace the largest, most splendid prison in the world.
But today, even that derisive nickname aimed at the Emperor seemed out of place.
“Affiliation and name.”
“I’m Hong, from Seok Family Manor. Here are the identity tags and inventory of the belongings of the people who came with me.”
“Ah, forgive me. You’re the steward of Seok Family Manor! Is your Family Head keeping well?”
“Thanks to Your Excellency’s concern, he’s as hale as ever.”
“Ha ha, I’m glad to hear it. We’ll have to continue our conversation later. All right, next!”
“Good day. I’m from the Continental Escort Bureau...”
A grand banquet on this scale required a great many supplies and people.

The Outer Palace, the palace’s outermost section, was bustling with outsiders—a sight rarely seen there over the past decade. Officials drafted from various departments to prepare for the banquet sorted the arrivals into groups.
Naturally, people were treated differently according to their status and importance.

The wealthy merchants, whose contributions would help fund the imperial treasury and the banquet, received the warmest welcome. Next came those who had brought rare tribute gifts, hoping to make an impression. Far below them were the performers who had come to enliven the festivities.
Circus troupes, for instance, whose livelihoods depended on performing all sorts of feats.
“Damn it. A circus troupe at my age...”
The Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, muttered as though lamenting his fate.
If the proud ancestors of the Fire Gate Clan had seen him now, they would have wept beneath the earth... or perhaps not.
Unlike those inflexible bastards from the Nine Sects and One Gang, they might be gathered in the heavens right now, peering down through the clouds and snickering.
“Hey, isn’t that Jeok Cheongang fellow over a hundred?”
“He passed a hundred ages ago. He’s probably lived longer than anyone in our sect’s history. Isn’t dying young practically a Fire Gate Clan tradition?”
“That’s what happens when a one-disciple lineage keeps picking the most hotheaded bastards in the land to teach. Anyway, the imperial palace. That ought to be interesting. Who was his master?”
“Me.”
“Me? You still haven’t learned your lesson? When an ancestor as exalted as I am calls on you, how are you supposed to answer?”
“I-I’m sorry.”
“Again.”
“Seventeenth Sect Leader, Hong. Wi. Ryang!”
Something like that, probably.
Imagining his master standing stiffly at attention, Jeok Cheongang felt a lump rise in his throat.
“I’m sorry. I raised my disciple so poorly that even you, Master...”
At the sorrowful sound of his voice, Taishan, standing beside him, spoke with a solemn expression.
“I want five-spice pork.”
“Namho, kill that bastard right now. I’ll allow it.”
“Really? You mean it? I can really do that?”
“No, you can’t!”
Namho eagerly reached for Taishan’s throat, but Sama Pyo hurriedly stopped him.
A few steps away, the Divine Physician watched the scene and chuckled.
“There’s no danger of our identities being exposed. Anyone can see we’re a fine circus troupe.”
Jeok Cheongang gave him a disgruntled look.
“To hell with that. Does it make any sense for me to be in a circus troupe at my age?”
“And what about at my age? At least you look young, Old Master. There’s no mistaking me for anything but an old man.”
“We’re already here, so what else can we do? Taishan—no, Geosan—is enormous. A circus troupe is about the only cover that won’t raise suspicion.”
For all his complaints, Jeok Cheongang couldn’t disagree.
“That... is true.”
The East Depot might not wield the power it once had, but it could still arrange a wide variety of thoroughly prepared false identities.

Half a day before they entered the palace, however, the East Depot specialist who came to deliver the human-skin masks and identity tags they needed had taken one look at Taishan. After a long silence, he’d asked:
“D-Does this man have to come too?”
“I’d love to leave him behind, but we have no choice. I swear he’d cause trouble if we did. If the Embroidered Uniform Guard caught him, he’d spill everything for one plate of five-spice pork.”
“Taishan not that kind of traitor! Taishan wouldn’t sell out his friends for just one plate!”
“Fine. Ten plates, then. Extra meat and spices.”
“Hmm. Hmmmmm. Taishan needs a little time to think.”
“See? That’s the bastard we’re dealing with.”
“What can we do?”
“We’ll have to change your cover. With a man that size, merchants are out of the question. A circus troupe would be best.”
“A circus troupe? You want to turn this old man into a street clown?”
“I-I’m sorry, but there’s no other way. You’re all highly skilled masters. A few feats should be enough to make you look the part.”
“Feats? You mean holding oil in your mouth and breathing fire?”
“That’s right.”
“But that won’t be enough for a grand banquet at the imperial palace.”
“We’ve already made arrangements, so you only need to look convincing. That large fellow will draw particular attention, though. To be safe, he should practice a few feats beforehand.”
“Feats. Such as?”
“As you said, holding oil in his mouth and...”
“That bastard doesn’t keep anything in his mouth. Whatever goes in, he chews up and swallows without mercy.”
“Then... tearing firewood apart with his bare hands...”
“That won’t be a problem. He tears people apart with his hands.”
“...Please never say things like that inside the imperial palace. You absolutely must promise me.”

After the specialist’s desperate, repeated warnings, Jeok Cheongang, the Divine Physician, and the Fire Dragon Pavilion members had received new names and faces and been allowed into the imperial palace.
Of course, there was no doubt the East Depot’s immense power had made it possible.
“So everything in the letter was true. I can’t believe we got into that magnificent imperial palace so easily.”
At Jeok Cheongang’s mutter, the pretty, freckled girl beside him—who had been looking around carefully—answered.

“It was probably easier because this is the Outer Palace. Security at the Inner Palace is on another level. The Imperial Guards protecting the Outer Palace are elite soldiers, but the Inner Palace is guarded by the Embroidered Uniform Guard, the Emperor’s personal guard.”
“How do you know so much?”
“My grandfather told me. The imperial family entrusted him with several important jobs a long time ago.”
“Huh. I suppose that makes sense, given that he’s the Escort King. And you remember stories you heard as a child remarkably well.”
Jeok Cheongang looked at Ju Hwaran with an affection he never showed anyone else. A faint smile touched her face, tense until now.
That was when someone called out.
“Is everyone here?”
A court official swept an arrogant gaze over the gathering. His loose robes did nothing to hide his bulk or the belly that bulged like a well-fed pig’s.
“As the official in charge of the music for this grand banquet, I will inspect and sort you all before the festivities begin.”
Clank. Clank.
A heavy metallic sound rang out the moment he finished speaking.

The newcomers wore gleaming golden armor and carried an aura far more imposing than that of any Imperial Guards the group had seen so far. The other circus troupes who had come to perform at the banquet, along with the courtesans and musicians, swallowed nervously.
“The Embroidered Uniform Guard...”
There was no mistaking them.
Permitted to wear gold, one of the Son of Heaven’s symbols, they were the Great Nation’s finest troops. Alongside the East Depot, they were its most powerful watchers.
Unlike the Imperial Guards, who could be seen throughout the Imperial Capital, the Embroidered Uniform Guard rarely appeared. When they did, their authority was unmistakable.
As formidable as the man who now stepped forward, his eyes gleaming.
“I am Jeong Hogun, a Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
His voice was calm, but a heavy aura pressed down in every direction.
Jeok Cheongang sensed his intent well before that wave of energy reached the crowd and swiftly sent a Sound Transmission.
—Everyone, be on your guard.
The inspection and sorting the fat official had mentioned would be neither ordinary nor easy.
They’re using the Embroidered Uniform Guard to weed out possible assassins.
Flies always gathered around a well-laid feast.
It would be one thing if they were merely a nuisance. Flies armed with swords and spears and aiming for the Emperor’s life were another matter entirely.
Fortunately, Jeok Cheongang’s group and the East Depot had anticipated this.
I knew it.
Know your enemy and know yourself, and you can fight a hundred battles without peril.

To prepare for just such a situation, the Divine Physician had personally made Energy-Dispersing Poison, which disrupted internal energy, and given it to the group. Jeok Cheongang had already reached the realm of Returning to Simplicity and could conceal his qi at will without it.
The only problem is that bastard Taishan...
But contrary to his fears, Jeong Hogun’s gaze rested on Taishan only briefly before moving away.
Or rather, trouble broke out elsewhere before he could examine Taishan closely.
“You there. Step forward.”
“M-Me, sir?”
The sparrow-mustached man, who looked like the steward of a pleasure house, asked in a trembling voice. Jeong Hogun shook his head.
“No. The courtesan behind you.”
“W-Whatever could be the reason...?”
“She knows better than I do. Don’t you?”
The courtesan, who looked barely twenty, had a pure, lovely face. She blinked in surprise, then threw herself face-first onto the ground.
“T-This girl has done nothing wrong!”
Jeong Hogun replied flatly.
“I think so too.”
“Th-Then why...?”
“But the sachet at your waist smells of bitter poison.”
“Will you explain yourself?”
The courtesan raised her head and stared up at Jeong Hogun in bewilderment.
Then she yanked the hairpin from her hair and swung it in a flash.
Whoosh! Thunk!
A faint sound of air being cut, followed by a spray of blood.
Jeong Hogun watched with a lowered gaze as the courtesan plunged the hairpin into her own neck.
“Why?”
“T-Twelve years ago. Grrk. My father and mother, my younger sibling... Cough.”
“Revenge. Yes, I suppose so.”
“The Emperor... I have to k-kill...”
Thump.
Still coughing up blood, the courtesan went limp and collapsed.
Jeong Hogun stared down at the corpse in silence for a while, then spoke abruptly.
“Remove the body. Take everyone who came with her to the prison.”
“Yes, sir!”
“W-Wait! We didn’t know anything about this! We really don’t know a thing...”
Clang-clang!
The cold sound of drawn blades drowned out their desperate excuses.
Realizing they had no choice, they disappeared somewhere under the Embroidered Uniform Guard’s escort, faces filled with despair.
Jeong Hogun watched until they were gone, then turned to the person he had put off questioning.
“You there.”
“Huh?”
“You said you belonged to a circus troupe.”
“Yeah.”
Taishan looked around blankly. Jeok Cheongang lowered his head, weighing whether to wait a little longer or step in himself.
Just as he cautiously curled his hand into a fist, a voice from far away reached his ears.
“Oh, Hogun. What are you doing here?”
At the familiar voice, Jeok Cheongang reflexively raised his head.
A young man was walking toward them with a wide grin.

chapters.title: Chapter 884
paragraphs: The moment I saw what was happening, I thought:
I knew this would happen.
It wasn’t as if I were some gifted shaman who’d come rushing over because a divine spirit told me to. I’d decided I should see for myself as soon as Hong Jin gave me the news.
“People from Young Master Jin’s group entered the palace a little while ago. Disguised as a circus troupe. But...”
“Did something go wrong?”
“I think so. They seem to have attracted more attention than we expected. You know that huge man in the group?”
“Ah, fuck. I told them not to do that.”
“...I haven’t even said anything yet.”
“What’s the point? I know what they’re usually like. I’d better go take a look.”
Wait. Eunuch Ma must have made arrangements. Let’s give it a little longer.
“I know my companions better than anyone. Even if it’s only to be safe, I should see for myself.”
“Captain, you’re absolutely right. I’ll escort you and have you back in no time, so Comrade Hong can relax.”
“Mujin.”
“Yes, Captain.”
“Quit showing off and stay here.”
“That bastard would only go and cause another mess.”
I’d left the pavilion without a moment’s hesitation half an hour ago.

For some reason, ever since I’d met the Emperor two days earlier, the Embroidered Uniform Guard surrounding the pavilion had only watched from a distance. They hadn’t tried to stop me. And the place Hong Jin had told me about was much closer than I’d expected.
I’d had to take a roundabout route to avoid looking suspicious, but fortunately, I’d arrived just in time.
Right now.
“Oh, Hogun. What are you doing here?”
At my casual greeting, the air around us, taut as a bowstring, eased.
Then every eye turned to me. Among the faces were a few that looked unfamiliar and familiar at the same time.
I don’t know if those are human-skin masks or what, but they’ve done a hell of a job with the disguise technique.
The smallest change to someone’s features could give them a completely different look.
Pretending to sweep my gaze over the crowd, I spotted my companions huddled in one corner. Then I waved to Jeong Hogun.
“There’s an old saying that you can’t spit in a smiling face, but looking at you, Hogun, I guess that isn’t always true. Could you at least answer when someone speaks to you?”
Jeong Hogun opened his mouth, his expression subdued.
“Who are you calling ‘our Hogun’?”
“Fine, then. Your Hogun.”
“As always, it’s impossible to have a sensible conversation with you.”
“What’s the point of a bunch of smelly, black balls understanding each other? Are you interested in me, by any chance?”
“Not at all. But I am interested in why you’ve suddenly appeared here.”
That was the Embroidered Uniform Guard for you.
His tone was blunt, but the meaning behind it was sharp as a needle. Still, I hadn’t spent all my time stumbling around Murim training only my martial skills.
And the half hour I’d spent getting here had given me plenty of time to think about how to avoid the enemy’s suspicion—and what to do if I drew it anyway.
“What the hell do you mean, why? I was bored and taking a walk nearby. Things looked tense, so I came over.”
I pointed to the blood splattered across the ground. It had to have come from someone.
“Thought I might find something, and sure enough.”
“On my way here, I saw about fifteen people being dragged off in a line. What did they do, commit treason?”
Jeong Hogun stared at me for a long while without answering, then abruptly spoke.
“They were trying to attend the banquet disguised as courtesans.”
I wasn’t lying about seeing people dragged away.
I remembered the corpse one of the Embroidered Uniform Guard had hauled off, rolled up in a straw mat. That was probably the courtesan Jeong Hogun meant.
I wonder why she did it.

I had no way of knowing. She might have survived the destruction of her family at the Emperor’s hands, or she might have been an assassin sent by someone who considered themselves a champion of loyalty and righteousness.
There were plenty of possibilities. The problem was that the incident had put Jeong Hogun even more on edge. He might start suspecting my companions.
This can’t be how things go from the start.
I spoke as naturally as I could, with the same hint of contempt in my eyes and voice I’d used until now.
“You brought down a traitor who dared raise a blade against His Majesty the Emperor. You’re definitely getting promoted this time, Thousand Captain Jeong.”
“I didn’t kill her. She took her own life.”

“It’s basically the same thing. Why do you think she killed herself? Because being dragged off and tortured to death would’ve been worse. She’d failed anyway, so dying cleanly was a hundred, a thousand times better. You know that too, don’t you?”
Jeong Hogun was silent for a moment, then answered evenly.
“Yes. You’re right.”
What?
He’d always been like that, but there was something strange about how little my sharp words seemed to affect him. I wondered to myself,
Has he noticed something?
His instincts seemed sharper than those of the other Embroidered Uniform Guards. I couldn’t rule it out, and if he had noticed something, I couldn’t leave things as they were.
I smiled broadly and stepped forward.
“Nice to see you admit I’m right for once. How about I lend you a hand while I’m here?”
“You want to help?”
“It’s easy enough. Who knows? If I catch a traitor even the Embroidered Uniform Guard couldn’t weed out, maybe His Majesty the Emperor will grant me a wish.”
“What are you up to?”
“There you go again. That’s an occupational disease, you know. At this stage, even the Divine Physician couldn’t cure you.”
Thank goodness every eye was on me.
I pretended not to notice the Divine Physician flinching on reflex among the crowd, then shrugged at Jeong Hogun.
“Anyway, say the word if you don’t want my help. Otherwise, I’ll take a quick look around. I’m better at that sort of thing than you are. You know that.”
I wasn’t just saying that.
Jeong Hogun was far better at surveillance and interrogation, but when it came to judging someone’s martial skill, I was a step ahead of him. I’d crossed the threshold of Supreme Peak, after all.
No—if I could use Qi Sense, which I couldn’t right now, to get precise information, I’d be the perfect person for the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
Of course, my offer probably sounded strange to everyone else.
—Is this madman serious...?
—What are you plotting?
Two Sound Transmissions reached me in succession. The first came from Jeok Cheongang. The second came from Jeong Hogun.
I gave a quiet laugh and replied in kind, addressing only the man staring at me as though determined not to miss the slightest opening.
—Why bother with Sound Transmission? It’s not that big a deal.
—Answer me properly. Why are you doing this?
—Why? Isn’t it obvious?
I looked Jeong Hogun straight in the eye and moved my lips.
—What if some lunatic starts swinging a sword at the banquet? And what if that stern Emperor you love so much gets hurt? Who do you think’s going to take the blame for it all?
—I’m not doing this for the master you serve. I’m doing it to protect His Highness Prince Shangshan, you idiot.
It was an explanation that made perfect sense from start to finish. I’d come up with it in a hurry on the way here, but it worked.
The muscles in Jeong Hogun’s rigid face relaxed, if only a little.
Success.
But I wasn’t finished.
I swallowed the sigh of relief that was about to escape me, clicked my tongue, and turned away.
—From what I can see, there’s no one particularly suspicious right now. Just do your job properly from here on out. Both of us have someone to protect, don’t we?
That was it.

I walked back the way I’d come, at an easy pace, crossing through the now-quiet crowd. I didn’t forget to pause and react when I reached Taishan, whose face had changed but whose massive build hadn’t.
“Whoa, damn. Look at the size of you. What on earth do you eat to get that big?”
Taishan answered haltingly.
“I like... I like five-spice pork.”
“Liar.”
“You look like you’d eat anything.”
“Oh. Uh, yeah. I do.”
“Those muscles and bones of yours are ridiculous. You’ve trained in external arts, haven’t you?”
“Geosan. Sold to circus troupe when young. Had to learn to survive.”

Circus troupes traveled the land putting on shows. You could find one in just about any sizable city, and there was nothing strange about performers who pushed their bodies so hard learning external arts.
What’s strange is how huge he is to begin with.
I thought to myself, then ran my hands over Taishan’s arms and legs, which were packed with muscle.
“With a build like this, you could beat most First Rate masters with your fists... Where are you from?”
Namho, an old man with dark skin standing beside us, promptly bowed and answered.
“We’re based north of the Yangtze, sir. We mostly perform in Hebei and Liaoning Province.”

“Oh, that’s close. If you’re interested, stop by the Jin Family of Taiyuan in Shanxi Province sometime. He may have missed his chance, but if he has enough internal energy to back it up, he could still become a great martial artist.”
“We’re grateful for the offer, but we’d rather not. As you can see, he’s not as bright as most, but he’s the treasure of our circus troupe...”
His time in the Hidden Shadow Pavilion had certainly made Namho a hell of an improviser.
Namho was showing the kind of acting that could kick one of Chungmuro’s rising stars in the shins. After exchanging a few more words with him, I left with an exaggeratedly disappointed look.
Inside, I was certain.
That did it.

Anyone who’d heard us would now know that the giant had learned enough external arts to defeat a First Rate master, that his troupe performed north of the Yangtze, far from the Imperial Capital, and that there wasn’t much reason to suspect them.
And the potbellied official turned out to be an ally I hadn’t even known about.
“If there’s nothing more to investigate, let them through. They’ve already been thoroughly vetted several times, and I have a mountain of work to do.”
Hong Jin’s words flashed through my mind.
Wait. Eunuch Ma must have made arrangements. Let’s give it a little longer.
Those words hadn’t been a lie.
Rather than draw attention by mobilizing the East Depot, Ma Sanbao must have planted an ally where no one would notice.
Luckily, my arrival fit right in.
After I’d walked a little over ten jang, my keen hearing picked up Jeong Hogun’s blunt voice.
“Let them through.”
I cheered inwardly, then found myself at a loss for words when a Sound Transmission came from Jeok Cheongang.
—As expected, you had a plan all along. This old man never doubted you.
No, Old Master.
A moment ago, you called me a madman.

chapters.title: Chapter 885
paragraphs: Naturally, there was no moving reunion beyond that.
We’d only been apart for a few days, and we couldn’t exactly acknowledge each other here.
There’ll be a chance soon enough.
I crossed the vast grounds of the imperial palace, taking in the layout of the buildings, the Imperial Guards posted everywhere, and the outsiders brought in to prepare for the banquet.
That was when I noticed something unexpected.
What’s that?
I stopped and narrowed my eyes at a group carrying boxes about ten paces ahead.
“Hold on. Take that this way.”
“One, two. Hup!”
“Those are offerings from Grandee Guanglu. They’re worth more than all your lives put together, so handle them carefully.”
“Yes, sir. Of course.”
Their clothes were clean but old and mended in places. Hardship had etched lines into their faces.

Sweat poured off them as they bowed and smiled at a man who looked like a low-ranking official, then went straight back to hauling the mountains of goods. They looked like ordinary laborers living from one day’s wages to the next.
But...
They’re different.

I could feel a faint wrongness about them. It was an instinct honed through countless real battles and brushes with death—so subtle that I wouldn’t have noticed it if I hadn’t reached my current realm.
They’re not ordinary laborers.
I couldn’t sense any internal energy from them, but one thing gave them away.
The stench of blood.
It was like a brand no amount of washing could remove. The sour smell of sweat and the mustiness of old clothes couldn’t quite cover it.
Martial artists?

Were they martial artists who’d voluntarily taken Energy-Dispersing Poison to hide their internal energy? Or was it just my imagination, brought on by the fact that I had to be sensitive to everything happening around me right now?
I’ll know if I check.
I started toward them for a closer look—or tried to.
A cart, unable to bear its load, tipped toward me.
Crack. Crash!
Wooden splinters flew. Silver yuanbao and all kinds of ornaments spilled from the boxes, and the official clutched his head.
“What the hell do you think you’re doing?”
“I-I’m sorry. I loaded the cart wrong, and...”
“You stupid old fool! Forget apologizing and pick it all up! If even one thing is damaged, you’ll pay dearly!”
“Yes, sir. Right away.”
An old man bowed so low he looked ready to snap as the official stormed off. Small and gaunt as a tree that had lost all its life, he limped over and looked up at me with frightened eyes.
“Are you all right, sir? This old man’s mistake didn’t hurt you, did it...?”
A mistake. Sure.
“I’m fine. Not a scratch.”
“Phew. Thank goodness.”
“It gave me a fright, though. That cart looked perfectly sound before it suddenly fell over.”
He saw my smile and bowed again, flustered.
“I apologize once more, sir.”
“Don’t worry about it. Want some help? Looks like there’s a lot to pick up.”
“Oh, how could I ask that of you? It’s more than I deserve that someone of your standing would speak so politely to me...”
“I’m not someone of high standing. You know that already, don’t you?”
For an instant, something shifted among the laborers coming over to clear the mess. In a pause too brief for anyone else to notice, the old man slowly opened his mouth.
“If you’d help us, we’d be very grateful.”
“Then that’s settled.”
I nodded, crouched down, and began gathering the scattered goods. I worked in silence as though picking them up had been my only intention, but I kept my eyes on the old man.
He broke the silence first.
“How did you know?”
I let out a quiet laugh at the admission.
“You gave that up fast.”
“I hate wasting time. Especially when I’m an old man without much of it left.”
“Are you a martial artist? Who do you belong to?”
“Answering a question with a question is rude. Remember that.”
“What does that—oh.”
“How did you know? I was sure no one would notice.”
His eyes gleamed now, the frightened laborer gone as if he’d never existed.
“The stench of blood,” I said.
He didn’t look surprised. He frowned, sniffed at various parts of himself, and smacked his lips.
“My nose must be failing with age. All I smell is old-man stink.”
“That’s there too. Since you brought it up, could we put a little distance between us? I’m having trouble breathing.”
“I thought you were just skilled in martial arts, but you’ve got a hell of a nose, too.”
“You know me?”
“Of course. Information is essential in this line of work. But even without being told about you, I’d have known right away.”
“How?”
The stench of blood.
That shut me up. The old man went on.
“Didn’t you know? You reek of it yourself. Enough that no one would blink if they called you a Killing Ghost instead of a Divine Dragon.”
“No need to look at me like that. I mean it as a compliment. You know what they say.”
He grinned, releasing a terrible stench from between his blackened, yellow teeth.
“Kill a hundred and you’re a Killing Ghost. Kill a thousand and they call you a hero. Kill ten thousand and you become... a king.”
My mouth felt gritty, like I’d been chewing sand. I stared at the old man, whose breath stank right in my face.
What the hell is this?
Something about him felt wrong. Just facing him sent a chill down my spine. Even in Murim, with every sort of person roaming it, you rarely came across someone like this.
“Who are you? No—who are all of you?”
“You address a Senior of Murim as ‘you’? Does your master know his Disciple has such poor manners?”
“Someone I met recently told me it was rude to answer a question with a question.”
The old man stared at me, eyes wide, then burst out laughing.
“Well, you got me there.”
“Finished laughing? Then answer me.”
“Why ask when you already know? Those children and I are martial artists. Not so different from you.”
“I’d say you’re very different. Am I imagining it?”
“There’s no need to worry. We may not belong to the Murim Alliance, but we’re in the same boat.”
“What does that...”
I trailed off as a thought struck me.
“No way...”
“Eunuch Ma. Is that answer enough?”
“Everyone has their own place and role. Go back and wait for the right moment. Any more attention will only make things troublesome.”
The old man rose and bowed to me.
“We can manage the rest, sir. You needn’t trouble yourself any longer.”
It was a clear dismissal—and a performance for whoever might be watching us. No, calling it a performance almost did him a disservice. He was an old laborer, every movement perfectly in character.
“Please get back safely, sir. Then this old servant will be off...”
Step. Step.
I watched him limp away carrying a box, and at last I thought I knew what the people disguised as laborers were.
Even in all of Murim, only a few sorts of people could hide themselves and move about so completely. Add that stubborn stench of blood, and only one word came to mind.
Assassins.
Even martial artists, surrounded as they were by lunatics and people with no sense of self-preservation, had certain sorts they preferred to avoid. The same few always made the list.
Killing Ghosts. Fiends. Mysterious old men. Beautiful women in veils.
Like Japan’s legendary first-string team, they weren’t easy to find. But martial artists with a shred of sense and dreams of retiring to a village for the elderly someday knew to steer clear.
Why? Simple.
Even messing with them—and sometimes just being near them—made a sense of doom creep over you.
And right up there with Killing Ghosts and fiends, among the three most avoided professions, were assassins.
The three kings of utter bastards.
Nobody argued with the list. Plenty of people even put assassins at the top. Someone close to me had once given me much the same advice.
His sobriquet was the Slaughter Saint, which made it a little ironic.
Actually, that’s well past ironic. It’s practically black comedy.

I kept walking as I muttered to myself. It suddenly occurred to me that I didn’t know where this road led. But that thought was quickly buried by the conversation with the Slaughter Saint that came to mind.
“A Killing Ghost or a fiend would be better. But whatever you do, stay away from assassins.”
“Why? Aren’t they all the same kind of lunatic?”
“Your head is a solid lump of rock, so let me give you a simple example. Say you’re eating at an inn and a Killing Ghost or fiend suddenly walks in. What do you do?”
“That’d be fucking awful. I’m trying to eat.”
“Well... you’re not wrong. But think a little harder before answering.”
“You just called me a blockhead. I don’t want to think. Can’t you tell me?”
“In case you’ve forgotten, I can break rocks with my fist. A head made of stone is no exception.”
“I spoke too soon. May I have a moment to think?”
“You’ve gotten a little smarter.”
“Thank you. Hmm. First, I’d watch the Killing Ghost or fiend, then carefully...”
“Yes. Your first priority is to carefully get out of there.”
“No. I’d hit them first.”
“...What the hell did the Fire King teach you?”
The Slaughter Saint had looked up at the sky and sighed. Then he’d hit me on the head a couple of times with that rock-breaking fist before continuing.
“To put it more simply, Killing Ghosts and fiends are no different from madmen who don’t think about the consequences.”
“Ow, my head. Doesn’t that make them more dangerous? Like you said, if I met one at an inn, the whole place could turn into a sea of blood.”
“But you’d still have a good chance of surviving.”
“Well, sure, if your martial skill is high enough...”
“It has nothing to do with skill. You can never predict people like that. They kill or spare people on a whim.”
“They really are crazy.”
“But what about an assassin?”
“An assassin... Oh.”
“Now you’re beginning to understand. They aren’t merely madmen. They’ll do anything to kill their target. That’s how an assassin can kill a master a level or two above them.”
“They’ll do anything to assassinate their target...”
“That’s why you must be most wary of assassins and keep your distance. Understood?”
“Yes. Understood.”
“They’ve lost their place in the world, so you won’t find many these days. Still... what are you doing?”
“Packing my things.”
“Why?”
“You told me to stay away from assassins.”
“Oh. Does that not include former assassins?”
Man, I got beaten up a lot that day.
Then again, that was why I remembered the advice so clearly. And now I’d run into those very assassins in the middle of the imperial palace.
If Ma Sanbao was going to bring in martial artists, why bring assassins into the imperial palace?
Just as a question I couldn’t answer right away rose in my mind—
“Stop.”
A clear, bright voice pierced my ears.
