sentences.text: The pledge Ma Sanbao pulled from his robe was worn with age.
The paper had yellowed, and stains marked it here and there.
But the names and positions, crowded onto it in each signer’s own hand, were still clear.
At the center stood one name in larger, bolder script than all the rest.
Wei Zhong, Seal-Holding Eunuch of the East Depot.
“Lord Cang Gong,” Ma Sanbao said, noticing where I was looking.
“He was the first to draw up the pledge and sign it.
He made us promise, again and again, that even if he died, we would see the coup through.”
“He must have thought he might die.”
“His Internal Injury was so severe it would have been no surprise if he’d died on the spot.
Thankfully, he survived...”
Ma Sanbao sighed, regret on his face.
“But it’s not good.
He still hasn’t recovered completely.
Of course, if he hadn’t been injured that badly, he wouldn’t still be alive.”
“What do you mean?”
“Why else would the Emperor have spared Lord Cang Gong?
He was the foremost of the old retainers who served the late Emperor.
The Emperor couldn’t execute him outright without facing the consequences.”
I’d wondered about that myself.
That meticulous Emperor had spared Lord Cang Gong, the man who stood in his way—and the head of the East Depot, the most threatening force of all.
“Is there something else I don’t know?”
Ma Sanbao nodded quietly.
“There was a bargain.
The fate of the Great Nation hung on it.”
“What kind of bargain?”
“The life of a child who hadn’t even learned to walk.
Traded for the lives of countless loyal officials.”
“Yes, exactly what you’re thinking.
Nearly a hundred senior officials were sacrificed to save His Highness Prince Shangshan.
Not just the officials themselves, but their entire families.”
The air around us seemed to grow heavy.
A fire flickered in Ma Sanbao’s eyes.
“With the late Emperor, His Highness the Crown Prince, and the other princes all gravely ill, we had to protect His Highness Prince Shangshan, our last hope, even at that cost.
It was the only way.”
“What did the Emperor get out of the bargain?”
“Legitimacy and time.
The late Emperor, after securing a promise about His Highness Prince Shangshan’s future, formally abdicated the throne.
Lord Cang Gong calmed the opposition forces that had wanted to fight the new Emperor.”
The Imperial Capital might be the center of the realm, but it wasn’t the whole realm.
The Great Nation’s vast territories were held together by countless officials and armies.
Even with the legitimacy of a formal transfer of power, the new Emperor would have needed time to quell the unrest simmering across the land.
Cang Gong was the most respected of the late Emperor’s old retainers.
Cang Gong’s safety, along with Prince Shangshan’s, must have been what kept those forces in check.
“The bargain dealt us a terrible blow, but it let us achieve what we had to.
The Emperor wasn’t the only one who needed time to recover.”
The Emperor had probably expected Cang Gong to die before long.
Instead, Cang Gong had miraculously survived his terrible Internal Injury.
The East Depot he led had endured, too.
And so had the restoration army, which dreamed of rebellion under his leadership.
“So the two sides split apart and faced off against each other.
And they’ve been doing that for more than a decade.”
“That’s right.
This clash has been inevitable for a long time.
We’ve had our blades pointed at each other, but neither side could make the first move.
Not openly, at least.”
I frowned at that last part.
“Not openly?”
“There have been several assassination attempts.
The Emperor went after Lord Cang Gong, and we went after the Emperor.”
I didn’t need to ask how those attempts had turned out.
Both men were still alive.
The Emperor lived under heavy guard in Qianqing Palace, though.
Cang Gong’s survival was the surprising part.
“When I went to Qianqing Palace, I saw that the Emperor had one hell of an assassin working for him.
How did you stop them?”
“The Emperor has several Supreme Peak masters under his command, of course.
But our forces are no weaker.
Have you heard of the Twelve Palaces of the Zodiac?”
“I’ve heard the name a few times.
Aren’t those constellations?”
“Usually.
But it’s also a title for the twelve Supreme Peak masters who protect the Imperial Capital.”
What?
My eyes widened.
Twelve Supreme Peak masters, all here in the Imperial Capital?
They were rare even in Murim.
I knew much of the Great Nation’s strength was concentrated here, but that was still astonishing.
What Ma Sanbao said next surprised me even more.
“Half of those twelve Supreme Peak masters belong to our side.
Some of them are staying with Lord Cang Gong.”
“And that’s not all.”
Ma Sanbao pointed to the names and positions on the pledge, one after another.
Among them was an old scholar who enjoyed the overwhelming support of the realm’s Confucian scholars, along with senior court officials of the highest rank, such as the Three Dukes.
But the most important names belonged to military officers.
Commanders guarding the Imperial Capital and the borders beyond it.
One was even a governor-general who commanded tens of thousands of troops.
“Do you understand why this standoff has lasted so long?”
I nodded gravely.
The names on that pledge represented no less than half the Great Nation.
If either side struck first, the result would be a sea of corpses and blood.

Children of this era generally grew up faster than children in the modern world.
But Prince Shangshan was still too young to shoulder the burden of an empire this vast.

chapters.title: Chapter 897
paragraphs: That day, everything was different from usual.

The streets, usually filled with laughter and music, were quiet. Clouds that had yet to clear cast shadows over the people below, and the canal, swollen by unprecedented rainfall, churned uneasily, as if reflecting the mood of the city.
At the end of it all, and at its center, stood the imperial palace.
Rumble.
It was the dim hour before dawn. Even when the massive iron gates began to open with a heavy metallic groan, no one thought anything strange was happening.
The palace gates always closed at the hour of the Rat and opened at the hour of the Rabbit.

Before long, dawn would break. Ministers from the various courts would make their way to the palace, while the people of this beautiful, dangerous metropolis—high and low alike—began another day in their own places.
Like precisely meshing gears.
As if that were simply the natural order of things.
But the dazzling light that appeared between the slowly opening gates was proof that this day would not begin like any other.
“H-Hey. Is that...?”
“Hm?”
A vendor who had set up his stall along the main road in front of the palace, as usual, turned at the call of a fellow merchant. His narrow eyes swelled wide.
“T-The Embroidered Uniform Guard?”
The words had barely escaped his lips when—
“Ha!”
With a short battle cry shouted in unison, a thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards mounted on their fine steeds poured through the wide-open gates.
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
Hooves thundered, waking the dawn.
The ground shook. Dust, settled by the cool morning air and rainwater that had yet to dry, rose into the air.
The thousand riders shot forward like a single arrow, crossing the main road before the palace in the blink of an eye. At a hand signal from their commander, they scattered in every direction.
From a thousand to hundreds. Hundreds to a hundred. A hundred to dozens.
They split up, then split again, exactly as planned.
The people who had started their day early watched in a daze. But when they saw the notices left behind by the golden tide that had swept through the Imperial Capital, they understood.
Tomorrow. The hour of the Goat.
The grand banquet for the imperial prince’s birthday. Begins.

That was how the first line of the hundreds of proclamations began, each written by the imperial court calligrapher whose elegant handwriting was renowned throughout the realm. The faces of the people already suffering from the untimely flood twisted with anger.
“Three days? He’s holding that damn banquet for three whole days in a situation like this?”
“Shh. Keep your voice down. Want to get arrested for treason?”
“Treason, my ass. I worked like an ox my whole life to buy my house, and now I’ve lost it and every last thing in it. What have I got left to be afraid of?”
“Exactly!”
“Fuck, so to hell with what the people think? His own kid’s birthday comes first, is that it?”
Some had lost their property. Others, their families.
And they were all neighbors who had been closer than family.
So the people trying to calm those furious at the proclamation didn’t look happy, either.
The Son of Heaven. Or the Emperor.
How could the supreme ruler, descended from the dragon appointed by Heaven and charged with caring for all his subjects, do such a thing?
Those who had lost what they treasured in the flood were furious. And the people watching them suddenly realized that they too might one day be standing there, furious over their own losses.
Something’s wrong with this country...
At first, they had done nothing but look up to the Son of Heaven. He was so far above them that they couldn’t dream of seeing him, no different from the sun overhead.
But the current Emperor had violated the bonds of kinship.
He was a monster in human skin who had seized the throne by slaughtering his parents, his siblings, and countless loyal officials and their families.
And so Heaven’s favor must have turned away from him.
At the Shaolin Temple, known to everyone under Heaven, eminent monks had been dying. In Sichuan, thousands of martial artists had turned the broad daylight into a sea of corpses and blood.
And that wasn’t all.
Unbelievable rumors had come from Hubei of an imugi gone on a rampage. Sinister tales said that the barbarians of the harsh lands of Nanman had formed a vast army and marched north.
The northern tribes, quiet as mice for a hundred years, were showing signs of unrest. And now an unprecedented downpour had struck the Imperial Capital.
What could this string of disasters mean?
Heaven has forsaken this country. No—the heavens are trying to punish the Emperor.
If these had been peaceful, prosperous times, no one would have given such rumors and superstitions a second thought.
A house earned through hard work, a beloved family, plenty of grain and money—that would have been enough.
For more than a decade, the realm had been as calm as the waters of West Lake. The people hadn’t complained about their new Son of Heaven as much as one might have expected.
They could condemn the Son of Heaven for defying the natural order, but their lives and livelihoods hadn’t changed all that much.
Some had even cheered when corrupt officials who’d run rampant during the late Emperor’s peaceful reign were caught up in the purge for treason. Good riddance, they’d said.
But things were different now.

In barely two years, strange phenomena that could only be called supernatural powers had appeared throughout the realm. A young king beloved by the people had been summoned to the capital. And the Son of Heaven, ignoring his suffering subjects, had poured a fortune into a banquet celebrating his heir.
“Is this... is this truly the right thing to do?”
A man in a worn bamboo hat pulled low over his face muttered the question on everyone’s mind.
“The people’s will is Heaven’s will, and Heaven’s will is the people’s. Why, then, has the Emperor turned his back on Heaven and his people?”
His voice rang clearly through the crowd, which had fallen silent.
The invisible air pressed down on them, heavy and still.
In the suffocating silence, people clenched their teeth and their eyes shone. For some reason, they strained to hear every word of the man’s voice, which sounded unusually clear.
“The azure heaven’s power is waning, and dark clouds gather. The storm that will soon descend will soon swallow the realm whole.”
It was strange.
Hundreds of people had gathered there, yet not one of them spoke. They all listened to the man.
The rough laborer who had never learned to read. The street vendor who lived from day to day. Even the elderly Confucian scholar, whose learning was likely as extensive as his years.
There was something mysterious in the man’s words and voice, a profound insight and conviction that drew them all in.
And left them with a question they couldn’t help asking.
“Um, sir. Forgive me for interrupting, but could I ask you one thing?”
At the laborer’s cautious approach, rough as he looked, the man in the bamboo hat nodded.
“Go ahead.”
“If it’s not too much trouble, what should a poor man like me do to escape the storm you mentioned?”
“Head for the mountain.”
“What?”
The laborer’s eyes widened at the answer, given without a moment’s hesitation. The man in the bamboo hat continued slowly.

“Find the highest mountain in the realm and take shelter there. It has a stream that never runs dry, fruit growing ripe, and animals roaming free. Its forests will provide timber for homes and firewood. It could shelter all the people under Heaven and still have room to spare.”
The laborer was dumbfounded.
So was most of the crowd.
The highest mountain in the realm?
Where was there a mountain vast enough to shelter everyone, with food and resources to spare?
While the laborer searched for words, another man, more impatient, blurted out,
“I don’t know who you are, but you seem to be a master of profound cultivation. Do you mean the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains?”
A few people gave soft cries of recognition and nodded.
The five famous mountains, said to be the highest in the realm and filled with sacred energy—yes, that would make sense, they murmured.
“Which of the Five Sacred Mountains do you mean? Mount Song in Henan? Taishan in Shandong? Huashan in Shaanxi? Or...”
“You’re all wrong. I didn’t mean the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains.”
“What? What do you mean? If not the Five Sacred Mountains, then what—”
The man’s calm, firm reply left the crowd speechless. Just then, an elderly voice came from somewhere among them.
“There’s one place left. No, it was the only place from the beginning.”
Every head turned.
An elderly Confucian scholar in faded but neat clothes gazed at the gloomy sky and murmured, almost to himself,
“Shangshan.”
A few people understood what those words meant, and their eyes widened. Most remained confused.
Until the old scholar continued.

“Yes. That place could shelter all the people under Heaven. No matter how fiercely the storm swallowed the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains, it would never dare reach Shangshan. The mountain’s master is under Heaven’s protection, a descendant of the dragon who commands rain and lightning.”
For a moment, the world seemed to stop.
Everyone stood frozen like statues, looking at one another. Then they realized they had all reached the same conclusion.
Shangshan.
Higher and wider than the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains, a mountain capable of sheltering all the people under Heaven.
And its master—a descendant of the dragon, protected by Heaven.
How had they failed to see it? How could they have been so foolish?
The man had never been talking about a mountain. Every word had pointed to one person who could shelter this troubled realm.
Prince Shangshan...!
Was this what it felt like to have a bolt of lightning strike through the crown of your head?
Everyone’s whole body trembled as if they’d been electrocuted.
Mouths agape. Teeth clenched. Fists balled, as they fought to cool their heads, burning hot with excitement.
And at the same time, they pictured a future they had never imagined before.
What if... what if His Highness Prince Shangshan took the throne?
Heaven’s favor had already departed. The people’s hearts were wavering.
And a child who had survived the vast, brutal purge years ago had returned to the capital, to the very place where he had first cried out at birth.
Was it fate, or coincidence? Another sinister plot by an Emperor who had already violated the bonds of kinship once?
Or...
Was it the Mandate of Heaven?
No one dared speak. Slowly, they turned their heads.
They wanted an answer.
They wanted to face the man who had put this startling possibility before them.
But in the next moment, their anticipation and excitement came crashing down.
The place where the man in the bamboo hat had stood only moments ago was empty.

And left them with a question they couldn’t help asking.
“Um, sir.
Forgive me for interrupting, but could I ask you one thing?”
At the laborer’s cautious approach, rough as he looked, the man in the bamboo hat nodded.
“Go ahead.”
“If it’s not too much trouble, what should a poor man like me do to escape the storm you mentioned?”
“Head for the mountain.”
“What?”
The laborer’s eyes widened at the answer, given without a moment’s hesitation.
The man in the bamboo hat continued slowly.
“Find the highest mountain in the realm and take shelter there.
It has a stream that never runs dry, fruit growing ripe, and animals roaming free.
Its forests will provide timber for homes and firewood.
It could shelter all the people under Heaven and still have room to spare.”
The laborer was dumbfounded.
So was most of the crowd.
The highest mountain in the realm?
Where was there a mountain vast enough to shelter everyone, with food and resources to spare?
While the laborer searched for words, another man, more impatient, blurted out,
“I don’t know who you are, but you seem to be a master of profound cultivation.
Do you mean the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains?”
A few people gave soft cries of recognition and nodded.
The five famous mountains, said to be the highest in the realm and filled with sacred energy—yes, that would make sense, they murmured.
“Which of the Five Sacred Mountains do you mean?
Mount Song in Henan?
Taishan in Shandong?
Huashan in Shaanxi?
“You’re all wrong.
I didn’t mean the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains.”
“What?
What do you mean?
If not the Five Sacred Mountains, then what—”
The man’s calm, firm reply left the crowd speechless.
Just then, an elderly voice came from somewhere among them.
“There’s one place left.
No, it was the only place from the beginning.”
Every head turned.
An elderly Confucian scholar in faded but neat clothes gazed at the gloomy sky and murmured, almost to himself,
“Shangshan.”
A few people understood what those words meant, and their eyes widened.
Most remained confused.
Until the old scholar continued.
“Yes.
That place could shelter all the people under Heaven.
No matter how fiercely the storm swallowed the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains, it would never dare reach Shangshan.
The mountain’s master is under Heaven’s protection, a descendant of the dragon who commands rain and lightning.”
For a moment, the world seemed to stop.
Everyone stood frozen like statues, looking at one another.
Then they realized they had all reached the same conclusion.
Shangshan.
Higher and wider than the Five Sacred Mountains of the Central Plains, a mountain capable of sheltering all the people under Heaven.
And its master—a descendant of the dragon, protected by Heaven.
How had they failed to see it?
How could they have been so foolish?
The man had never been talking about a mountain.
Every word had pointed to one person who could shelter this troubled realm.
Prince Shangshan...!
Was this what it felt like to have a bolt of lightning strike through the crown of your head?
Everyone’s whole body trembled as if they’d been electrocuted.
Mouths agape.
Teeth clenched.
Fists balled, as they fought to cool their heads, burning hot with excitement.
And at the same time, they pictured a future they had never imagined before.
What if... what if His Highness Prince Shangshan took the throne?
Heaven’s favor had already departed.
The people’s hearts were wavering.
And a child who had survived the vast, brutal purge years ago had returned to the capital, to the very place where he had first cried out at birth.
Was it fate, or coincidence?
Another sinister plot by an Emperor who had already violated the bonds of kinship once?
Or...
Was it the Mandate of Heaven?
No one dared speak.
Slowly, they turned their heads.
They wanted an answer.
They wanted to face the man who had put this startling possibility before them.
But in the next moment, their anticipation and excitement came crashing down.
The place where the man in the bamboo hat had stood only moments ago was empty.

chapters.title: Chapter 898
paragraphs: Someone once said humans are creatures of adaptation.
But everyone has at least one thing they can never get used to, no matter how many times they experience it.
For me, one was being responsible for other people’s lives. Another was waking up to someone’s ugly face.
“What are you doing?”
Hyuk Mujin answered, “Checking on you, Captain.”
“Why?”
“You barred everyone from coming in and spent two whole days shut up in your room circulating your qi. I thought you might’ve suffered qi deviation, so I slipped in to check.”
“Two days?”
“Yes. You didn’t know?”
“No, I knew.”
That was a lie. I’d thought half a day had passed at most. Two whole days?
I looked toward the sunlit window and sighed inwardly.
“I appreciate you worrying about me, but next time, just leave me alone.”
“Why?”
“Because seeing your face first thing when I woke up nearly gave me qi deviation.”
“Isn’t that a bit harsh?”
“Your face is harsh.”
“Then I’ll just stay nearby. You need someone to stand guard, don’t you?”
“Don’t stand guard, either.”
“Why not?”
“Your snoring will give me qi deviation.”
“...At this point, I’d be better off not being here at all. Keep this up and I might get fed up and head back to our family on my own.”
I had just uncrossed my legs and was about to get up. Instead, I stared at Hyuk Mujin and his halfhearted attempt to threaten me.
“W-Why are you looking at me like that? Is there some rule that says I have to follow you around, Captain?”
Despite his words, he was watching me nervously. A laugh escaped me.
Hyuk Mujin had been hunching his shoulders, ready to dodge a punch that might come at any moment—or at least make it hurt less. Now he looked baffled.
“What’s going on? Am I seeing things? Why are you acting like this all of a sudden, Captain?”
“Like what?”
“You’d normally have hit me at least twelve times by now, but you’re just smiling like some virtuous gentleman.”
I barely held back the laugh bubbling up inside me.
Then I kicked off the floor and shot forward like a flash of light.
Whoosh!
Hyuk Mujin instinctively tried to defend himself. In that split second, he moved with a speed and composure that made it hard to believe he was still only a First Rate martial artist.
Of course, against me, his defense had failed before it began.
“Hup.”
Realizing it was hopeless, Hyuk Mujin let out a strangled breath and squeezed his eyes shut. He was probably bracing for the hard blow that usually followed.
But for all his preparation, it never came.
Tap.
Instead of smacking him as I usually did, I lightly tapped the back of his head and clicked my tongue.
“You’ve been learning martial arts wrong all this time. Who told you to close your eyes?”
“Even if you’re getting hit, keep your eyes wide open. Even just keeping your eyes on your opponent puts you halfway there.”
Hyuk Mujin rubbed the back of his head, looking dazed, then blurted out, “Why are you acting like this all of a sudden?”
“Like what?”
“It’s strange. Normally...”
“So you want me to hit you like I usually do?”
Hyuk Mujin answered at once. “No. Not that.”
“Then shut up. I’m keeping you fit to fight.”
“Fit to fight?”
“Yeah. We’ll be fighting like hell soon. What good would hitting you on the back of the head do? If you caught a stray blade because of it, I’d end up having bad dreams for nothing.”
Hyuk Mujin grinned.
“Ohhh. So that’s what it is. You could be a little more honest, you know.”
“What?”
“I know all about it. When I said I might leave, it bothered you, didn’t it, Captain? Right?”
I started to answer, then just let out a quiet laugh.
“Yeah, you little shit. Must be nice to be so perceptive.”
“I knew it. I thought so. Even you need someone like me, your right-hand man, stuck to your side if you want to get anything done.”
“Right-hand man, my ass. You’re a little toe.”
“Come on, now. Calling myself your right-hand man is already a big concession on my part.”
“A concession?”
“Yes. Where else are you going to find a subordinate as loyal as me? I’m not your right hand—I’m your heart. Your heart.”
“Not a chance. You’ve got balls. How dare you call yourself my heart?”
“Then if I get them removed, do I qualify?”
Whack!
This time I put some force into it. For some reason, Hyuk Mujin groaned and clutched the back of his head, but his face lit up.
“Now that’s more like it.”
“It’s still a little weak, though. Hit me harder.”
What was with that creepy reaction?
Just as I began to question Hyuk Mujin’s tastes, he grinned and went on.
“It’s nothing, really. You’ve been so different from usual that I couldn’t help worrying.”
“I know you’ve had a lot on your mind lately, but it’ll all work out. So do what you always do. Just like you always have.”
For a moment, I couldn’t speak.
At the same time, the truth I’d kept buried in my heart welled up and tickled the back of my throat.
But...
I can’t.
I couldn’t let a passing rush of emotion make me speak. To survive and win this enormous gamble, surrounded by monsters, I had to choose my words carefully.
In the end, after thinking it over, I managed only one question.
“Aren’t you scared?”
“Hm? Of what?”
“The situation we’re in. And whatever it is we’re about to face.”
Hyuk Mujin blinked at me for a long while, then answered, “What kind of question is that? Of course I’m scared.”
“You don’t act like it.”
“I’m used to being scared.”
“You’re used to it?”
“Yes. How do I put it? I’ve always been kind of a coward.”
Hyuk Mujin scratched the back of his head, looking embarrassed.

“When I was little, I was afraid my younger sibling would take all my parents’ love, so I cried every day. Then, when I got older and decided to become a martial artist, just holding a sword made me tremble. I thought I’d gotten better after joining the Jin Family of Taiyuan, but once I started following you around, Captain... I felt like I was going to piss myself every single day.”
That was the first I’d heard of it.
Thinking back, I’d never really asked Hyuk Mujin about his past.
I’d learned by chance that he was the eldest son of a large textile shop that had been in his family for three generations. It wasn’t as if I’d tried to find out.
Maybe that was why, instead of cutting off his long-winded story with a flick to the forehead as I normally would have, I found myself wanting to hear more.
“...Anyway, somehow I wound up stuck to your side.”
Hyuk Mujin finished with a shrug, then suddenly looked at me.
“This is all your fault, Captain.”
“Mine?”
“Yes. You’re like a ghost, always finding your way to places where people go to die. I got so much practice along the way that now I’m scared, but I’m not. You know what I mean?”
“So it was hard on you?”
“Hard? I thought I was going to die. But I never actually did. Or, to be precise, whenever I thought I was going to die, you saved me.”
Maybe not this time.
I swallowed the words that had been circling in my mouth.
Unaware of what I was thinking, Hyuk Mujin went on as if nothing were wrong.
“Maybe that’s why I’m not all that scared this time, either. Even when I heard what you told Comrade Hong and me recently, I felt pretty calm.”
“Because you figure I’ll save you again?”
“No.”
“No?”
“No. I just had a thought.”
For a moment, Hyuk Mujin looked straight at me and spoke.
“Oh, I thought, maybe this time I can be the one to save you, Captain.”
“You said it was dangerous. That even you and Great Hero Jeok would have to risk your lives. That it was basically a gamble. Then couldn’t even someone as weak as me be useful this time?”
Hyuk Mujin added with a bright smile, “I’m still a First Rate nobody with a long way to go, but they say when you’re in trouble, even a cat’s paw is worth borrowing. Right?”
I didn’t answer.
No, I couldn’t.
It felt as if an invisible hand had closed around my throat, cutting off my breath. If I opened my mouth, I was afraid the truth might slip out before I could stop it.
So I looked at his smiling face in silence, then smiled back.
“Yeah. Now you’re finally going to be useful.”
“Ahem. This time, just trust me. I, Hyuk Mujin, am your right hand and your heart. I’m the Tenfold Man of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, aren’t I?”
Watching Hyuk Mujin thump his chest with exaggerated force, I let go of every worry still weighing on my mind.
And I was certain.
Every choice I made from here on out would be the right one.
“Remember what I told you two days ago?”
Hyuk Mujin’s smile faded, and he nodded.
“Which part...?”
“The Murim Alliance reinforcements.”
“Oh, of course. But when did you manage to get in touch with the Murim Alliance, Captain?”
“That’s not important, so forget it. I have a mission for you.”
“Just me?”
“No, everyone in the Fire Dragon Pavilion.”
“The entire pavilion means... you’re coming with us, Captain?”
“I’m not going. And neither is my Master. You’ll lead the rest of the group to the place I tell you and wait there.”
“Are we meeting the Murim Alliance reinforcements there?”
“Yeah. They’ll arrive within half a day at the earliest, and by tomorrow at the latest.”
Hyuk Mujin nodded as if he understood, then suddenly furrowed his brow.
“That’s longer than I expected. Leaving you here at a time like this is a bit... You’re not in your usual condition, either.”
“I’m not. So, are you afraid a Supreme Peak master who isn’t in his usual condition will keel over coughing blood at any moment?”
Hyuk Mujin grinned.
“Right. I was a crow-tit worrying about a Heavenly Eagle.”
“Usually, it’d be a stork you were worried about, not a Heavenly Eagle.”
“For the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, even a Heavenly Eagle isn’t enough. Anyway, is that the whole mission?”
“Yeah. Right now.”
I answered and took a neatly folded note from inside my robe, then handed it to him.
I’d prepared it two days ago, but until the last moment, I’d wavered over whether to take it out at all.
“Anyone besides me and my Master should be able to leave the imperial palace without much trouble. Once you’re sure no one’s following you, check the destination written there.”
“This is starting to feel less like the Fire Dragon Pavilion and more like the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.”
Hyuk Mujin carefully took the note and tucked it away. Then he clasped his hands in a salute.
“I’ll get going, then.”
“One last thing.”
“Yes?”
“Be careful. You and everyone else.”
Hyuk Mujin looked puzzled, then gave me a playful grin. He turned and disappeared.
Once his presence had faded completely, I slowly left the room and came face to face with the one person still there.
Whoosh.
A slow exhalation. Hong Jin looked at me through the cloudy smoke from his long-stemmed tobacco pipe, then murmured as if to himself, “Martial artist Hyuk seemed pretty busy.”
“He is. I gave him a mission.”
“It must be important, to send him off at a time like this.”
“Yes. It is.”
“I understand how you feel.”
Creak.
The old wooden chair groaned. Hong Jin rose with elegant poise and spoke through the haze of smoke.
“In a dangerous gamble where no one knows what will happen, you must want to save even one more person.”
“So, Young Master Jin, are you ready?”
I nodded with a bitter smile.
“I’ve always been ready.”
A little while later, golden-armored guards lined up in front of the pavilion to escort us to the Grand Banquet Hall.

chapters.title: Chapter 899
paragraphs: Maybe it was because everything around me gleamed gold, but for a moment, I felt like the richest man in the world.
Sadly, reality was a long way from that.
Clank. Clank.
I might’ve been able to enjoy the feeling a little longer if not for those ominous metallic sounds.
But the Embroidered Uniform Guards surrounding Hong Jin and me as they marched along showed no sign of offering that kind of consideration.
To be fair, I’d be crazy to expect it.
A laugh slipped out before I could stop it. I felt a heated gaze from beside me. Hong Jin was staring at me in disbelief.
“What is it?”
“...You do know why I’m looking at you, right? I’m asking just in case.”
“Hmm. Because I suddenly laughed at a time like this?”
“Thank goodness. I thought Young Master Jin had completely lost his mind.”
“Don’t worry. I’m holding on to my sanity.”
It wasn’t as if I could stand there grinning like a lunatic with my life hanging by a thread.
When you’re backed up against a cliff, your mind actually grows calmer.
Everything else falls away, leaving only one word: survival.
Just like right now.
“I’ll take your word for it. I have no choice.”
Hong Jin muttered as if to himself, then slowly drew on his still-lit long-stemmed tobacco pipe.
The ember glowed red. He exhaled a plume of white smoke that drifted among the guards.

Smoking so boldly as he walked through the imperial palace, when his head might roll at any moment. I was privately impressed by Hong Jin’s nerve when I noticed his eyelashes trembling and his face growing languid.
Then the smoke’s distinctive scent reached me.
Now that I think about it, I always smell that when I’m near Hong Jin.
Normally, I’d thought nothing of it.
I wasn’t some anti-smoking spokesperson. There was nothing strange about Hong Jin smoking a pipe, and no reason for me to stop him.
I’d simply assumed he was making up for what he lacked as a man by filling himself with nicotine.
But even so, I’d occasionally felt a strange sense of déjà vu.
Something about the smell was familiar, and I had no trouble remembering when I’d felt that way before.
Right. Immediately after I returned from my audience with the Emperor. That very day.
An idea flashed through my mind.
I watched Hong Jin slowly exhale smoke, then spoke up.
“It seems to taste better than I expected. The smell didn’t appeal to me.”
“What are you talking about? Oh, this?”
I gave a quiet nod. Hong Jin lightly waved the pipe in his hand.
“I wouldn’t say it tastes good. It’s just... a habit. A very bad one.”
Of course smoking was bad for your health.
At least by modern standards.
But in this era, it wasn’t exactly frowned upon.
This world had no place in any history passed down to the twenty-first century, but it was remarkably similar in many ways. The names of its regions, the clothes and food, even people’s attitudes.

And by those standards, smoking wasn’t considered a bad habit. If anything, the powerful, who indulged in every sort of pleasure, encouraged it. Tobacco leaves were expensive, though, so it was a luxury most commoners could hardly afford.
But Hong Jin is one of those powerful people, and even he calls it a bad habit?
Something clicked.
There was more to this. Something I hadn’t figured out yet.
I held out my hand to Hong Jin.
“Can I try it?”
“Hmm? You want to smoke? This?”
“Yes. I thought I’d give it a try while I had the chance.”
Our eyes met for an instant. Hong Jin’s eyebrow twitched so slightly no one else could have noticed.
A sign that he’d understood exactly what I meant.
“How curious. The martial artists I know drink readily enough, but they rarely touch poppy.”
“Poppy...?”
“It’s the dried sap of the poppy. If you smoke it when your mind is troubled, sometimes it calms you down and makes you feel drowsy. It’s often used to relieve pain, but it’s highly addictive, so—”
Hong Jin’s voice faded to a distant echo.
Only one word floated through my mind.
Opium!
I might’ve treated school lessons as a chance to catch up on sleep, but at least a little basic knowledge had stuck.
Especially since my world history teacher had a booming voice so passionate it could chase away the sleep that had already claimed me.
“Hey! Jin Taekyung!”
“Hrk. Huh?”
“You punk. What did the teacher just say? Don’t roll your eyes around—tell me.”
“Uh, well...”
“Right. You don’t know. Of course you don’t. You’ve slept through the entire third period back there. Is this a hotel or a school?”
“Oh, I remember now.”
“What? You remember? Fine, let’s hear what kind of creative bullshit you heard in your dream. What was it?”
“Hey, Jin Taekyung.”
“No, that’s right. It is. But... you really are a nutcase. The Opium War! I was talking about the Opium War. I swear, you’re driving me crazy. Repeat after me. The Opium War!”
“What? The Youth Protection War?”
“Youth Protection... Hey, class president! Kim Minjeong!”
“Yes?”
“Call the cops right now. I’m going to beat this punk and get arrested for assaulting a student.”
Fortunately, the police never came. After my teacher finished shouting at me, I was sentenced to copy out an entire section on the Opium War by hand.
That was how I’d managed to cram all sorts of trivial details into my thick skull—including the fact that the white-skinned island chinks had invaded the genuine mainland chinks.
And that opium came from a plant called the poppy.
So that’s useful now.
I silently thanked my world history teacher, who’d been more passionate than anyone.
Thanks to him, I’d just learned something new.
Opium. No, that distinctive scent of poppy... I’ve smelled it before. Stronger than Hong Jin’s.
Just a few days ago.
I’d definitely felt that déjà vu. And only now did I realize what I’d overlooked at the time.
Listen carefully. Don’t react.
Hong Jin kept walking as though nothing had happened. Barely moving my lips, I sent him a Sound Transmission.
If the Emperor smokes opium, why do you think he does it?
That day. That time. That moment.
The first person who’d stirred that sense of déjà vu was the man above all others—the one I’d met in Qianqing Palace.
“Hah.”
With a ragged exhale, the man suddenly opened his eyes.
Faint torchlight flickered beyond the darkness. Long lengths of thin, colorful silk hung around him.
Where am I...
There was no mistaking the place. It was his bedchamber and his fortress, where he’d spent most of the past decade or so.
He lay there for a while, soaked in cold sweat as he caught his breath. Then he spoke.
“Is anyone there?”
The dry sound of his voice had barely faded when—
Rustle.
A breeze from somewhere stirred the silk curtains. A thread of Sound Transmission slipped between them and reached his ear.
—At your command.
The man said nothing for a while. He ran a hand over his face.
The deep furrows, too pronounced for his age, showed the marks of fatigue.
Though some time had passed since he’d awoken, his heart still pounded fiercely.
“It seems the sun has already set.”
—It will soon be the hour of the Dog.
“The hour of the Dog. And the grand banquet?”
—The appointed hour of the Goat has long since passed. The civil and military officials have all gathered.
“Then is he there, too?”
He.
Hardly enough to identify one person among the many gathered for the grand banquet. Yet the shadow in the darkness answered without hesitation.
—Yes.
“...Unexpected. Martial artists may rush headlong into danger, but this is absurdly reckless.”
The Emperor seemed to be speaking to himself, but he went on.
“Then again, someone had already foreseen it. His Master must have stayed, too.”
—He has also attended. However...
“Go on.”
—The other martial artists, apart from those two, have left the imperial palace.
“Left?”
—Yes. They appeared to be moving with some purpose, but we could not follow them any farther.
“You couldn’t follow them?”
The man frowned, but the shadow’s next words silenced him.
—Yes. ‘She’ personally intervened and stopped us.
“...I see.”
—If you command it, we can act at once.
“No. No.”
He shook his head and slowly rose from his bed.
The room was far too vast to be one person’s bedchamber. Clad in sleeping robes embroidered with golden thread, he stood before a large mirror.
Rustle. Thud.
The soft silk slid over his skin and fell to the floor.
An ordinary person would have shivered at the sudden chill. But the man stood firm as an iron tower.
As he had when he led a great army to crush the rebels.
As he had that day, more than a decade ago.
But for all his enduring spirit, the figure reflected in the mirror bore little resemblance to the man he’d once been.
I’ve aged. Beyond recognition.
He felt no regret.
The path he’d walked was one someone had to take.
He’d simply been the one chosen.
He’d put on a dragon robe so dazzling no one dared raise their head to look at him, and been granted the title Son of Heaven.
He had no regrets.
Only the path ahead remained. Just one step left to take.
“It’s time for me to leave Qianqing Palace.”
At his words, the darkness where the shadow had melted stirred, and Qianqing Palace, silent as a grave, sprang to life.
No. They had been ready from the beginning.
Ready to kill and to die at the Emperor’s command.
And on the roof of Qianqing Palace, its pulse throbbing like a volcano on the verge of eruption, a woman gazed up at the cloudy sky.
“Will it rain again today?”
So Gyo stroked the weapons hanging at either side of her waist.
She had them back after a long time. They were cold as ice, while the qi within them boiled hot as fire.
The Grand Banquet Hall was unbelievably vast and impossibly quiet. Countless officials, high and low, had gathered, yet not one of them spoke.
For that moment, they were all blind, unable to see, and mute, unable to speak.

Those who already knew what was happening quietly reflected on the lives they’d led up to then. Those who didn’t know were frozen in place by the suffocating presence that had swallowed the Grand Banquet Hall.
Who would speak first?
Who would be the first to... draw a sword?
As the same thought passed through every mind—
“There he is.”
A voice broke the silence.
“Five hours late. Are you kidding me?”
Jin Taekyung’s gaze pierced the darkness beyond the flickering torches.
More precisely, it pierced the enormous golden procession approaching from beyond, like a dragon.

chapters.title: Chapter 900
paragraphs: Thud. Thud-thud.
The earth trembled. Blazing torches roused the night.
A thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards marched in formation beneath fluttering imperial banners. Behind them came countless eunuchs and palace maids.
At the center of the procession was an enormous, magnificent imperial carriage built for one person alone.
Boom!
At last, the thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards entered the Grand Banquet Hall and stamped their feet in unison.
The powerful wave of qi they unleashed shook the air and washed over everyone’s skin.
“At last...”
Those who heard the voice slip from someone’s lips suddenly wondered:
Who had said that?
Which side were they on, and what outcome were they waiting for?
But there was no time to think of an answer.
From the enormous procession that had come to a halt, someone slowly rode forward on a fine steed and let out a thunderous cry.

“The sovereign of the Great Nation, master of Heaven and Earth and all things beneath them, has deigned to appear in person! All civil and military officials, great and small, kneel and pay your respects to His Majesty the Emperor!”
Whoosh!
Not even the golden armor encasing his body or the helmet pulled low over his head could hide his truly overwhelming presence.
At the shout, infused with internal energy, from Baek Yeon—the Emperor’s right hand in name and deed, and Commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard—everyone in the Grand Banquet Hall rose and knelt.
Clatter.
There were hundreds of civil and military officials, and thousands of soldiers already standing guard all around them.
They moved as one, bowing their heads to the ruler of this vast continent.
Even if, for some of them, it was nothing more than an empty show of respect, the fuse that would bring this banquet to an end had not yet burned all the way down.
“Long live His Majesty the Emperor.”
At Ma Sanbao’s quiet murmur, everyone joined in.
“Long live His Majesty the Emperor! Long live! Long, long live!”
At the very end of that resounding cheer, the Emperor stepped down from his sedan chair and walked slowly through the human curtain of guards.
Step. Step.
His footsteps rang out with unusual clarity.
But with their heads bowed, they couldn’t see the Emperor as he passed. Only after he had taken his place on the throne atop the lofty stairs could they straighten up and face him.
The ruler of all under Heaven, who had shut himself away in Qianqing Palace for years on end while attending to the affairs of state.
The Great Nation’s fourth prince turned rebel, then rebel turned Emperor: a notorious unfilial wretch and butcher who had finally seized the throne.
And a man of tempestuous fortune, standing at the highest place beneath Heaven.
They were stunned.
In an instant, shock and disquiet swept across the Grand Banquet Hall like an invisible wave.
There was no trace of the Emperor’s once-youthful, handsome appearance in the man who had emerged after his long seclusion.
But the Emperor paid it no mind.
He looked down haughtily at the countless gazes fixed on him.
Though he had aged beyond recognition, his eyes shone brighter than anyone else’s in the hall as he surveyed the gathered officials, great and small, one by one.
The pillars that held up this vast empire. Its very heart.
Among them were generals who commanded armies, and old scholars whose backs were bent but whose eyes remained unbowed.
Ma Sanbao, the East Depot’s de facto leader and the Emperor’s greatest adversary, was there as well.
But the last place the Emperor’s gaze fell was far off at the end of the hall, where a young man watched him in silence.
Jin Taekyung.
Their eyes met across the hall.
The Emperor looked at Jin Taekyung. Jin Taekyung looked at the Emperor.
They stared at each other for a while without saying a word. At last, the Emperor’s firmly closed lips parted.
“Begin.”
Perhaps it wasn’t just a few people who imagined it.
Boom. Boom. Bwoom!
The drums heralding the start of the grand banquet sounded like war drums announcing the opening of a battle.
The atmosphere, frozen like a glacier, began to thaw little by little when musicians and dancers entered with an astonishing spread of delicacies and began to perform.
The melody stirred the heart, and sleeves fluttered in time with the music.
On top of that, the imperial chefs had displayed all their skill, and the finest wines were served without limit.
Perhaps it was only natural that those who’d had a drink to settle their nerves began to relax a little.
“Whew. I can finally breathe.”
“Indeed. I really thought something was about to happen...”
“Shut your mouth. You want to say the wrong thing and invite needless suspicion?”
“M-My apologies, sir.”
“If I hear you say something that disrespectful again, I won’t let it pass.”
The middle-aged man reprimanded the young official beside him in a carefully lowered voice, then swept a sharp gaze around them.
He seemed worried someone might have overheard.
I casually picked up a bite of food from the appetizer in front of me.
The next moment, I felt the middle-aged man across from me fixing me with an unusually persistent stare.
The young official’s voice reached my ears, too.
“S-Sir. I did misspeak, but no one could’ve heard me. The Embroidered Uniform Guards are far away, too.”
He wasn’t wrong.
The hall being used for today’s grand banquet was large enough to train thousands of soldiers at once. The officials, seated at regular intervals, were quite far apart.
And though every Embroidered Uniform Guard was an exceptional master, only a few, including their commander, Baek Yeon, remained by the Emperor’s side.
The rest were far away, holding their assigned positions.
But even after hearing the young official, the middle-aged man kept watching me closely for a while before asking,
“Do you know anything about that man?”
“Pardon? W-Well, I’ve heard in passing that he’s a ruffian from the martial world.”
“Is that all?”
“I’m not sure what you mean...”
“Tsk. You really don’t think, do you? Be grateful that your father and I have a connection. Otherwise, you wouldn’t have made it this far.”
The middle-aged man clicked his tongue and continued in the same low whisper.

“How could some ruffian attend a banquet like this? He’s Prince Shangshan’s bodyguard and guest, brought here by His Highness. He’s also the third son of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, whose influence has recently spread all the way south of the Yangtze.”
“The Jin Family of Taiyuan. The Jin Family of Taiyuan... Do you mean the family that runs the Jin Family Trading Company and the Jin Family Escort Bureau?”
“That’s right. And that Jin Family of Taiyuan is based in Shanxi, Prince Shangshan’s fief.”
“Ah.”
The young official let out a faint exclamation.
“A family of that standing must wield considerable influence in Shanxi Province.”

“With Prince Shangshan’s protection, how could it be otherwise? Martial artists who defy the Great Nation’s solemn laws have no business wielding that kind of power... but apparently they rule as de facto overlords across Shanxi Province.”
“Is that why you’re paying attention to him, sir? Because he’s the son of a martial arts family?”
“It’s more than that.”
“Then...”

“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon. That’s his sobriquet. A tremendous master, barely in his twenties, who’s already accomplished countless feats of arms. There’s no one in the martial world who hasn’t heard of him.”
“You’ve done your homework.”
“There was no need to look into it in detail. Even among the people of the Imperial Capital, there are countless who know of Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung...”
The middle-aged man, who hadn’t taken his eyes off me as he spoke, suddenly frowned.
“Did you just speak casually to me?”
But the young official didn’t answer.
Normally, he would’ve scrambled to make excuses. Now his face had gone white as he stared at someone standing behind him and the middle-aged man.
One second.
Two seconds.
Three.
After a silence in which the world seemed to stop, the middle-aged man slowly turned to follow the young official’s gaze.
Then he froze like a statue.
“Y-Your Majesty...!”
It wasn’t just my imagination: the words, forced from deep in his lungs, sounded like a scream.
The Emperor.
The absolute ruler called the Son of Heaven, a descendant of Heaven, looked down at the two men without a word.
As if considering how to kill them.
Perhaps he seemed all the more likely to do just that because Baek Yeon stood tall behind him—the very man who had led the purge of tens of thousands of “traitors” more than a decade ago.
“Y-Your Majesty. Please...”
Flap.
The Emperor made a small gesture, and the man’s voice cut off.
That was right. This arrogant and cruel absolute ruler still hadn’t spoken.
And he would allow no one to speak before him.
By now, the Grand Banquet Hall had fallen into deathly silence. The Emperor abruptly turned his head and looked at me.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
I could feel it.
The air trembling.
Countless gazes piercing me from head to toe.
The Emperor had spoken first to me, the only outsider among the high officials who supported the empire and the gathered civil and military officials.
And he’d walked all the way to my lowly seat at the far end of the hall, well away from his throne, to do it.
“I ask you: what should I do with these people?”
If this had happened a few days ago, I would’ve been shocked.
Why the fuck is this crazy bastard pulling this shit out of nowhere? I probably would’ve thought something like that—and started to feel like I needed to piss.
But not today.
Yeah. No.
I’d already stepped into a gamble where everyone had staked their lives.
Perhaps all of this had been inevitable from the moment I entered the tiger’s den that was the imperial palace.
The time had come.
The die had been cast. Now it was time to see how it landed.
“Well, before I answer, would it be all right if I had a drink?”
Whoosh.
The air trembled again.
No, trembled might not be quite the word.
If the earlier disturbance had been a ripple from a stone dropped into a lake, this was a triangular wave—a disaster.
Everyone in the Grand Banquet Hall gaped as that wave swept over them in an instant. I looked at the Emperor, who gave a small nod, and spoke.
“Then I’ll take that as permission.”
Glug.
Instead of answering, I tossed back the wine already poured into my cup. Cries of shock and angry shouts erupted from every direction.
The wave that hadn’t seemed real even when they’d seen and heard it for themselves had finally hit them.
“What a lunatic!”
“H-How dare that man...!”
“How can there be such a lawless man in this world?”
“Commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, what are you doing? Why haven’t you cut down that high traitor yet?”
“Your Majesty! Punish that outrageous ruffian at once for insulting Your Majesty and the imperial household!”
“Please punish him!”
Listen to that decibel level.

They say the more people curse you, the longer you live. If this raucous enthusiasm had lasted another fifteen minutes, my sobriquet might’ve become Three Thousand Jiazi instead of Blazing Flame Divine Dragon.
Beheading was the basic option, and they kept piling on extras: cut off my balls, torture me slowly, then tear me limb from limb by quartering.
...No, I mean, the balls are a bit much.
Was that guy from the Sichuan Tang Clan or something?
I took a good look at the face of the man who’d proposed castrating me, then put down my cup.
Then I looked at the Emperor and spoke.
“Kill them if you want, or spare them if you want. Isn’t that what Your Majesty does best?”
Well.
I was starting to feel like I needed to piss.

sentences.text: Thud.
Thud-thud.
The earth trembled.
Blazing torches roused the night.
A thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards marched in formation beneath fluttering imperial banners.
Behind them came countless eunuchs and palace maids.
At the center of the procession was an enormous, magnificent imperial carriage built for one person alone.
Boom!
At last, the thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards entered the Grand Banquet Hall and stamped their feet in unison.
The powerful wave of qi they unleashed shook the air and washed over everyone’s skin.
“At last...”
Those who heard the voice slip from someone’s lips suddenly wondered:
Who had said that?
Which side were they on, and what outcome were they waiting for?
But there was no time to think of an answer.
From the enormous procession that had come to a halt, someone slowly rode forward on a fine steed and let out a thunderous cry.
“The sovereign of the Great Nation, master of Heaven and Earth and all things beneath them, has deigned to appear in person!
All civil and military officials, great and small, kneel and pay your respects to His Majesty the Emperor!”
Whoosh!
Not even the golden armor encasing his body or the helmet pulled low over his head could hide his truly overwhelming presence.
At the shout, infused with internal energy, from Baek Yeon—the Emperor’s right hand in name and deed, and Commander of the Embroidered Uniform Guard—everyone in the Grand Banquet Hall rose and knelt.
Clatter.
There were hundreds of civil and military officials, and thousands of soldiers already standing guard all around them.
They moved as one, bowing their heads to the ruler of this vast continent.
Even if, for some of them, it was nothing more than an empty show of respect, the fuse that would bring this banquet to an end had not yet burned all the way down.
“Long live His Majesty the Emperor.”
At Ma Sanbao’s quiet murmur, everyone joined in.
“Long live His Majesty the Emperor!
Long live!
Long, long live!”
At the very end of that resounding cheer, the Emperor stepped down from his sedan chair and walked slowly through the human curtain of guards.
Step.
Step.
His footsteps rang out with unusual clarity.
But with their heads bowed, they couldn’t see the Emperor as he passed.
Only after he had taken his place on the throne atop the lofty stairs could they straighten up and face him.
The ruler of all under Heaven, who had shut himself away in Qianqing Palace for years on end while attending to the affairs of state.
The Great Nation’s fourth prince turned rebel, then rebel turned Emperor: a notorious unfilial wretch and butcher who had finally seized the throne.
And a man of tempestuous fortune, standing at the highest place beneath Heaven.
They were stunned.
In an instant, shock and disquiet swept across the Grand Banquet Hall like an invisible wave.
There was no trace of the Emperor’s once-youthful, handsome appearance in the man who had emerged after his long seclusion.
But the Emperor paid it no mind.
He looked down haughtily at the countless gazes fixed on him.
Though he had aged beyond recognition, his eyes shone brighter than anyone else’s in the hall as he surveyed the gathered officials, great and small, one by one.
The pillars that held up this vast empire.
Its very heart.
Among them were generals who commanded armies, and old scholars whose backs were bent but whose eyes remained unbowed.
Ma Sanbao, the East Depot’s de facto leader and the Emperor’s greatest adversary, was there as well.
But the last place the Emperor’s gaze fell was far off at the end of the hall, where a young man watched him in silence.
Jin Taekyung.
Their eyes met across the hall.
The Emperor looked at Jin Taekyung.
Jin Taekyung looked at the Emperor.
They stared at each other for a while without saying a word.
At last, the Emperor’s firmly closed lips parted.
“Begin.”
Perhaps it wasn’t just a few people who imagined it.
Boom.
Boom.
Bwoom!
The drums heralding the start of the grand banquet sounded like war drums announcing the opening of a battle.
The atmosphere, frozen like a glacier, began to thaw little by little when musicians and dancers entered with an astonishing spread of delicacies and began to perform.
The melody stirred the heart, and sleeves fluttered in time with the music.
On top of that, the imperial chefs had displayed all their skill, and the finest wines were served without limit.
Perhaps it was only natural that those who’d had a drink to settle their nerves began to relax a little.
“Whew.
I can finally breathe.”
“Indeed.
I really thought something was about to happen...”
“Shut your mouth.
You want to say the wrong thing and invite needless suspicion?”
“M-My apologies, sir.”
“If I hear you say something that disrespectful again, I won’t let it pass.”
The middle-aged man reprimanded the young official beside him in a carefully lowered voice, then swept a sharp gaze around them.
He seemed worried someone might have overheard.
I casually picked up a bite of food from the appetizer in front of me.
The next moment, I felt the middle-aged man across from me fixing me with an unusually persistent stare.
The young official’s voice reached my ears, too.
“S-Sir.
I did misspeak, but no one could’ve heard me.
The Embroidered Uniform Guards are far away, too.”
He wasn’t wrong.
The hall being used for today’s grand banquet was large enough to train thousands of soldiers at once.
The officials, seated at regular intervals, were quite far apart.
And though every Embroidered Uniform Guard was an exceptional master, only a few, including their commander, Baek Yeon, remained by the Emperor’s side.
The rest were far away, holding their assigned positions.
But even after hearing the young official, the middle-aged man kept watching me closely for a while before asking,
“Do you know anything about that man?”
“Pardon?
W-Well, I’ve heard in passing that he’s a ruffian from the martial world.”
“Is that all?”
“I’m not sure what you mean...”
“Tsk.
You really don’t think, do you?
Be grateful that your father and I have a connection.
Otherwise, you wouldn’t have made it this far.”
The middle-aged man clicked his tongue and continued in the same low whisper.
“How could some ruffian attend a banquet like this?
He’s Prince Shangshan’s bodyguard and guest, brought here by His Highness.
He’s also the third son of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, whose influence has recently spread all the way south of the Yangtze.”
“The Jin Family of Taiyuan.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan...
Do you mean the family that runs the Jin Family Trading Company and the Jin Family Escort Bureau?”
“That’s right.
And that Jin Family of Taiyuan is based in Shanxi, Prince Shangshan’s fief.”
“Ah.”
The young official let out a faint exclamation.
“A family of that standing must wield considerable influence in Shanxi Province.”
“With Prince Shangshan’s protection, how could it be otherwise?
Martial artists who defy the Great Nation’s solemn laws have no business wielding that kind of power... but apparently they rule as de facto overlords across Shanxi Province.”
“Is that why you’re paying attention to him, sir?
Because he’s the son of a martial arts family?”
“It’s more than that.”
“Then...”
“Blazing Flame Divine Dragon.
That’s his sobriquet.
A tremendous master, barely in his twenties, who’s already accomplished countless feats of arms.
There’s no one in the martial world who hasn’t heard of him.”
“You’ve done your homework.”
“There was no need to look into it in detail.
Even among the people of the Imperial Capital, there are countless who know of Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung...”
The middle-aged man, who hadn’t taken his eyes off me as he spoke, suddenly frowned.
“Did you just speak casually to me?”
But the young official didn’t answer.
Normally, he would’ve scrambled to make excuses.
Now his face had gone white as he stared at someone standing behind him and the middle-aged man.
One second.
Two seconds.
Three.
After a silence in which the world seemed to stop, the middle-aged man slowly turned to follow the young official’s gaze.
Then he froze like a statue.
“Y-Your Majesty...!”
It wasn’t just my imagination: the words, forced from deep in his lungs, sounded like a scream.
The Emperor.
The absolute ruler called the Son of Heaven, a descendant of Heaven, looked down at the two men without a word.
As if considering how to kill them.
Perhaps he seemed all the more likely to do just that because Baek Yeon stood tall behind him—the very man who had led the purge of tens of thousands of “traitors” more than a decade ago.
“Y-Your Majesty.
Please...”
Flap.
The Emperor made a small gesture, and the man’s voice cut off.
That was right.
This arrogant and cruel absolute ruler still hadn’t spoken.
And he would allow no one to speak before him.
By now, the Grand Banquet Hall had fallen into deathly silence.
The Emperor abruptly turned his head and looked at me.
“Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
I could feel it.
The air trembling.
Countless gazes piercing me from head to toe.
The Emperor had spoken first to me, the only outsider among the high officials who supported the empire and the gathered civil and military officials.
And he’d walked all the way to my lowly seat at the far end of the hall, well away from his throne, to do it.
“I ask you: what should I do with these people?”
If this had happened a few days ago, I would’ve been shocked.
Why the fuck is this crazy bastard pulling this shit out of nowhere?
I probably would’ve thought something like that—and started to feel like I needed to piss.
But not today.
Yeah.
No.
I’d already stepped into a gamble where everyone had staked their lives.
Perhaps all of this had been inevitable from the moment I entered the tiger’s den that was the imperial palace.
The time had come.
The die had been cast.
Now it was time to see how it landed.
“Well, before I answer, would it be all right if I had a drink?”
Whoosh.
The air trembled again.
No, trembled might not be quite the word.
If the earlier disturbance had been a ripple from a stone dropped into a lake, this was a triangular wave—a disaster.
Everyone in the Grand Banquet Hall gaped as that wave swept over them in an instant.
I looked at the Emperor, who gave a small nod, and spoke.
“Then I’ll take that as permission.”
Glug.
Instead of answering, I tossed back the wine already poured into my cup.
Cries of shock and angry shouts erupted from every direction.
The wave that hadn’t seemed real even when they’d seen and heard it for themselves had finally hit them.
“What a lunatic!”
“H-How dare that man...!”
“How can there be such a lawless man in this world?”
